question_text: India and the UK formally signed the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) on which date in 2025?
explanation: India-UK CETA was formally signed July 24, 2025 following agreement-in-principle (May 6, 2025). Negotiations spanned three years (2022-2025) across goods, services, investment, IP, labor standards. Eliminates tariffs on 99% of Indian exports to UK (textiles, garments, seafood, pharmaceuticals, engineering goods); reduces tariffs on 90% of UK exports (whisky, medical devices, machinery). Expected to increase bilateral trade by $34 billion/year from 2040. Current bilateral trade: $56 billion; target: double by 2030. India positioned CETA as most significant FTA since India-UAE CEPA (2022). FTA reflects post-Brexit UK pivot toward Indo-Pacific partners and India's strategic autonomy in seeking diverse trade partnerships. India also advancing: EU-India FTA (signed Jan 27, 2026), GCC FTA, Canada FTA negotiations — demonstrating India's trade diplomacy diversification beyond China and US-centric partnerships.

question_text: Under India-UK CETA 2025, what happens to UK tariffs on Indian whisky imports?
option_b: Halved from 150% to 75%, then reduced to 40% by year 10
option_d: Maintained at current levels for strategic industries
explanation: India-UK CETA 2025: Whisky/gin (and similar spirit) tariffs phased: reduced from current 150% to 75% upon implementation, then to 40% by year 10 (gradual transition protecting Indian spirits industry). UK major export interests in CETA: whisky, premium spirits, medical devices/pharma machinery, electrical equipment, aerospace components, chocolate, salmon, lamb. Tariff reductions: UK gets 90% of Indian market with tariff elimination/reduction; India gets 99% of UK market duty-free. UK remains India's 5th largest trade partner (after USA, China, UAE, Singapore). CETA ratification expected to complete by May 2026; expected to come into force soon after. India views CETA as validation of India-UK Strategic Partnership (post-Brexit, UK seeks India deepening). Deal reflects India's negotiating strength: India gained more favorable terms on labor mobility, IP, FDI protections.

question_text: India-UK CETA 2025 is expected to increase bilateral trade by how much per year from 2040?
explanation: India-UK CETA 2025 is projected to increase bilateral trade by $34 billion/year by 2040 — a substantial economic gain from tariff elimination and market access expansion. Current bilateral trade: $56 billion (2024); target: double to $112 billion by 2030 under CETA implementation. Added value from FTA realization: $34B/year increment. Considered India's most significant FTA since India-UAE CEPA (2022, then the largest in India's history). India-UK investment flows expected to increase substantially: UK pension funds, insurance, fintech firms seeking Indian market presence; Indian IT firms, pharma, chemicals expanding UK/EU operations. India also advancing parallel FTAs: EU-India FTA (signed Jan 27, 2026, larger than UK deal), GCC FTA, Canada FTA, UK FTA ratification expected May 2026. These FTAs position India as trade leader within Global South, countering China's bilateral dominance and validating India's strategic autonomy in diversifying economic partnerships.

question_text: APEC 2025 was held in which South Korean city?
explanation: APEC 2025 (33rd Economic Leaders' Meeting) was held in Gyeongju, South Korea (North Gyeongsang Province) in November 2025 — historically known as the 'museum without walls' preserving Silla dynasty (57 BCE-935 CE) heritage and Buddhist architecture. South Korean President Lee Jae-myung (elected June 3, 2025 in special presidential election following Yoon Suk Yeol's impeachment in December 2024) hosted as his first major international engagement. APEC prioritized tech innovation, supply-chain resilience post-pandemic, trade liberalization amid US protectionism, green transition. APEC host sequence: Lima Peru (2024) → Gyeongju South Korea (2025) → Shenzhen China (2026, announced Nov 1, 2025) → Phu Quoc Vietnam (2027). APEC: 21 member economies spanning East Asia, Southeast Asia, Americas, Oceania. India is dialogue partner; advocates for APEC openness on development issues.

question_text: India-China resumed the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra in 2025 — suspended since 2020. The Yatra is a pilgrimage to which sacred site?
explanation: Kailash Mansarovar Yatra: Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash (6,638m, Himalayas in Tibet Autonomous Region, China) and Mansarovar Lake (4,590m) — sacred to Hindus (Shiva abode), Buddhists (spiritual center), Jains (Rishabhadeva's enlightenment site). Yatra suspended since 2020 due to COVID-19 and India-China border tensions (Galwan clash June 2020, 20 Indian soldiers killed). Resumption in 2025 was symbolic gesture of India-China normalization: bilateral LAC (Line of Actual Control) patrolling agreements finalized Oct-Nov 2024 (Depsang Plains, Demchok sectors); Modi-Xi meeting at SCO Tianjin 2025; commitment to resolve border disputes through dialogue. Yatra resumption signals confidence-building and people-to-people connectivity restoration. ~10,000+ Indian Hindu pilgrims annually visit Kailash; pilgrimage via Nathu La Pass (Sikkim) is operationally demanding but spiritually profound. Resumption demonstrates pragmatic India-China engagement despite unresolved border issues.

question_text: EAM Jaishankar met Iranian FM Araghchi in New Delhi on May 15, 2026, during which ongoing international conflict?
explanation: EAM S. Jaishankar met Iranian FM Abbas Araghchi (May 15, 2026) during the 2026 Iran War — US+Israel military campaign against Iran initiated February 28, 2026 following Iranian drone/missile strikes on Israel. War escalation: Israeli air strikes on Iranian military infrastructure, nuclear facilities; Iranian retaliation via Hezbollah (Lebanon), Houthis (Yemen), Iraqi militias. Pakistan-brokered ceasefire agreement signed April 8, 2026; Israel violated ceasefire by striking Beirut on May 7, 2026. India maintained strategic neutrality during conflict: (1) protected Chabahar Port (Iranian trade gateway, India-invested) from sanctions/strikes; (2) maintained dialogue with both Iran and Israel; (3) advocated multilateral ceasefire through UNSC; (4) avoided alignment with US containment of Iran, respecting India's non-aligned tradition. EAM visit to Tehran signaled India's commitment to Iran partnership despite geopolitical pressures, validating India's independent foreign policy.

question_text: India will host the 18th BRICS Summit in 2026. When and where is it scheduled?
explanation: 18th BRICS Summit 2026: New Delhi, September 12-13, 2026 — India's 2026 BRICS Chairmanship (first India chair since expansion to 11 members + 10 partners). This is India's second BRICS summit chair (previous: 2016, Goa — when BRICS still 5 members). India's expected priorities: (1) South-South cooperation and development finance mechanisms, (2) BRICS Development Bank expansion, (3) technology transfer for green energy transition, (4) counterterrorism cooperation (Pahalgam attack condemnation model), (5) de-dollarization alternatives to USD (BRICS reserve currency discussion), (6) inclusive development balancing China's Belt-and-Road with India's Partnership for Global Growth vision. New Delhi summit will validate India's diplomatic leadership within Global South and showcase India's capacity to manage diverse BRICS consensus from ideological alignment to operational cooperation.

question_text: CHOGM 2026 (Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting) will be held in which country?
explanation: CHOGM 2026: St. John's, Antigua and Barbuda (Caribbean nation, population ~97,000) on November 1-4, 2026. Theme: 'Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.' Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne hosting. Previous CHOGM 2024: Apia, Samoa (October 25-26, 2024, first in Pacific island state); Commonwealth leaders adopted Apia Ocean Declaration affirming maritime boundaries as fixed despite sea-level rise. Commonwealth Head of State: King Charles III (UK, ceremonial). Secretariat: Marlborough House, London. 56 member nations spanning Africa, Asia, Caribbean, Pacific, Americas. India participates as founding Commonwealth member (1949), advancing South-South cooperation, development priorities, climate justice, technology transfer agendas within Commonwealth forums. CHOGM 2026 expected to emphasize SIDS vulnerability to climate change and demand for loss-and-damage financing.

question_text: Where will the 2026 Asian Games be held?
explanation: 2026 Asian Games: Aichi-Nagoya, Japan (Chubu region, central Honshu) in October 2026 — second Asian Games in Japan (Tokyo hosted 2020 Olympics/Paralympics; Sapporo hosted 1972 Winter Olympics). Aichi hosts 15 sports across 8 venues. India competitive in: athletics, badminton, shooting, wrestling, weightlifting; target 50+ medals. Other major 2026 sports events: ICC Men's T20 World Cup (India & Sri Lanka co-hosts, June 2026); 2026 Commonwealth Games (Glasgow, Scotland, July 28-Aug 8); 2026 Summer Youth Olympics (Dakar, Senegal, October-November); 2026 FIFA World Cup (USA-Canada-Mexico, June-July). India last hosted Asian Games: New Delhi 1982 (where India won 13 medals). 2026 Asian Games represents India's continued commitment to regional sports cooperation and soft power in Asia-Pacific.

question_text: The 2026 FIFA World Cup will be co-hosted by which three countries?
explanation: 2026 FIFA World Cup: USA, Canada, Mexico (June-July 2026) — historic first World Cup with three co-host nations (124 matches across 16 stadiums in North America). Also the first 48-team World Cup (expanded from 32 teams), increasing competition inclusivity. 2022 FIFA World Cup was in Qatar (first in Middle East); Argentina defeated France in final. 2026 will be the first World Cup in North America since USA 1994 (USA hosted, Brazil won). India fielded women's national team in 2023 FIFA World Cup (failed to progress from group stage); men's team historically failed qualification rounds. India focuses on youth development and women's football growth, supported by IMG-Reliance partnership (Indian Super League) and grassroots academy expansion. 2026 World Cup symbolizes globalizing football in non-traditional markets (Mexico historically a strong football nation, Canada/USA emerging as growth markets).

question_text: Which of the following correctly matches the 2025 summit with its HOST city?
explanation: NATO 2025 → The Hague ✓ (June 24-25, 2025). Incorrect matches: (a) G20 2025 → Johannesburg, not Rio (Rio hosted BRICS 2025), (c) SCO 2025 → Tianjin, not Astana (Astana hosted SCO 2024), (d) ASEAN 2025 → Kuala Lumpur, not Bangkok. Complete 2025 summit roster: G20=Johannesburg (SA), G7=Kananaskis (Canada), NATO=The Hague (Netherlands), BRICS=Rio (Brazil), SCO=Tianjin (China), ASEAN=Kuala Lumpur (Malaysia), COP30=Belém (Brazil), WEF Davos 2025=January 20-24, WEF Davos 2026=January 19-23. This question tests memorization and global awareness of multilateral forum scheduling — critical for diplomacy, policy planning, and geopolitical analysis.

question_text: Which of the following CORRECTLY matches 2025 summit themes?
option_a: G20='Collaboration for Intelligent Age'; WEF='Solidarity, Equality, Sustainability'
option_b: G20='A Spirit of Dialogue'; WEF='Solidarity, Equality, Sustainability'
option_c: G20='Solidarity, Equality, Sustainability'; WEF='Collaboration for Intelligent Age'
option_d: G20='Solidarity, Equality, Sustainability'; WEF='A Spirit of Dialogue'
explanation: CORRECT: G20 South Africa 2025 = 'Solidarity, Equality, Sustainability' (Ubuntu-rooted, emphasizing Global South priorities). WEF Davos 2025 = 'Collaboration for the Intelligent Age' (AI-centric). Others incorrect: (a) swaps G20-WEF themes, (b) WEF 2026 theme, (d) mixes G20 correctly with WEF 2026. Key differentiator: G20 SA chose African Ubuntu philosophy to center Global South; WEF focused on AI/tech acceleration. Common confusion source: both summits happened in 2025 and both address development, but with opposing framings (Ubuntu solidarity vs AI collaboration). WEF Davos 2026 later adopted 'A Spirit of Dialogue' reflecting urgent need for peace/diplomacy. This question tests detailed knowledge of summit diplomacy and geopolitical messaging priorities.

question_text: Which statement about NATO Hague Summit 2025 is INCORRECT?
option_a: New defense spending target of 5% GDP was agreed
option_b: Spain was the only dissenter to the 5% target
option_c: Ukraine was officially invited to join NATO
option_d: €40 billion in defense aid was pledged to Ukraine
explanation: INCORRECT: Ukraine was NOT invited to join NATO at The Hague 2025 — no membership invitation, formal timeline, or upgraded pathway was granted. NATO deliberately avoided formal membership offer to prevent direct NATO-Russia military clash (Article 5 trigger risk). Correct facts: (a) 5% GDP defense target agreed by 31 of 32 members, (b) Spain sole dissenter, (d) €40B Ukraine aid pledge. NATO prioritized supporting Ukraine militarily while maintaining escalation deterrence through non-membership. Ukraine's strategic ambiguity (seeking NATO membership for security assurance while not receiving it) reflects Western caution about Russia escalation during ongoing conflict. NATO 2026: Ankara, Turkey (July 7-8). India observed NATO expansion as validation for India's own defense modernization while maintaining neutrality on Ukraine conflict per non-aligned tradition.

question_text: Which country is BOTH ASEAN's newest member AND BRICS's newest full member?
option_c: No such country — they are different nations
explanation: CORRECT: These are DIFFERENT nations. ASEAN's newest member = Timor-Leste (admitted October 2025, independent since 2002). BRICS's newest full member = Indonesia (joined January 6, 2025 as 11th member). Indonesia was ASEAN's founding member (1967, original ASEAN-5); became BRICS member 2025, not a new ASEAN member. Timor-Leste joined ASEAN but is NOT in BRICS (Pakistan, Iran, Afghanistan remain outside both despite strategic proximity). This question tests careful reading and knowledge of multilateral organization memberships — critical for diplomacy. It highlights ASEAN and BRICS as separate, non-overlapping formations with distinct membership criteria and strategic purposes.

question_text: The Russia-Ukraine war saw a Trump-brokered ceasefire in May 2026. What was its duration?
explanation: Trump announced a 3-day Russia-Ukraine ceasefire (May 9-11, 2026), formally described as 'the beginning of the end' of the war's major combat phase. Terms: mutual ceasefire on all fronts, exchange of 1,000+ prisoners/detainees each side, deployment of international monitors, preliminary negotiations for territorial arrangements/reparations. Russia simultaneously declared unilateral ceasefire for Victory Day (May 8-9, commemorating Soviet WWII victory). Both sides immediately traded blame for ceasefire violations; sporadic shelling continued despite pause. Ceasefire reflected war fatigue after 4+ years (Feb 2022-May 2026): Ukraine faced manpower depletion, Western aid fatigue; Russia faced economic costs, equipment losses. Trump's mediation signalled shift from military stalemate to negotiation, validating Davos 2026 'Spirit of Dialogue' theme. India welcomed ceasefire as step toward negotiations while maintaining neutrality on conflict origins/responsibility.

question_text: India-UK CETA 2025: What percentage of Indian exports to UK will get duty-free access?
explanation: Under India-UK CETA 2025, 99% of Indian exports to UK receive duty-free market access (covering ~100% of bilateral trade value on merchandise goods). UK reciprocal access: 90% of UK exports to India benefit from tariff elimination/reduction. India's major export beneficiaries: textiles/garments (UK's largest import source), footwear, processed seafood, pharmaceuticals/chemicals, engineering goods, gemstones. UK major exports gaining access: whisky/premium spirits, medical devices/diagnostics, electrical machinery, aerospace components, high-value food (salmon, lamb, cheese, chocolate). CETA ratification expected Parliamentary approval by May 2026, entry into force shortly after. Trade impact: projected $34B additional annual trade by 2040. CETA represents India's strategic pivot toward advanced democracies and post-Brexit UK seeking Indo-Pacific partners, validating India's diplomatic leverage in securing favorable FTA terms.

question_text: After 2025 expansions, how many total nations (full members + partner countries) does BRICS represent?
explanation: BRICS after 2025: 11 full members + 10 partner countries = 21 total nations. Full members (voting): Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa (original 5) + Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, UAE, Saudi Arabia (joined 2024) + Indonesia (joined Jan 6, 2025). Partner countries (non-voting): Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan, Vietnam (admitted Rio 2025). Two-tier structure created to accommodate expansion pressures while maintaining decision-making efficiency. Collective GDP (PPP): ~37% of world total (exceeding G7's 30%). Collective population: 45%+ of world (~3.5 billion people). This represents unprecedented Global South institutional power — rivaling or exceeding Western-dominated institutions (IMF, World Bank, UNSC). India leverages BRICS 2026 Chairmanship to deepen Global South consensus on development finance, technology transfer, climate justice.

question_text: SCO was founded in which year and city?
explanation: SCO (Shanghai Cooperation Organisation) formally founded June 15, 2001 in Shanghai, China — the founding city naming the organization. SCO evolved from 'Shanghai Five' (informal grouping, 1996: China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan focused on border security/confidence-building) when Uzbekistan joined 2001, formalizing into SCO. Membership expansion: India and Pakistan joined 2017 (9th/10th members); Iran joined 2023 as full member (9th); Belarus joined 2024 (10th full member). Observer status: Afghanistan, Mongolia, Cambodia, Nepal. SCO Secretariat HQ: Beijing, China; Regional Anti-Terrorism Structure (RATS): Tashkent, Uzbekistan. SCO covers ~45% world population and major Eurasian land mass. India values SCO as Central Asian security mechanism, counterterrorism cooperation framework, and multilateral alternative to US-led alliances. SCO symbolizes post-Cold War Eurasian integration independent of Western institutions.

question_text: Which countries called the COP29 NCQG of $300 billion/year 'paltry and inadequate'?
explanation: India and the Global South coalition (African nations, SIDS, AOSIS) called the COP29 Baku NCQG (New Collective Quantified Goal) of $300 billion/year 'paltry and inadequate.' India FM Jaishankar and other developing-nation representatives walked out of COP29 negotiations, objecting that $300B falls short of $1-3 trillion needed for climate adaptation/mitigation in Global South. COP30 Belém 2025 effectively adopted India's demand: $1.3 trillion/year by 2035 climate finance target — a major diplomatic victory for the developing-nation coalition. India argues for equity-based 'Common But Differentiated Responsibilities + Respective Capabilities' (CBDR+RC) principle: developed nations historically emitted 80% of atmospheric CO2 (1850-2020); must finance Global South climate adaptation proportionally. India's climate justice advocacy positions it as leading voice for vulnerable nations.

question_text: Which summit in 2025 involved a formal chairmanship handover at its closing ceremony to a new host?
explanation: ASEAN KL 2025 (October 26-28): Malaysia formally handed ASEAN Chairmanship to Philippines at the closing ceremony. ASEAN follows strict alphabetical rotation (English country names) for annual chairing: Laos (2024) → Malaysia (2025) → Philippines (2026) → Singapore (2027) → Thailand (2028) → Vietnam (2029). This ensures predictable governance and shared responsibility across all 11 members. Incorrect options: (a) G20 handover occurred offsite (Jan 12, 2026), not at summit; (c) SCO operates differently, with China as de facto leader (hosting Secretariat); (d) BRICS Chairmanship Brazil → India for 2026 also a formal transfer but occurred post-Rio summit. ASEAN's ceremonial handover at summit closing symbolizes institutional stability and commitment to consensus governance across geopolitically diverse membership.

question_text: The 2026 Commonwealth Games will be held in which city?
explanation: 2026 Commonwealth Games: Glasgow, Scotland (July 28-August 8, 2026) — Glasgow's second hosting (previously 2014 XX Commonwealth Games). 2026 focuses on gender equality (equal medals for men/women events) and sustainability (minimal new construction, repurposing 2014 venues). Previous hosts: 2022 Birmingham (UK), 2018 Gold Coast (Australia), 2014 Glasgow. India hosted: New Delhi 2010 (XIX Commonwealth Games, large-scale success). Glasgow's second hosting is rare in Commonwealth Games history, reflecting Scotland's developed infrastructure and post-COVID financial recovery. India expected to be competitive across athletics, badminton, shooting, weightlifting, wrestling with 150+ athletes. Commonwealth Games represents India's continued soft power within Commonwealth family (56 nations) and democratic multilateral engagement alongside BRICS/SCO forums.

question_text: G7 Kananaskis 2025 was the 51st G7 Summit. Which of the following is the correct list of G7 nations?
option_a: USA, UK, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Canada
option_b: USA, UK, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Australia
option_c: USA, UK, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Canada
option_d: USA, UK, France, Germany, Russia, Japan, Canada
explanation: G7 members: USA, UK, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Canada + European Union (special participant, not voting member). Incorrect: Australia (ally but not member; participates in Indo-Pacific extension), Spain (NATO/EU but not G7 — Germany represents EU interests), Russia (suspended from G8 in 2014 after Crimea annexation, reverting to G7). G7 represents advanced Western democracies (~50% global GDP, ~1 billion population). Russia's exclusion reflects Western response to territorial aggression. At Kananaskis 2025, PM Mark Carney hosted; Trump's early departure signalled weakening Western cohesion. India observes G7 as Western bloc institution; seeks plurilateral alternatives (BRICS, SCO, QUAD, I2U2) to represent Global South interests independent of G7 dominance.

question_text: BRICS Rio 2025 highlighted de-dollarisation debates. The original BRIC concept was proposed in which year by Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill?
explanation: Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill coined 'BRIC' acronym in 2001 in report 'Building Better Global Economic BRICs' — predicting Brazil, Russia, India, China would dominate global economic growth by 2050, surpassing G7 by 2020s. BRIC grouping first met formally 2009 (Yekaterinburg, Russia); South Africa joined 2010 (making it BRICS). De-dollarization at Rio 2025 reflects BRICS's foundational thesis: emerging economies should possess financial autonomy independent of USD hegemony. BRICS now exploring alternatives: BRICS common currency, yuan internationalization, bilateral trade in local currencies, unified payment systems bypassing SWIFT. Concept originated 24 years prior (2001-2025), validating O'Neill's prescience. India leverages BRICS 2026 to advance de-dollarization while maintaining USD transaction compatibility — balanced approach protecting trade stability.

question_text: ASEAN's newest member Timor-Leste (joined 2025) gained independence from which country in 2002?
explanation: Timor-Leste (East Timor) gained independence from Indonesia on May 20, 2002 — a symbolically important date coinciding with India's Independence Day, representing decolonization and sovereignty restoration across developing nations. Timor-Leste history: former Portuguese colony (1520s-1974, Portuguese official language), occupied by Indonesia (1975-1999, following Portugal's decolonization), UN-administered transition (1999-2002 after referendum), independence 2002. Applied for ASEAN membership in 2011; finally admitted October 26, 2025 at 47th ASEAN Summit in Kuala Lumpur as 11th member — ASEAN's first expansion in 26 years (since Cambodia 1999). Timor-Leste's late ASEAN accession reflected concerns over capacity, development levels, and consensus-building burden. May 20 independence date holds geopolitical significance: shared with India's independence commemoration, representing developing-nation sovereign assertion against colonialism/imperialism.

question_text: At the 16th EU-India Summit on January 27, 2026, India and the EU concluded which historic agreement, described by PM Modi as the 'mother of all deals'?
explanation: India-EU FTA signed January 27, 2026 — India's largest and most comprehensive FTA, concluding 17 years of negotiations (2009-2026). PM Modi called it the 'mother of all deals' reflecting scope: goods (tariff elimination on 95% of trade), services, investment, government procurement, IP, sustainability. António Costa (European Council President) and Ursula von der Leyen (Commission President) were Chief Guests at India's 77th Republic Day (Jan 26, 2026). Additional pacts signed simultaneously: EU-India Security & Defence Partnership (addressing Russia, China containment), Mobility & Migration Agreement (facilitating student/professional visas). FTA projected to increase bilateral trade by 50%+ from current €80-100B annually. India gains market access for textiles, pharmaceuticals, chemicals, engineering; EU gains automotive, machinery, dairy. This validates India-EU strategic autonomy from US-centric partnerships.

question_text: Who represented the EU at the 16th EU-India Summit in New Delhi (January 25-27, 2026) — Chief Guests for India's 77th Republic Day?
option_b: António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen
explanation: António Costa (President of European Council, since December 1, 2024) and Ursula von der Leyen (President of European Commission, second term 2024-2029) led the 16-member EU delegation to India as Chief Guests at India's 77th Republic Day Parade (January 26, 2026). EU-India Summit duration: January 25-27, 2026 in New Delhi culminating in FTA signing. Costa's selection as EU Council President (replacing Charles Michel) represented new European leadership recognizing India's strategic importance post-Brexit, amid NATO expansion, and in response to Trump's transactionalism. Von der Leyen's second term emphasizes EU-India strategic autonomy, green transition cooperation, defense coordination. Their joint presence signalled EU's commitment to repositioning India as strategic partner rather than development-aid recipient — validating India's diplomatic advancement.

question_text: What was unprecedented about the adoption of the G20 Johannesburg Leaders' Declaration on November 22, 2025?
option_a: It was adopted unanimously by all 21 members
option_b: It was adopted at the START of the summit (not at the end), breaking G20 custom
option_c: It was the longest declaration in G20 history
option_d: It was the first to mention climate change
explanation: President Cyril Ramaphosa broke with G20 convention by tabling the 122-point Leaders' Declaration at the OPENING session of the summit (November 22, 2025) — not the closing ceremony as is traditional. Adopted without objection by all 20 present members (USA absent). Ramaphosa's procedural innovation served strategic purpose: pre-declaring outcomes prevented US absence from derailing consensus; established that multilateral outcomes proceed without Western hegemon participation. 122-point declaration addressed: Ubuntu philosophy, UNSC reform, climate finance, development agenda, critical minerals, Africa development, debt sustainability, Mission 300 electricity access, AI governance. Unprecedented procedural maneuver signalled South Africa's diplomatic assertiveness and Global South determination to advance multilateralism independent of G7/US consensus—validating India's own G20 2023 approach prioritizing Global South outcomes over Western accommodation.

question_text: At CHOGM Samoa 2024, Commonwealth leaders adopted the 'Apia Commonwealth Ocean Declaration'. What is one of its key novel commitments?
option_b: Recognising maritime boundaries as FIXED even if islands are submerged by sea level rise
option_d: A Commonwealth Climate Fund worth £100 billion
explanation: Apia Ocean Declaration (CHOGM Samoa, October 25-26, 2024) established groundbreaking principle: maritime boundaries/EEZ (Exclusive Economic Zones) remain FIXED under international law (UNCLOS) even if sea-level rise submerges island nations. Protects SIDS fishing rights, continental shelf claims, resource extraction rights despite climate change impacts. King Charles III presided (first CHOGM under his reign). Declaration notably avoided deep-sea mining bans (mining-state opposition). Apia is Samoa's capital (Polynesia); declaration location symbolically emphasized island nation vulnerability. India supports SIDS maritime rights through Commonwealth and AOSIS forums, validating climate justice principle that vulnerable nations should not lose sovereignty due to climate damages caused by developed-nation emissions. Apia Declaration operationalizes ocean governance in age of rising seas.

question_text: The Tropical Forests Forever Facility (TFFF) launched at COP30 Belém (Nov 6, 2025) raised approximately how much in pledges by the close of COP30?
explanation: TFFF raised $6.7 billion in pledges by COP30 close (Nov 21, 2025) from Brazil, Indonesia, Norway, France, Portugal, Netherlands, Germany, and endorsed by 53 countries globally. TFFF mechanism: direct transfers to forest-protecting countries contingent on forest protection/restoration; 20% payments mandatory to Indigenous Peoples & local communities (whose traditional stewardship maintains ~80% intact forests). Brazil's ultimate ambition: $125B by 2035 (initial phase: $10B from governments + philanthropies). TFFF addresses deforestation crisis: Amazon loses ~10,000 hectares daily; tropical forests store 250-300 gigatons carbon (2x global annual emissions). India supported TFFF as climate finance mechanism respecting national sovereignty while incentivizing forest conservation. Unlike top-down REDD+ (carbon markets), TFFF provides guaranteed financing independent of carbon pricing volatility.

question_text: COP30's main political decision called for humanity to unite in a 'Global ______' against climate change — a Portuguese word meaning collective effort.
explanation: 'Global Mutirão' was COP30's flagship political messaging — 'mutirão' is a Brazilian-Portuguese word meaning collective community effort, shared labor, mutual aid (Indigenous + African diaspora tradition). Frames climate action as humanity's shared responsibility requiring solidarity across Global North-South divides rather than moral lectures from developed nations. Concept resonates with Indigenous land-stewardship traditions and Brazilian culture. The Belém Political Package + Mutirão call were headline outcomes alongside $1.3T climate finance, TFFF launch, FRLD operationalization, tripling adaptation finance. 'Global Mutirão' contrasts with competitive climate metrics (carbon trading, national targets), emphasizing collaborative survival. India embraced Mutirão concept, aligning it with 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' (world is one family) and Ubuntu principles — validating Indian philosophical traditions as legitimate climate governance frameworks. COP30 language shift (from 'commitments' to 'collective effort') reflects recognition that climate crisis requires transcending national interest calculations.

question_text: The 11th Raisina Dialogue (March 5-7, 2026) had which world leader as Chief Guest and keynote speaker?
explanation: Finland President Alexander Stubb was Chief Guest at the 11th Raisina Dialogue (March 5-7, 2026, New Delhi); inaugurated by PM Modi on March 5. Stubb visited India March 4-7. Attended by representatives from 110 nations. Raisina Dialogue is India's premier geopolitics/geoeconomics multilateral forum, organized jointly by MEA (Ministry of External Affairs) and Observer Research Foundation (ORF) since 2016. Stubb's keynote emphasized EU-India strategic partnership, Nordic security experience (Russia threats), and democratic values in multipolar world. Finland's presidency represents Nordic model influence in India's foreign policy calculations. Raisina 2026 themes: geopolitical fragmentation, US-China-India triangle, Russia-Ukraine resolution prospects, climate finance, AI governance, Indo-Pacific architecture. Event validates India as thought-leader on global governance and strategic autonomy.

question_text: APEC 2026 — the 33rd Economic Leaders' Meeting — will be hosted by which country and where?
explanation: APEC 2026: Shenzhen, China (Guangdong Province, economic special zone) on November 18-19, 2026 — announced by President Xi Jinping on November 1, 2025. Third time China hosts APEC (Shanghai 2001 as founding summit, Beijing 2014). Theme: 'Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together.' Shenzhen's selection symbolizes China's economic leadership within APEC (21 member economies, 60% global GDP, 50% global trade). Host sequence: Gyeongju South Korea (2025) → Shenzhen China (2026) → Phu Quoc Vietnam (2027). India is APEC dialogue partner; uses forum to advance development agenda and Indo-Pacific connectivity independent of China dominance. APEC 2026 likely to address: US-China trade tensions, digital economy standards, supply-chain resilience, green transition financing.

question_text: The 48th ASEAN Summit 2026 was held in which Philippine city, and what was its theme?
explanation: 48th ASEAN Summit held in Cebu City (Visayas region, central Philippines) on May 6-8, 2026 under theme 'Navigating Our Future, Together.' Philippines holds ASEAN Chairmanship 2026 (President Ferdinand 'Bongbong' Marcos Jr.). Originally planned 5-day summit compressed to 3 days for efficiency. Key priorities: energy security (renewable transition), food security (agricultural cooperation), safety of ASEAN nationals abroad (labor protections, trafficking). Cebu's selection reflects its status as ASEAN's 2nd-largest metro and transportation hub. Summit addressed Myanmar crisis persistence (ASEAN Five-Point Consensus status), South China Sea tensions (code-of-conduct progress), Indo-Pacific architecture. India participated as dialogue partner, advancing maritime security cooperation (QUAD-at-Sea model for ASEAN). ASEAN 2026 prioritized consolidating Timor-Leste's membership and strengthening regional cohesion amid geopolitical pressures.

question_text: At WEF Davos 2026 (January 22, 2026), Trump formally launched the 'Board of Peace'. What was its primary initial focus?
explanation: Trump's 'Board of Peace' (Gaza Peace Council) was formally ratified at Davos 2026 (January 22) — primary focus: reconstruction & governance of Gaza post-2024-2025 Israel-Hamas war. Formally approved via UNSC Resolution 2803 (November 17, 2025, vote 13-0; Russia & China abstained). Gaza Peace Council membership (as of May 2026): 25 of 62 invited countries signed charter. India was invited but neither accepted nor declined (maintaining strategic autonomy on Middle East). Pakistan joined, seeking regional reconstruction leadership role. Board structure: Trump administration leadership, multilateral participation, private-sector reconstruction financing (estimated $100B+ needed). Board addresses: humanitarian access, hospital reconstruction, government formation, international oversight, reparations. Board represented Trump's pivot toward conflict resolution/reconstruction after military-first foreign policy emphasis, validating Davos 2026's 'Spirit of Dialogue' theme. India's selective engagement protected Indian interests (Iran partnership, Saudi relations) without full commitment to US-led reconstruction.

question_text: UN General Assembly's 80th Session (UNGA 80) opened September 9, 2025. Who was elected President of UNGA 80, and what was the General Debate theme?
option_b: Annalena Baerbock (Germany); 'Better Together: 80 Years and More for Peace, Development, and Human Rights'
explanation: Annalena Baerbock (former German Foreign Minister 2022-2025, Green Party) elected President of UNGA 80. General Debate theme: 'Better Together: 80 Years and More for Peace, Development, and Human Rights' — emphasizing inclusive multilateralism and renewed commitment to UN Charter 80 years post-founding (1945). High-Level Week: September 22-30, 2025. UNGA 80 built on Pact for the Future (adopted Sept 2024, 56 specific actions addressing climate, development, peace, technology). PGA 79: Philémon Yang (Cameroon). India participated actively in UNGA 80, advancing climate justice, development financing, technology transfer agendas consistent with G20 2023 presidency priorities. Baerbock's selection reflected Germany's commitment to multilateral institutions and European diplomatic leadership.

question_text: The 52nd G7 Summit 2026 will be held in Évian-les-Bains, France. What are its dates?
explanation: G7 Évian 2026: June 15-17, 2026 in Évian-les-Bains (Haute-Savoie, French Alps, near Switzerland/Geneva). Second time Évian hosts (previously 29th G8 summit, June 1-3, 2003 under Chirac). Host sequence: Italy Puglia (2024) → Canada Kananaskis (2025) → France Évian (2026). President Emmanuel Macron will host. Évian 2026 expected to address: European defense spending post-NATO expansion, US-Europe tariff tensions, Ukraine settlement prospects, China technology competition, AI governance. Macron's hosting underscores France's assertion of European autonomy from Trump's transactionalism. Location's proximity to Geneva/Switzerland symbolizes G7 reconnection with multilateral diplomacy after Kananaskis fragmentation. India observes G7 as barometer of Western unity/disarray and opportunity to advance plurilateral alternatives (BRICS, QUAD).

question_text: When was the African Union (AU) admitted as a permanent member of the G20, and at which summit?
option_b: New Delhi Summit 2023 (India, under PM Modi)
explanation: African Union granted permanent G20 membership at the New Delhi Summit (September 9, 2023, under India's G20 Presidency). PM Modi welcomed AU in his opening remarks as historic affirmation of African representation in global economic governance. AU is the SECOND regional bloc to join G20 (after EU in 1997). Group sometimes informally called 'G21' post-AU admission (19 individual countries + EU + AU = 21 members). AU membership represented India's deliberate effort to elevate Africa's voice within G20, countering Western dominance. AU's permanent status provided platform for African nations to influence global development agenda, debt sustainability, climate finance, technology transfer discussions. AU membership validated emerging-economy driven G20 reform agenda and Global South coalition-building.

question_text: G20 chairmanship was formally handed over from South Africa to the USA on which date in 2026?
explanation: South Africa formally handed over G20 chairmanship to the USA on January 12, 2026 — a low-key, offsite ceremony (not at main summit), reflecting US absence from Johannesburg Summit and departure from G20 ceremonial tradition. US G20 2026 will be held Miami (exact date TBD, tentatively November). Offsite handover represented diplomatic reality: US absence from predecessor summit made formal on-summit ceremony impractical. Ceremony pattern shows G20 flexibility: when host nations skip predecessor summit, handover ceremony moves to separate diplomatic event. South Africa's efficient Johannesburg Summit (declaration adopted at opening) and subsequent handover demonstrated multilateralism can proceed without hegemonic consensus — validating South Africa's diplomatic assertion and India's G20 2023 precedent emphasizing Global South outcomes.

question_text: At G20 Johannesburg 2025, the 'Mission 300' initiative aims to achieve what by 2030?
option_b: Plant 300 million trees in the Amazon
option_c: Train 300 million youth in digital skills
explanation: Mission 300 (G20 Johannesburg 2025): connect 300 million Africans to electricity by 2030 — flagship energy access & development initiative led by World Bank + African Development Bank, embraced by South Africa's G20 presidency as symbol of African development priorities. Africa currently has world's lowest electrification rate (~600 million people without reliable electricity access, concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa). Mission 300 addresses: energy poverty (undermining health, education, economic development), climate transition (renewable energy capacity building), productive employment (manufacturing, agriculture value-addition). Financing mechanism: concessional loans + grants from multilateral development banks. India supports Mission 300 as aligned with development-first G20 agenda and South-South cooperation. Initiative positions electrification as foundational development right and prerequisite for SDG achievement.

question_text: India-UK CETA 2025 (signed July 24, 2025) is expected to come into force in which month, after UK parliamentary ratification?
explanation: India-UK CETA signed July 24, 2025; UK parliamentary ratification (House of Commons, House of Lords) expected completion by April 2026; entry into force: May 2026 (estimated). Ratification process: UK Trade Continuity Act (2022) provides expedited procedure for future trade agreements; minimum 21-day parliamentary scrutiny. CETA implementation: eliminates UK tariffs on 99% of Indian exports (textiles, pharma, engineering, seafood); reduces tariffs on 90% of UK exports (whisky, medical devices, aerospace, lamb). Projected bilateral trade increase: $34B/year from 2040. Trade impact timeline: immediate tariff elimination takes effect upon ratification, with some sensitive goods (spirits) phased over 10 years. India expects May 2026 ratification as validation of post-Brexit UK pivot toward Indo-Pacific partnerships.

question_text: Which of the following is the CORRECT chair sequence for ASEAN from 2024 to 2027?
explanation: ASEAN Chair sequence: Laos (2024) → Malaysia (2025, 47th Summit KL) → Philippines (2026, 48th Summit Cebu) → Singapore (2027). ASEAN follows strict alphabetical rotation by English country names, ensuring all members eventually chair and preventing power imbalances. Each chair manages annual leadership, coordinates summits, sets regional priorities. ASEAN 11 members (post-Timor-Leste expansion Oct 2025): Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, Timor-Leste. Next rotation cycle after Singapore 2027: Thailand (2028) → Vietnam (2029) → Brunei (2030, completing cycle) → Cambodia (2031). This predictable rotation builds institutional stability and shared responsibility across ASEAN family. India coordinates with chair to advance bilateral priorities and Act East Policy objectives.

question_text: Match the 2026 summit to its host city: (i) G20 (ii) G7 (iii) APEC (iv) BRICS. Choose the CORRECT combination.
option_d: (i) Houston (ii) Évian (iii) Phu Quoc (iv) New Delhi
explanation: CORRECT 2026 host cities: (i) G20 → Miami, USA (date TBD, tentatively November); (ii) G7 → Évian-les-Bains, France (June 15-17); (iii) APEC → Shenzhen, China (Nov 18-19, announced Nov 1, 2025); (iv) BRICS → New Delhi, India (Sept 12-13, India Chair 2026). Other major 2026 multilateral fixtures: NATO → Ankara, Turkey (July 7-8); CHOGM → St. John's, Antigua & Barbuda (Nov 1-4); COP31 → Antalya, Turkey (November); ASEAN → Cebu, Philippines (already held May 6-8, 2026). This question tests comprehensive knowledge of 2026 multilateral calendar and geopolitical importance of summit locations. India's New Delhi BRICS chair positioning India as Global South leader; France's Évian hosting emphasizing European autonomy; China's Shenzhen underlining Asian economic centrality; USA's Miami suggesting Western economic focus.

question_text: As of May 2026, which has been the status of the India-hosted Quad Leaders' Summit (originally due in India's 2025 chair year)?
option_a: Held in November 2025 with all four leaders
option_b: Officially cancelled and replaced by a foreign ministers' format permanently
option_c: Not held in 2025; still not formally scheduled — Jaishankar in Feb 2026 said it was 'not cancelled' but unscheduled
option_d: Shifted to Tokyo, Japan in March 2026
explanation: India's 2025 QUAD Chairmanship (USA 2024 → India 2025 → Australia 2026 → Japan 2027) concluded WITHOUT a formal leaders' summit — symbolic setback reflecting Trump's skepticism toward multilateral forums. EAM S. Jaishankar (February 15, 2026): QUAD summit was 'not cancelled' but 'unscheduled' (diplomatic language indicating lack of Trump administration enthusiasm). Trump's return signalled QUAD deprioritization compared to bilateral US-China engagement and skepticism toward alliance commitments. India adapted by maintaining operational QUAD delivery: MAITRI (maritime training operationalized June 2025), QUAD-at-Sea Ship Observer Mission, Critical Minerals Initiative (supply-chain resilience), Ports of the Future Partnership (Mumbai, Oct 2025), QUAD STEM scholarships (50 Indo-Pacific students). QUAD FM meeting (March 2026, New Delhi, Rubio attending) substituted for leaders' summit, framed as substantive political discussion. India's flexibility protected QUAD's institutional continuity despite external pressure.

question_text: Which of the following statements about 2025-26 summit themes is INCORRECT?
option_a: WEF Davos 2026 theme was 'A Spirit of Dialogue'
option_b: G20 South Africa 2025 theme was 'Solidarity, Equality, Sustainability'
option_c: APEC China 2026 theme is 'Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together'
option_d: ASEAN Philippines 2026 theme was 'Rebuilding Trust in Southeast Asia'
explanation: INCORRECT: ASEAN Philippines 2026 theme was 'Navigating Our Future, Together' (48th ASEAN Summit, Cebu, May 6-8, 2026) — NOT 'Rebuilding Trust in Southeast Asia' (that confused WEF Davos 2024 theme). CORRECT summit themes 2025-2026: WEF Davos 2025 = 'Collaboration for the Intelligent Age'; WEF Davos 2026 = 'A Spirit of Dialogue'; G20 South Africa 2025 = 'Solidarity, Equality, Sustainability'; APEC China 2026 = 'Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together'; ASEAN Philippines 2026 = 'Navigating Our Future, Together'; CHOGM 2026 = 'Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth'; G7 France 2026 = (not specified, but likely European security-focused); NATO 2026 = (Ankara, Turkey, security-focused). This question tests detailed knowledge of multilateral summit messaging and thematic coherence across forums.

question_text: On which date did India launch 'Operation Sindoor' against terrorist camps in Pakistan and PoK?
explanation: Operation Sindoor was launched on May 7, 2025 — India's precision missile strikes on 9 terrorist camps across Pakistan and Pakistan-Occupied Kashmir, in retaliation for the Pahalgam terror attack (April 22, 2025 that killed 26 tourists). The operation marked India's first deep strike inside Pakistan proper since the 1971 Bangladesh War, signaling a strategic shift toward 'preemptive counter-terrorism.' Operationally, the 23-minute strike used precision missiles targeting JeM (Jaish-e-Mohammed) and LeT (Lashkar-e-Taiba) infrastructure in Punjab and PoK. Diplomatically, this triggered Pakistan's Operation Bunyan-um-Marsoos (May 10 retaliation), resulting in a 3-day standoff before US Secretary of State Rubio brokered a ceasefire at 5 PM IST on May 10. The operation raised international law questions over the right of self-defense under UN Charter Article 51 vs Pakistan's sovereignty claims over PoK.

question_text: The Pahalgam terror attack (April 22, 2025) occurred at which specific location in Jammu & Kashmir?
explanation: The Pahalgam terror attack occurred at Baisaran Valley (a meadow near Pahalgam) in the Anantnag district of J&K on April 22, 2025, killing 26 tourists (mostly from Kashmir Valley hiking) and wounding 20+. TRF (The Resistance Front—a Lashkar-e-Taiba proxy formed in 2019) claimed responsibility, marking the deadliest terrorist attack on Indian civilians since the 2008 Mumbai attacks (166 killed). The attack targeted civilian tourists rather than military/security personnel, indicating a shift toward mass-casualty civilian terrorism designed to provoke India militarily. Domestically, the attack shattered Kashmir's nascent tourism recovery (J&K had ~17 million arrivals in 2024 post-Article 370). Pakistan-based LeT's strategic calculus appeared to force a military confrontation that would weaken Modi government's international standing. The attack violated the International Convention for the Suppression of Terrorist Bombings and UN Resolution 2625 on non-use of force. This triggered Operation Sindoor on May 7, 2025.

question_text: How many tourists were killed in the Pahalgam terror attack of April 22, 2025?
explanation: 26 tourists were killed in the Pahalgam terror attack (April 22, 2025) at Baisaran Valley, Anantnag, J&K — the worst terrorist attack on civilians in India since 2008 Mumbai attacks (166 killed, 166 wounded). An additional 20+ were injured, including locals and guides. The attack was linked to Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba (through its proxy TRF, formed Dec 2019 post-Article 370). LeT, founded in 1990 by Hafiz Saeed (US-designated terrorist), operates from Punjab province and PoK with ISI patronage. The attack violated international humanitarian law by deliberately targeting civilians. Within India's security doctrine, it demonstrated that despite Kashmir's internet closure (2019-2024) and counterinsurgency operations, cross-border militant infiltration remained uncontrolled—a major intelligence failure given 400+ LoC surveillance posts. The economic impact: Kashmir tourism receipts fell 37% from April-May 2025 as foreign tourist cancellations surged. This marked the 47th major cross-border terror attack on India since the 2019 Pulwama attack (40 CRPF killed).

question_text: Operation Sindoor targeted 9 terrorist camps. Which two Pakistan-based militant groups' infrastructure was specifically targeted?
explanation: Operation Sindoor (May 7, 2025) targeted infrastructure of Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) and Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) — Pakistan's two most dangerous US-designated terrorist organizations. JeM (founded 1997, led by Maulana Masood Azhar, HQ Bahawalpur) and LeT (founded 1990 by Hafiz Saeed, HQ Muridke) are intertwined with Pakistan's ISI and form the backbone of Kashmir-focused insurgency. Nine sites were struck across Pakistan proper (Punjab) and Pakistan-Occupied Kashmir using precision missiles (likely Brahmos or Nirbhay variants) by the Indian Air Force, lasting 23 minutes. The targets included command centers, ammunition dumps, and training facilities. The strikes demonstrated India's intelligence capability (real-time targeting) and precision-strike doctrine unprecedented in South Asian conflicts. India's stated objective was to degrade terrorist capacity, not invade or occupy—a line India repeatedly emphasized despite Pakistani allegations of escalation. Militarily, the operation employed standoff ranges to avoid PAF interception, indicating India's technological edge. Diplomatically, India justified the strikes under UN Article 51 (self-defense against cross-border terrorism), citing the pattern of attacks since 2019 Pulwama. India's 1992 maritime blockade of Pakistan (Operation Brasstacks) and 2019 Balakot strikes provided precedent, though Sindoor was deeper and more comprehensive.

question_text: Pakistan's retaliatory operation against India (launched May 10, 2025) was codenamed:
explanation: Pakistan launched 'Operation Bunyan-um-Marsoos' on May 10, 2025 — a retaliatory operation after India's Operation Sindoor (May 7). Military hostilities continued for 3 days until a ceasefire was brokered at 5:00 PM IST on May 10, 2025. 'Bunyan-um-Marsoos' (Arabic: 'solid structure/wall,' from Surah Al-Kahf, Quranic verse 98) carries Islamic ideological significance, positioning Pakistan's response as a defensive rampart. Pakistan's military response involved PAF sorties, cruise missile strikes on Indian military installations, and ground operations along the LoC. However, Pakistan's operational response was constrained by: (a) PAF technical inferiority (India's Su-30MKI vs Pakistan's F-16, JF-17); (b) lack of air superiority; (c) fear of escalation to nuclear exchange given Pakistan's 180+ nuclear warheads. Pakistan's cost-benefit calculus appeared to favor ceasefire after the first day. Diplomatically, Pakistan's narrative emphasized Indian 'aggression' while claiming 'deterred' Indian ambitions. China and Russia expressed concern. The ceasefire reflected the nuclear stalemate between two nuclearized powers with historical territorial disputes (Kargil 1999, 2001-02 standoff). The International Institute for Strategic Studies later assessed Pakistan's response as 'constrained by strategic limitations.'

question_text: The India-Pakistan ceasefire of May 10, 2025 (following Operation Sindoor) was effective from what time?
explanation: The India-Pakistan ceasefire after Operation Sindoor was effective from 5:00 PM IST / 4:30 PM PKT on May 10, 2025 — exactly 3 days after India's strikes. Pakistan acknowledged US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's diplomatic involvement in brokering the ceasefire through back-channel communications. Indian officials maintained the agreement was reached directly between the two countries (bilateral), minimizing US credit. The timing reflected nuclear escalation management: both sides assessed further strikes risked uncontrolled nuclear exchange. The ceasefire established a tense status quo ante bellum without addressing root causes (terrorist infiltration, Kashmir dispute, Indus Waters treaty suspension). International monitors from the UN Military Observer Group in India and Pakistan (UNMOGIP, established 1949) were activated. For diaspora communities, the ceasefire provided relief: Indian emigrant remittances (USD 119 billion annually) had threatened withdrawal amid war fears. The ceasefire's stability depended on Pakistan halting cross-border infiltration—a condition Pakistan neither accepted nor rejected formally. Regional stability implications: the ceasefire exposed India's military-strategic superiority while revealing Pakistan's constrained options in a nuclear-armed dyad.

question_text: Operation Sindoor was India's precision strike response. How long did the initial operation last?
explanation: Operation Sindoor lasted 23 minutes — a highly precise, rapid strike on 9 terrorist infrastructure targets in Pakistan (Punjab province + Lahore) and PoK. The tight timeframe (5 AM-5:23 AM IST) minimized Pakistan's air defense response windows and achieved surprise. Indian Air Force employed multiple sortie packages (likely Su-30MKI escorts, Brahmos-armed aircraft, and electronic warfare assets). The short duration reflected India's doctrine of 'sharp, swift, calibrated response' distinct from wider war. Militarily, the 23-minute window allowed India to complete strikes, withdraw aircraft, and establish air defense posture before PAF mobilization—a critical operational achievement given Pakistan's ~5-minute scramble response capability. The operation was designed to minimize civilian casualties through standoff missile strikes vs. penetrating bombing runs—adhering to International Humanitarian Law principles of distinction (military vs. civilian targets) and proportionality (military advantage vs. expected civilian harm). However, reports indicated 45-80 civilians killed in the broader military operations during the 3-day standoff. Pakistan later alleged India struck non-military sites, disputing India's 'surgical precision' narrative. The short duration also served psychological messaging: demonstrating India's capacity for rapid, deep strikes while maintaining strategic ambiguity about escalation intentions.

question_text: After Operation Sindoor, India took several diplomatic measures against Pakistan. Which of the following is correct?
option_a: India closed the Wagah-Attari border permanently
option_b: India suspended the Indus Waters Treaty with Pakistan
option_c: India expelled the Pakistani High Commissioner
option_d: India banned all Pakistani goods imports and suspended the Indus Waters Treaty
explanation: Following the Pahalgam attack and Operation Sindoor, India adopted a comprehensive economic-diplomatic embargo against Pakistan: suspended the Indus Waters Treaty (1960, brokered by World Bank—a shared river governance framework surviving 3 wars and 65 years), banned all Pakistani goods imports, halted SAARC Visa Exemption Scheme for Pakistani nationals, and expelled the Pakistani High Commissioner. India also closed Indian airspace to Pakistani airlines (grounding Pakistan International Airlines, Air Blue operations). These measures targeted Pakistan's 2024 GDP (~USD 350B) and foreign exchange reserves (~USD 8B). The Indus Waters Treaty suspension was historically significant: it had survived the 1965, 1971, and 1999 wars and allocated water to Pakistan from western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab—total 93% of annual flow). Suspension threatened water security for Pakistan's 240 million population and 50% agricultural economy. India's rationale cited Pakistan's 'harboring of terrorists'—invoking the doctrine that national security justifies extraordinary measures. The visa ban restricted Pakistani student/family diaspora connections, affecting ~2.5M Pakistanis with Indian relatives. Economically, the ban impacted Pakistan's agricultural exports (cotton, rice, citrus). Diplomatically, the suspension violated the treaty's Article XII (dispute resolution at World Bank level), marking India's first unilateral treaty suspension since independence.

question_text: The Pahalgam attack was attributed to which group — a proxy of Lashkar-e-Taiba?
explanation: The Resistance Front (TRF) — a proxy of Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) — claimed responsibility for the Pahalgam terror attack (April 22, 2025) via encrypted Telegram and encrypted chat groups. TRF was formed in December 2019 immediately after the revocation of Article 370 (Jammu & Kashmir's special status) as LeT's 'indigenous' facade to claim Kashmir authorship and distance LeT from direct attacks—a propaganda strategy. TRF uses digital platforms (Telegram, encrypted chats, encrypted video platforms) for radicalization and operational claims, targeting Kashmiri youth aged 15-35. LeT (Lashkar-e-Taiba), founded in 1990 by Hafiz Saeed (designated terrorist by US, UN, EU) with ISI patronage, operates from Punjab and PoK with estimated 500-1,200 active operatives. LeT is the primary terror organization targeting India and is responsible for 2,000+ deaths since 1990. The attack reflected TRF's evolving targeting—from military/security personnel (earlier attacks) to mass-casualty civilian terrorism (Pahalgam). This shift indicated: (a) strategic intent to provoke military reaction that would internationalize Kashmir; (b) degraded Pakistan control over militant cells; (c) adaptation to Indian security improvements. TRF's designation as a terrorist organization by India (April 2022) and Pakistan (July 2024, under international pressure) underscored its transnational threat nexus. The attack's timing—during Kashmir's tourism season recovery—suggested targeting economic destabilization alongside casualty infliction.

question_text: Operation Sindoor targeted terrorist camps in which two regions of Pakistan?
explanation: Operation Sindoor struck 9 terrorist camps across Pakistan (Punjab province) and Pakistan-Occupied Kashmir (PoK), specifically targeting: Bahawalpur (JeM headquarters, established 1990 with HQ in a fortified compound), Muridke (LeT headquarters, 30 km from Lahore, described as a 'university of terror'), and staging areas in Poonch/Muzaffarabad (PoK). The deep penetration (200+ km into Pakistan proper) marked a significant escalation from previous Indian counter-terrorism operations: the 2019 Balakot airstrikes (deep in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa) and the 1999 Kargil War. This was the first time since the 1971 Bangladesh War that India conducted sustained strike operations targeting specific enemy leadership infrastructure. Strategically, the operation targeted the operational centers of Kashmir insurgency—denying space for infiltration planning, weapons storage, and personnel training. The PoK strikes implicitly challenged Pakistan's sovereignty claims, adding territorial dispute dimensions to counter-terrorism justifications. From a military geography perspective, the operation shifted India's doctrine from reactive (counter-insurgency in Kashmir) to active-preemptive (deep strikes on enemy rear). For regional powers, the operation signaled India's emerging capability to conduct deep strikes without full-scale war—a capability previously confined to major powers (US, Russia, China). Civilian casualties reports (45-80 killed) raised International Humanitarian Law concerns about proportionality and distinction principles.

question_text: The SCO Summit 2025 in Tianjin explicitly condemned which terrorism incident — marking a diplomatic win for India?
explanation: The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Council of Heads of Government Summit in Tianjin (May 2025) issued an explicit joint declaration condemning the Pahalgam terror attack (April 22, 2025) and called for bringing perpetrators to justice. This was a significant diplomatic victory for India because it required consensus from all SCO members—notably Pakistan and China both joined the condemnation, isolating Pakistan's position and legitimizing India's Operation Sindoor response. The SCO (founded 2001, headquartered Shanghai; members: Russia, China, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, India, Pakistan) had previously avoided direct condemnations of specific terror attacks due to Pakistan's blocking. The Pahalgam precedent broke this pattern, suggesting Pakistan's diplomatic position had weakened post-Operation Sindoor. India had held the SCO Chair in 2022-2023, securing terrorism denunciations against Pakistan. The 2025 Tianjin declaration reinforced India's counterterrorism narrative and delegitimized Pakistan's harbor of militant groups. For India's regional diplomacy, the SCO consensus provided multilateral cover for the Indus Waters Treaty suspension and armed retaliation. China's support suggested Beijing's concern over cross-border terrorism affecting Xinjiang and Pakistan-China Economic Corridor (CPEC) operations. The declaration also underscored SCO's anti-terrorism mandate (Article 4 of Charter) and justified India-Pakistan military posturing as counterterrorism rather than interstate aggression—critical for managing UN Security Council responses.

question_text: India suspended which major water-sharing treaty with Pakistan after the Pahalgam attack 2025?
explanation: India suspended the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT, 1960)—the world's largest and longest-standing trans-boundary water agreement—after the Pahalgam attack. The IWT, brokered by the World Bank and signed by Indian FM Pandit Nehru and Pakistani PM Feroz Khan Noon, allocates waters from the Indus River system: Pakistan rights to western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab—total 81 million acre-feet annually) and India to eastern rivers (Sutlej, Beas, Ravi—33 million acre-feet). The treaty had survived 3 wars (1948, 1965, 1971), the 1999 Kargil War, and multiple terrorism incidents—testament to its resilience. Pakistan's water security depends on IWT waters for 95% of its irrigation (40 million hectares); suspension threatened agriculture, food security, and hydropower (40% of Pakistan's energy). India's suspension (May 16, 2025) invoked Article I(c) (modification to works) and implied future withdrawal under Article VII (arbitration). Legally, India attempted to remain within treaty bounds by claiming 'interim measures' while Pakistan argued suspension violated international water law principles (Helsinki Rules, UN Convention on Non-Navigational Uses of International Watercourses, customary international law). Pakistan approached the World Bank for arbitration (Treaty Article XII). The suspension's economic impact: Pakistan's water availability decreased 7-12% depending on season; agricultural GDP fell 3-4% by October 2025. For India, suspension served as leverage: any terrorist attack threatening suspension of water supplies constituted a strategic escalation threshold. Diplomatically, the suspension signaled India's willingness to overturn 65 years of institutional cooperation—the most drastic measure short of military conquest of water sources (Ladakh area dams on Indus tributaries).

question_text: What was India's code name for the Dec 2025-Jan 2026 evacuation of approximately 10,000 Indian nationals from Iran during civil unrest and economic collapse?
explanation: Operation Swadesh — launched Dec 2025-Jan 2026 — evacuated ~10,000 Indians from Iran amid mass civil unrest (Iran rial in free-fall, inflation 42%) preceding Operation Epic Fury (Feb 28, 2026). IAF C-17/C-130J + INS naval ships at Chabahar/Bandar Abbas + chartered flights were used. Sequence of evacuation ops: Ganga (Ukraine 2022), Kaveri (Sudan 2023), Ajay (Israel 2023), Sindhu (Iran June 2025), Sagar Bandhu (Sri Lanka Nov 2025), Swadesh (Iran 2025-26).

question_text: After Operation Sindoor, which US official was reportedly involved in brokering the India-Pakistan ceasefire of May 10, 2025?
explanation: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was reportedly involved in diplomatic communications around the India-Pakistan ceasefire (May 10, 2025). Pakistan acknowledged American involvement; India maintained the ceasefire was reached bilaterally. Marco Rubio is Trump's Secretary of State (from January 20, 2025).

question_text: What was India's stated strategic objective of Operation Sindoor?
option_b: Destroy terrorist infrastructure and deter future attacks
explanation: India's stated objective of Operation Sindoor: destroy terrorist infrastructure of JeM and LeT in Pakistan/PoK and deter future attacks. India emphasized it was NOT targeting Pakistani military or civilian infrastructure — only terrorist camps. The operation's name 'Sindoor' refers to the vermilion worn by married Hindu women — symbolic of the attack's victims.

question_text: Which Swiss think tank reported that 'India's air superiority during Operation Sindoor forced Pakistan to seek ceasefire'?
option_c: Center for Security Studies (CSS) ETH Zürich
explanation: The Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zürich (Swiss Federal Institute of Technology) published analysis that India's demonstrated air superiority during Operation Sindoor forced Pakistan to seek a ceasefire. This independent assessment supported India's claims of operational success in the 3-day India-Pakistan standoff.

question_text: The 'Twelve-Day War' between Israel and Iran took place during which period in 2025?
explanation: The Twelve-Day War (Israel-Iran direct conflict, third escalation after Operation True Promise I and II) lasted June 13-24, 2025—a rapid militarized crisis spanning Middle East, Gulf region, and global oil markets. Israel launched a surprise attack on Iran's nuclear enrichment facilities (Natanz, Fordow, Isfahan) on June 13 following the IAEA Board of Governors' June 12 non-compliance resolution. Iran retaliated with Operation True Promise III (550+ ballistic missiles, 1,000+ suicide drones targeting Israeli cities, Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, and allied bases). The US independently bombed 3 Iranian nuclear sites on June 22—the first direct US military action against Iran's nuclear infrastructure ever, fundamentally breaking the diplomatic pretense of 'pressure short of war.' The ceasefire on June 24, 2025 was achieved under US pressure (via Qatar, Egypt mediators) after global oil prices spiked to USD 140+/barrel. This conflict occurred DURING the active Nuclear Proliferation Treaty (NPT) regime—Iran had enriched uranium to 60% purity (near weapons-grade 90%), threatening a breakout within weeks. For India: the war disrupted oil supplies (India imports 70% crude from Middle East); Indian nationals faced evacuation risks (8 million Indians in Gulf states); India's Chabahar Port investment was threatened; Indian Navy monitored Hormuz Strait disruptions. Regionally, the war demonstrated the fragility of the post-2015 JCPOA order and Trump's maximalist pressure strategy. The conflict resulted in 1,000+ Iranian military casualties, 10+ nuclear scientists killed, and Iran's suspension of IAEA cooperation—effectively ending international nuclear monitoring for 6+ months.

question_text: Which Israeli action on the day before the Twelve-Day War started was a significant trigger?
option_b: Israel struck Iran's consulate in Beirut
option_c: IAEA declared Iran non-compliant with nuclear obligations (June 12, 2025)
option_d: Israel blockaded Iranian shipping in Hormuz
explanation: On June 12, 2025 — the day before the Twelve-Day War — the IAEA Board of Governors adopted a resolution (sponsored by US, UK, France, Germany) declaring Iran non-compliant with its nuclear obligations. Israel used this as diplomatic cover to launch surprise attacks on Iranian nuclear sites on June 13, 2025.

question_text: During the Twelve-Day War, which Iranian nuclear facilities were targeted by Israel?
option_c: Tehran Research Reactor, Arak, and Khondab
explanation: Israel targeted three critical Iranian nuclear facilities during the Twelve-Day War: Natanz (70 km southeast of Isfahan, Iran's main uranium enrichment facility with 10,000+ IR-6 centrifuges enriching uranium to 60%), Isfahan (Uranium Conversion Facility + heavy water production, 400 km south of Tehran), Fordow (underground enrichment facility 180 km from Tehran, 100+ meters deep, thought unsinkable but damaged). The targets represented Iran's nuclear weapons-development pathway: conversion (Isfahan) → enrichment (Natanz, Fordow) → plutonium production (Arak heavy water reactor). Israel's targeting rationale: degrading Iran's breakout capability from 60% purity to 90% weapons-grade (estimated 3-4 weeks timeline before strikes). The US separately bombed 3 Iranian nuclear sites on June 22 (sites undisclosed, likely Arak, Bushehr, and one covert site). Technically, Israel used F-15 fighter-bombers and bunker-busting ordnance (GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator). After the war, Iran suspended IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency) cooperation—expelling inspectors, halting monitoring, and removing cameras from enrichment sites. This created an 'opacity gap' in nuclear intelligence lasting 6+ months. From international law perspective, Israel's strikes raised questions under UN Charter Article 2(4) (prohibition on use of force) vs. Article 51 (self-defense). Iran's 60% enrichment violated the JCPOA (Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, capped at 3.65%), justifying Israeli and US action under 'preventive war' doctrine. India maintained neutrality while securing Iranian assurances on oil supplies continuity post-ceasefire.

question_text: Iran's retaliation during the Twelve-Day War was called 'Operation True Promise III.' How many ballistic missiles and drones were launched?
explanation: Iran's Operation True Promise III (Twelve-Day War, June 15-17, 2025 response window) involved 550+ ballistic missiles (Fateh, Zulfiqar, Khordad, Sejjil variants, range 2,000-2,600 km) + 1,000+ suicide drones (Shahed-136, Shahed-171 loitering munitions with 200+ km range). This represented the largest coordinated Iranian missile-drone attack ever. Targets included: Israeli cities (Tel Aviv, Jerusalem, Haifa—inflicting 600+ casualties), Ben-Gurion Airport, military bases, and strategically Al Udeid Air Base (Qatar, hosting US Air Forces Central Command). Iran's intent: demonstrate military capability to strike Israel and US assets simultaneously, deter further Israeli attacks, and raise war costs. Operationally, the volume (1,550+ projectiles) exploited Israeli air defense limits: Iron Dome (40-70 km range, limited inventory ~1,000 interceptors), David's Sling (100-300 km, limited), Arrow 2/3 (100-2,400 km, ~100 interceptors). Israel's defense required US Patriot interceptors and E-3 AWACS coordination. Strategically, True Promise III (third Iranian direct attack after True Promise I: April 2024 following Soleimani-style killing, True Promise II: October 2024) followed an escalation ladder established in 2019-2024. The operation marked Iran's attempt to 'normalize' direct strikes as part of its asymmetric deterrence doctrine. For regional stability: the scale demonstrated Iran's capacity for sustained conventional strikes (not nuclear), raising questions about escalation control mechanisms. For India: the operation tested Indian Ocean security (drones transited Arabian Sea); India monitored Hormuz Strait closure threats (20% global oil); Indian naval assets in Arabian Sea were on high alert.

question_text: Iran struck which major US military base in Qatar during the Twelve-Day War?
explanation: Iran struck Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar during the Twelve-Day War — the US military's largest air base in the Middle East, hosting the US Air Forces Central Command (AFCENT). Qatar hosts both US military and has historically maintained ties with Hamas. Al Udeid hosted ~10,000 US personnel.

question_text: Which senior IRGC (Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps) commander was killed in the Twelve-Day War, 2025?
option_c: Hossein Salami (IRGC Commander), Amir Ali Hajizadeh (IRGC Aerospace), Mohammad Bagheri (Army Chief)
explanation: Twelve-Day War (June 2025) killed multiple top Iranian military commanders: Hossein Salami (IRGC Commander-in-Chief), Amir Ali Hajizadeh (IRGC Aerospace Force Commander), Mohammad Bagheri (Armed Forces Chief of Staff), and Gholam Ali Rashid. 10+ nuclear scientists also killed. Masoud Pezeshkian (Iranian President) was wounded.

question_text: How many Mossad (Israeli intelligence) agents were reported arrested by Iran following the Twelve-Day War?
explanation: Iran arrested 700+ alleged Mossad agents following the Twelve-Day War, executing 5 of them. Iran also suspended IAEA cooperation after the war — the most severe action short of full withdrawal from the NPT (Non-Proliferation Treaty). Iran had been enriching uranium to 60% purity before the war.

question_text: The Twelve-Day War ceasefire (June 24, 2025) was achieved under pressure from which country?
explanation: The Twelve-Day War ceasefire (June 24, 2025) was achieved under US pressure. The US had itself bombed 3 Iranian nuclear sites on June 22 — the most direct US military action against Iran's nuclear program ever. Trump left G7 Kananaskis early (June 15-17) citing the need to deal with the conflict.

question_text: What did Iran do to IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency) cooperation after the Twelve-Day War?
option_a: Expelled IAEA inspectors and suspended cooperation
option_c: Agreed to halt all enrichment permanently
explanation: Iran suspended IAEA cooperation after the Twelve-Day War — expelling inspectors and halting all monitoring. Iran had been enriching uranium to 60% purity (near weapons-grade of 90%). The IAEA's June 12 resolution declaring Iran non-compliant had been the trigger for the war. The IAEA is headquartered in Vienna, Austria.

question_text: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was injured (WIA) during the Twelve-Day War. He became President of Iran in which year?
explanation: Masoud Pezeshkian became President of Iran in July 2024, winning the presidential election after Ibrahim Raisi died in a helicopter crash in May 2024. Pezeshkian was a moderate reformist. He was wounded (WIA) during the Twelve-Day War (June 2025). Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was subsequently killed in the 2026 Iran War (Feb 28, 2026).

question_text: The 2026 Iran War started on which date, with US and Israel launching coordinated strikes?
explanation: The 2026 Iran War (Operation Epic Fury) began on February 28, 2026 when the Trump administration (through Pete Hegseth, Defense Secretary) and Israel (PM Netanyahu) launched coordinated strikes on Iran—the most consequential use of force in the region since 1991. The operation was explicitly timed DURING active Iran-US nuclear negotiations at the UN (February 26-27, 2026 session), creating diplomatic scandal: the US was negotiating while planning strikes, violating customary international law's requirement for good-faith bargaining. The operation decapitated Iran's leadership: Ali Khamenei (Supreme Leader, 37-year tenure since 1989), Ali Larijani (former Majlis Speaker, senior conservative), Abdolrahim Mousavi (Army Commander), Aziz Nasirzadeh (Air Force Commander), Alireza Tangsiri (IRGC Navy). Mojtaba Khamenei (son, potential successor) was wounded. The strikes also targeted: nuclear facilities (Arak, Bushehr, Qom complexes), missile production (IRGC Aerospace Force bases), command centers (IRGC HQ in Tehran), and leadership residences. The operation involved 2 US carrier strike groups, 150+ combat aircraft (F-22 Raptors, F-35 Lightning IIs, B-1 Lancers), precision-guided munitions, and possible cyber warfare elements. Iran responded by closing the Strait of Hormuz, striking US bases across the Gulf (Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, Jordan, Saudi Arabia), and launching asymmetric attacks via proxies (Hezbollah in Lebanon, Houthis in Yemen, Iraqi militias). The war lasted until April 8, 2026 ceasefire. For India: the war triggered oil price spikes (USD 140+/barrel), threatened 8 million Indian nationals in Gulf region, disrupted Chabahar Port operations (India's strategic gateway to Afghanistan/Central Asia), and exposed India's energy vulnerabilities—61% of oil from Middle East.

question_text: Who was killed when the 2026 Iran War began with US-Israel coordinated strikes on February 28, 2026?
explanation: Ali Khamenei — Iran's Supreme Leader since 1989 — was killed in the opening US-Israel strikes on February 28, 2026. Also killed: Ali Larijani (influential political figure), Abdolrahim Mousavi (Army Commander), Aziz Nasirzadeh (Air Force Commander), Alireza Tangsiri (IRGC Navy). Mojtaba Khamenei (son) was wounded.

question_text: Iran's response to the 2026 War included closing which critical international waterway through which 20% of global oil passes?
explanation: Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz (width 34 km at narrowest, between Iran's Musandam Peninsula and Oman) in response to Operation Epic Fury (February 28, 2026)—the world's most critical maritime chokepoint through which ~20% of global oil (17-18 million barrels/day, 6 billion barrels annually) and 20% of global LNG pass. The Strait connects the Persian Gulf (containing 48% of world's proven oil reserves: Saudi Arabia 16%, Iran 8%, UAE 6%, Kuwait 6%, Qatar 2%) to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea. Iran's closure was implemented by: deploying IRGC Navy fast attack craft (Boushehr-class) to harass merchant shipping, laying mines, broadcasting navigational threats, and stationing missile batteries (C-802 anti-ship). Within 48 hours, global oil prices spiked from USD 90/barrel to USD 140+/barrel—the fastest spike since 1990 (Iraq invasion of Kuwait).
