For India: the closure was catastrophic—India imports 70% of its 4 million barrels/day from Middle East, with Hormuz transit serving 60% of Indian imports. Oil prices at USD 140 increased India's import bill by USD 20 billion annually (3.6% inflation impact). India's strategic reserve (Strategic Petroleum Reserve, 5.33 million barrel capacity, 50 days consumption) was activated. For global trade: closure added USD 200-400 per container for ships rerouting around Africa's Cape of Good Hope (10-14 extra days, 5,000+ nm additional voyage). Shipping insurance premiums in Hormuz doubled to 2-3% of cargo value. The closure lasted 39 days (until April 8 ceasefire) before US naval presence and diplomatic pressure (Pakistan mediation) reopened transit. Strategically, Iran's Hormuz closure was its most powerful conventional asymmetric weapon—costlier to global economy than military strikes.

question_text: During the 2026 Iran War, Iran struck US military bases in multiple countries. Which of the following was NOT struck by Iran?
explanation: Iran struck US military bases in: Bahrain (NSA Bahrain/5th Fleet HQ), Jordan (Al-Tanf area), Kuwait (Camp Arifjan), Qatar (Al Udeid), Saudi Arabia (Prince Sultan Air Base), and UAE (Al Dhafra). Egypt was NOT struck — Egypt hosts Sinai peacekeepers and maintains separate diplomatic relations. UK's Akrotiri base in Cyprus was also struck by drone.

question_text: The 2026 Lebanon War ran parallel to the Iran War. How many Hezbollah fighters were killed in the 2026 Lebanon War?
explanation: The 2026 Lebanon War (concurrent with 2026 Iran War) resulted in 1,000-1,900 Hezbollah fighters killed and 2,000+ total casualties. Hezbollah fired rockets at Israel from Lebanon. Israel struck Beirut again on May 7, 2026 — killing the then-current Hezbollah leader. Hezbollah SG Naim Qassem had taken over after Nasrallah's death in September 2024.

question_text: Pakistan mediated the April 8, 2026 conditional Iran-US ceasefire and then hosted follow-up talks. When did the Pakistan-hosted US-Iran talks at Islamabad collapse?
explanation: Pakistan (under PM Shehbaz Sharif, post-Operation Sindoor reputational recovery) brokered the April 8, 2026 'conditional ceasefire' between Iran and the US-Israel coalition, ending the active kinetic phase of the 2026 Iran War after 39 days and 15+ US soldiers killed, 3,636+ Iranians killed. The ceasefire was conditional: parties agreed to halt strikes, reopen Strait of Hormuz, and pursue negotiations. Pakistan's mediation role reflected: (a) Pakistan-Iran 900 km border and shared Shi'a-Sunni tensions; (b) Pakistan's interest in regional stability (energy imports, trade via Iran); (c) Pakistan's strategic desire to raise its profile post-Sindoor. Follow-up US-Iran negotiations at Islamabad (April 11-12, 2026 session) convened with US, Iran, Pakistan, and Qatar as participants. The talks collapsed over three irreconcilable demands: (a) Iran's demand for full US withdrawal from Persian Gulf bases (5th Fleet, CENTCOM forward HQ in Qatar, Al Udeid)—the US rejected, viewing these as core strategic architecture; (b) US insistence on permanent nuclear dismantlement (Arak reactor mothballing, centrifuge destruction, full IAEA access)—Iran rejected, viewing these as sovereignty violations; (c) Iran's reparations claim of USD 270-1 trillion for destroyed nuclear infrastructure, leadership casualties, economic damage—the US countered with USD 50-200 billion liability framework (US-flagged shipping damages, Gulf allies' losses). The collapse reflected the incompatibility of Iranian revolutionary ideology (resistance to US dominance) and US strategic interests (containing Iran's regional influence). Pakistan's mediation failure indicated even third-party powers lack leverage when core interests diverge. For India: the collapsed talks meant prolonged tensions in the Gulf (strategic interest), continued elevated oil prices (energy security), and uncertainty over India's positioning between Iran and US (diplomatic balancing act).

question_text: US casualties in the 2026 Iran War were:
explanation: US casualties in the 2026 Iran War: 15 soldiers killed, 538 wounded (as of ceasefire, April 8, 2026). Iran casualties (HRANA human rights group): 3,636 killed, 26,500 wounded; $270 billion to $1 trillion economic damage. Israel: 18 soldiers + 28 civilians killed; $50 billion economic damage.

question_text: What was the scale of US military deployment during the 2026 Iran War — described as the largest Middle East buildup since 2003?
explanation: US deployed 2 aircraft carrier strike groups for the 2026 Iran War — the largest Middle East military buildup since the 2003 Iraq invasion. US military leadership: Pete Hegseth (Defense Secretary), Michael Kurilla (CENTCOM Commander), Dan Caine (Joint Chiefs Chairman). US and Israel coordinated strikes starting February 28, 2026.

question_text: Who was Israel's Defense Minister during the 2026 Iran War?
explanation: Israel's key leaders during the 2026 Iran War: PM Benjamin Netanyahu, Defense Minister Israel Katz, IDF Chief Eyal Zamir. US Defense Secretary: Pete Hegseth (appointed by Trump). Iran's Revolutionary Guard was severely weakened after Twelve-Day War (June 2025) commanders killed.

question_text: Ali Khamenei had been Iran's Supreme Leader since which year?
explanation: Ali Khamenei became Iran's Supreme Leader in 1989 following the death of Ayatollah Khomeini (the founder of Islamic Republic). Before becoming Supreme Leader, Khamenei was Iran's President (1981-1989). He held the Supreme Leader position for 37 years until killed in the 2026 Iran War (February 28, 2026).

question_text: The 2026 Iran War caused Iran to close the Strait of Hormuz. What percentage of global LNG (Liquefied Natural Gas) also passes through the Strait?
explanation: The Strait of Hormuz carries ~20% of global oil AND approximately 20% of global LNG — including major exports from Qatar (world's top LNG exporter). Closure impacted global energy markets, driving oil prices above $100/barrel. India's Chabahar Port (in Iran) was also strategically affected.

question_text: Iran's economic damage from the 2026 Iran War was estimated at:
explanation: Iran's economic damage from the 2026 Iran War: $270 billion to $1 trillion (wide range due to ongoing conflict and estimation difficulties). Includes: infrastructure destruction, Strait of Hormuz closure economic impact, sanctions, oil revenue loss. Israel's damage: $50 billion. US deployed 2 carrier strike groups in the largest Middle East buildup since 2003 Iraq invasion.

question_text: US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was appointed under which president, and when did he take office?
explanation: Pete Hegseth was appointed US Secretary of Defense by President Donald Trump, taking office January 20, 2025 (Trump's inauguration day). Hegseth was a Fox News host and Army National Guard veteran before becoming Defense Secretary. He led US military decisions during Operation Sindoor (India-Pakistan), the Twelve-Day War, and the 2026 Iran War.

question_text: Israel struck Beirut on May 7, 2026 — killing a Hezbollah leader. Who had become Hezbollah's Secretary-General after Nasrallah was killed in September 2024?
explanation: Naim Qassem became Hezbollah's Secretary-General after Hassan Nasrallah was killed in an Israeli airstrike on September 27, 2024. Qassem had been Hezbollah's Deputy Secretary-General for many years. He was killed in Israel's May 7, 2026 Beirut strike. The Hezbollah-Israel ceasefire of November 2024 broke down with the 2026 Lebanon War.

question_text: In the Russia-Ukraine War, which country launched a historic surprise military incursion into Russia's Kursk Oblast in 2024, and what was its 2025 status?
option_a: Ukraine incursed Kursk August 2024; Russian forces recaptured most by early 2025
option_b: Russia incursed Ukraine's Sumy Oblast in 2024
option_d: Ukraine launched missiles at Moscow in August 2024
explanation: Ukraine's surprise incursion into Russia's Kursk Oblast (August 6-9, 2024) — first time since WWII that foreign forces directly held Russian sovereign territory—was a strategic gambit by Ukraine's military (SBU Chief Budanov planning). Ukrainian forces (1st Tank Brigade, 22nd Mechanized Brigade) penetrated 40+ km into Kursk, capturing 1,200+ sq km and 15,000+ Russian POWs. The operation's strategic intent: (a) break the stalemate on Ukrainian soil; (b) demonstrate Ukrainian offensive capability (after years of Russian offensive); (c) create a 'bargaining chip' for future negotiations; (d) boost Ukrainian morale (first foreign invasion of Russia proper); (e) expose Russian mobilization deficiencies. By early 2025, Russian forces (with North Korean 10,000-12,000 troop reinforcements) had recaptured 60-70% of Kursk, though Ukraine retained 400-600 sq km as of May 2026. Militarily, the operation demonstrated Ukraine's tactical resourcefulness despite material disadvantage (outgunned 3:1 in artillery). Legally, the incursion raised questions under International Humanitarian Law: Ukraine's occupation of Russian territory (technically violating UN Charter Article 2(4)) was justified as counter-occupation response to Russian control of 20% of Ukrainian territory. Diplomatically, Kursk became leverage in Trump-mediated negotiations (January-May 2026), with Russia demanding Ukrainian withdrawal as ceasefire condition. For India: the Kursk operation revealed limitations of larger military forces against smaller, innovative adversaries—relevant to India-Pakistan asymmetric warfare doctrine. The operation's success rate (initial 40 km penetration before stabilization) contradicted pre-war assessments of Russia's overwhelming military dominance.

question_text: North Korea sent approximately 10,000-12,000 troops to support Russia in the Ukraine war. How were these troops deployed?
option_a: Defensive positions in Russia's western border
option_b: Direct combat in Kursk Oblast against Ukrainian forces
option_c: Logistics and supply chain support only
explanation: North Korea (DPRK) deployed ~10,000-12,000 troops to Russia (October 2024 onwards) in direct combat roles in Kursk Oblast against Ukrainian forces, marking the first DPRK combat deployment outside Korean peninsula since 1950-53 Korean War. DPRK troops were primarily deployed in the 1st Guards Tank Army (western front against Ukraine's Kursk incursion). North Korea also supplied 3-5 million artillery shells (122mm, 152mm) and ballistic missiles (KN-02 Toksa, range 120 km), addressing Russia's critical ammunition deficit. Russia signed the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty with DPRK (October 2024), establishing mutual defense obligations (Article 4). Putin visited Pyongyang; Kim Jong-un visited Moscow (August 2023, then follow-ups). The deployment raised international law concerns: (a) UN Security Council prohibitions on DPRK foreign military activities; (b) potential violations of UN sanctions on DPRK; (c) expansion of DPRK's international combat experience (previously relegated to cyber warfare, proxy operations). Casualties: 1,500+ DPRK soldiers killed/wounded (first 3 months), exposing DPRK's poor combat training and outdated tactics. For India: DPRK-Russia cooperation indicated consolidation of anti-US axis (Russia, DPRK, Iran, China) against Western-aligned powers—relevant to India's strategic autonomy doctrine and China-Pakistan axis. The deployment also exposed DPRK's economic dependence on Russia (food, fuel shipments in return for soldiers + arms). The operation's personnel losses threatened DPRK's military regeneration capacity, suggesting potential instability in Korean peninsula (2026-2027).

question_text: Trump announced a 3-day Russia-Ukraine ceasefire in May 2026. What prisoner exchange was included?
explanation: Trump's 3-day Russia-Ukraine ceasefire (May 9-11, 2026) included an exchange of 1,000 prisoners each side — a significant humanitarian element. Trump called it potentially 'the beginning of the end' of the war. US Secretary of State Rubio struck a somber tone, saying US mediation had not led to a 'fruitful outcome' and efforts had 'stagnated.'

question_text: Russia declared a unilateral ceasefire in Ukraine for May 8-9, 2026 to mark which occasion?
explanation: Russia declared a unilateral ceasefire for May 8-9, 2026 for its annual WWII Victory Day commemorations. Ukraine declared its own truce for May 5-6, calling Russia's ceasefire 'not serious' (overlap only on May 8). Trump then brokered the 3-day joint ceasefire (May 9-11). The WWII Victory Day (May 9) is Russia's most important national holiday.

question_text: According to ACLED 2025 data, which conflict was the world's deadliest in 2025 with almost 78,000 fatalities?
explanation: The Ukraine War was the world's deadliest conflict in 2025 with almost 78,000 battle-related and 2,000+ civilian deaths (Armed Conflict Location & Event Project—ACLED, US dataset). Top 10 deadliest conflicts globally: Ukraine (78,000), Sudan (60,000+), Israel-Palestine (30,000+), Myanmar (9,000+), Nigeria (8,000+), Somalia (5,000+), Syria (4,000+), Mexico (3,000+), Brazil (2,500+), DRC (2,000+). Ukraine's lethality reflected: (a) sustained state-on-state warfare (conventional militaries, not insurgency); (b) Russian indiscriminate targeting of Ukrainian civilian areas (Kharkiv, Lviv, Odesa bombardments killing 2,000+); (c) attritional tactics (trench warfare, WW1-style casualties); (d) advanced weapons usage (drones, cruise missiles, artillery); (e) scale of forces engaged (1.5+ million combatants). Russia's strategy shifted from quick-victory blitzkrieg (February 2022) to grinding attrition, resulting in 500,000+ cumulative casualties (Russian + Ukrainian combined, killed + wounded). The Ukraine War's intensity exceeded recent conflicts: Syria 11-year civil war (500,000 deaths), Yemen (300,000+), Afghanistan (20 years, 200,000+). For India: the Ukraine War highlighted the costs of prolonged state conflict in the modern era and provided strategic lessons on: (a) defensive advantages (Ukraine 'holding' despite being outgunned initially); (b) asymmetric warfare effectiveness (drones, MANPADS vs. armor); (c) international support importance (NATO weapons, intelligence); (d) civilian resilience under bombardment. The 78,000 figure represented only counted deaths; total mortality (including famine, disease, displacement) was estimated 2-3x higher.

question_text: US-Ukraine-Russia trilateral talks were announced at WEF Davos 2026 to begin in which city?
explanation: At WEF Davos 2026, Zelenskyy met Trump and announced US-Ukraine-Russia trilateral peace talks to begin in Abu Dhabi on January 23, 2026. Abu Dhabi (UAE) was chosen as a neutral location. The talks followed multiple failed ceasefire attempts. US Secretary of State Rubio acknowledged negotiations had 'stagnated.'

question_text: In the Russia-Ukraine conflict, Ukraine has used which NATO nation's F-16 fighter jets, delivered in 2024-2025?
option_c: Netherlands and Denmark (transferred with US approval)
explanation: Netherlands and Denmark transferred F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine (with US approval) in 2024-2025 — a major boost to Ukraine's air force. The F-16s required Ukrainian pilot training in Romania. Germany supplied Leopard 2 tanks; UK supplied Storm Shadow cruise missiles. Russia condemned F-16 deliveries as NATO escalation.

question_text: Russia's war in Ukraine began on February 24, 2022. How many years had the conflict lasted by May 2026?
explanation: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began February 24, 2022. By May 2026, the conflict had lasted over 4 years and 3 months. The conflict was preceded by Russia's annexation of Crimea (2014) and support for Donbas separatists. By 2025, it was the world's deadliest conflict with 78,000+ fatalities.

question_text: NATO pledged €40 billion in defense aid to Ukraine in 2025 (at The Hague Summit). What controversial issue regarding Ukraine's NATO membership remained unresolved?
option_c: No NATO membership pathway, timeline, or invitation offered
explanation: Despite €40 billion in aid, NATO's Hague Summit 2025 offered Ukraine NO membership invitation, NO timeline, NO significant upgrade in membership language — deeply disappointing Kyiv. NATO's position was that Ukrainian NATO membership must be considered after the war ends. Meanwhile, NATO's defense spending was raised to 5% GDP.

question_text: The Gaza ceasefire 'Phase 1' was agreed on January 15, 2025. Who mediated this ceasefire?
explanation: The Gaza ceasefire Phase 1 (January 15, 2025) was mediated by Qatar, Egypt, and the USA — the same troika that mediated all Gaza ceasefire talks. Phase 1 involved a 42-day pause and hostage releases. The conflict had started on October 7, 2023 with Hamas's attack on Israel. By 2025, Gaza rebuilding faced immense challenges.

question_text: Which country was described as having the 'world's worst humanitarian crisis' in terms of absolute numbers of displaced persons by mid-2025?
explanation: Sudan's civil war (started April 2023: SAF vs RSF) caused the 'world's worst humanitarian crisis' by mid-2025 — 10 million internally displaced + 3 million fled to neighboring countries; 2/3 of Sudan's 50 million people needed assistance. RSF captured El Fasher (North Darfur capital) on October 27, 2025 after an 18-month siege.

question_text: Sudan's civil war (2023-2025) is between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and which rebel group?
explanation: Sudan's civil war: SAF (Sudanese Armed Forces) vs. RSF (Rapid Support Forces) — started April 2023. RSF was led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo ('Hemeti'). RSF captured El Fasher in October 2025. Sudan's conflict was rated the most likely to escalate in 2026 by International Crisis Group. Casualty estimates: 150,000+ killed.

question_text: On January 3, 2026 the US launched 'Operation Absolute Resolve' against which country, capturing its sitting president?
explanation: Operation Absolute Resolve (January 3, 2026, pre-dawn coordinated assault)—the Trump administration's direct military intervention in Venezuela, capturing sitting President Nicolás Maduro and extracting him to New York for federal indictment on narcotics trafficking, corruption, money laundering charges. The operation employed ~150 US combat aircraft (F-22 Raptors, F-35 Lightning IIs, B-1 Lancers, F-16s), establishing air superiority, followed by special operations forces (SOCOM Delta Force, Navy SEAL Team 6) insertion into Miraflores Palace (presidential residence) in Caracas. The operation lasted 18 minutes, with Maduro subdued and flown via US aircraft to Guantanamo Bay, then to New York federal courthouse. The capture of a sitting head of state and extrajudicial transfer to foreign courts violated multiple international law principles: UN Charter Article 2(4) (prohibition on use of force), UN General Assembly resolutions on sovereignty, and established norms against 'regime change' operations (post-2003 Iraq War international consensus). Venezuela's opposition leader María Corina Machado (Nobel Peace Prize 2025 winner) was subsequently sworn in as interim president with US recognition. Venezuela holds 303 billion barrels of proven oil reserves (20% of global reserves), making the resource-control dimension controversial. For India: the operation raised strategic concerns about US willingness to unilaterally intervene in sovereign states (applicable to India-Pakistan disputes, China-Taiwan, etc.), setting precedent for unilateral power projection. The operation destabilized regional oil markets, raised crude prices, and displaced Venezuelan refugees (500,000+ asylum-seekers). The legality under UN Charter was contested; China, Russia, Iran, and Non-Aligned Movement states condemned it as imperialism. The capture marked a return to 19th-century 'gunboat diplomacy' after 75 years of post-WWII UN Charter restraint.

question_text: Myanmar's civil war since 2021 has caused how many deaths and displacements by 2025?
option_b: 50,000+ deaths (per ACLED estimates), 3+ million internally displaced and 1 million fled
explanation: Myanmar's civil war (February 1, 2021 coup by General Min Aung Hlaing onward): approximately 50,000+ deaths per ACLED (Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project) estimates (battle-related + extrajudicial killings), 3+ million internally displaced, 1+ million fled abroad (Bangladesh 1M+, Thailand 100K+, India 50K+) by 2025. The ACLED estimates, refined through the conflict's 5-year trajectory, indicate ~50,000 casualties rather than earlier high-end projections. The conflict is described as 'under the radar' globally relative to Ukraine, Iran, Gaza—despite higher intensity (2021-2025 comparable to Ukraine War casualty rate per capita). ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus (April 2021) calling for dialogue, non-interference, and military aid cessation remained largely unimplemented. Myanmar's junta, backed by Russia and China, resisted ASEAN mediation. Key combatants: Myanmar Military (Tatmadaw) vs. 150+ ethnic armed organizations (EAOs: Karen National Liberation Army, Shan State Army, Arakan Army) plus People's Defence Force (PDF, anti-junta militia). The conflict involves: (a) ethnic separatism (Karen, Shan, Arakan, Rakhine autonomy demands); (b) post-coup democratic resistance (civil disobedience, armed rebellion); (c) humanitarian crisis (2M+ food insecure, 50%+ health system collapse). For India: Myanmar's instability threatened India's Northeast region (Mizoram, Nagaland) via cross-border rebel bases; India's regional influence in Myanmar declined post-coup; BIMSTEC economic integration stalled. Bangladesh's refugee absorption from Myanmar (1M+ Rohingya + Myanmar protesters) created burden-sharing pressures. At ASEAN KL 2025, leaders reviewed Myanmar's crisis but achieved no breakthrough. Min Aung Hlaing was 'elected' president in April 2026 in a junta-managed election—formalizing the coup's consolidation. International sanctions (US, EU, UK) had minimal impact on junta's behavior. The conflict represented the largest humanitarian crisis in Southeast Asia post-1990s Cambodia.

question_text: Russia was the FIRST country to officially recognise the Taliban government of Afghanistan. When did this happen?
explanation: Russia became the FIRST country to officially recognize the Taliban government of Afghanistan on July 3, 2025 — breaking a 3.5-year international consensus of non-recognition. Russia established formal diplomatic relations with the Taliban-led Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan. This was seen as Russia's strategy to expand influence in Central Asia.

question_text: The Houthi group (Yemen) has been led by which figure, conducting attacks on Red Sea shipping since 2023?
explanation: Abdul-Malik al-Houthi leads the Houthi movement (Ansar Allah) in Yemen since 2003 (founding) and expanded to national insurgency post-2015 Saudi coalition intervention. Since October 7, 2023 (Hamas-Israel war start), Houthis conducted systematic attacks on Red Sea commercial shipping via anti-ship missiles (Yemeni-modified cruise missiles, range 1,500+ km), naval mines, and unmanned boats—claiming 'solidarity with Gaza' and targeting US-allied shipping. The attacks disrupted 12-20% of global shipping through the Red Sea/Bab el-Mandeb Strait (34 km chokepoint carrying $700B+ annual trade). Houthis hit 100+ vessels by May 2026. US-UK Operation Poseidon Archer (January-May 2025) conducted airstrikes on Houthi military targets (drone bases, missile sites, ports in Hodeidah) but failed to deter attacks. The campaign reflected Houthis' asymmetric strategy: low-cost drones/missiles vs. expensive destroyers providing escorts (cost asymmetry of 1:100). For global trade: Red Sea disruption forced rerouting around Africa's Cape of Good Hope, adding USD 200,000+ per container and 10-14 voyage days. Insurance premiums tripled. For India: Houthi attacks threatened Indian shipping (5,000+ Indian vessels transiting Red Sea annually); Indian Navy provided escorts to Indian merchant vessels; oil import costs surged (India imports 70% crude from Middle East). Houthis received funding and weapons from Iran's IRGC Quds Force (Iran-backed proxy network). Yemen's civil war (SAF vs. STC vs. Houthis, 2015-2025) killed 300,000+; Houthis controlled 70% of population (northwest Yemen). The Red Sea disruption persisted until May 2026, causing estimated USD 10 billion in additional global shipping costs.

question_text: The New START nuclear arms control treaty between USA and Russia expired in February 2026. What was Russia's decision regarding the treaty?
option_a: Russia agreed to extend for 5 more years
option_b: Russia suspended participation in 2023 and treaty lapsed
option_c: Russia signed a replacement treaty with China
explanation: Russia suspended participation in the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START, signed Prague April 2010 by Obama-Medvedev) on February 21, 2023 (citing US support for Ukraine as pretext). The treaty capped US and Russian deployed strategic nuclear warheads at 1,550 each, deployed delivery systems (ICBMs, SLBMs, strategic bombers) at 700, and total warheads at 6,000 each—the last bilateral binding nuclear arms control agreement post-Cold War. The treaty lapsed in February 2026 when it expired, leaving no nuclear arms control framework between the two largest nuclear powers (Russia 5,459 warheads, USA 5,177) for the first time since 1972 (SALT-I era). The lapse created strategic ambiguity: (a) unknown force levels (Russia may have deployed 2,000+ warheads vs. treaty's 1,550 cap); (b) no verification mechanisms (IAEA inspections ceased); (c) destabilized mutual deterrence (both sides feared surprise disarming strike capability). For nuclear-armed India: the lapse illustrated risks of bilateral arms control collapse—relevant to India-Pakistan nuclear standoff stability. India had advocated for US-Russia nuclear talks as global security imperative at the UN. The lapse also accelerated China's nuclear modernization (estimated 500+ warheads by 2030) due to perceived US-Russia disarmament inequities. Trump administration (2025-2026) showed no interest in reviving New START, instead pursuing unilateral advantages. Pakistan's nuclear arsenal (170-180 warheads) benefited from reduced superpower oversight, complicating India-Pakistan deterrence calculations. The New START lapse marked the end of 50+ years of bilateral strategic arms control architecture.

question_text: 'Operation Poseidon Archer' was conducted by which countries against Houthi targets in Yemen in 2025?
explanation: Operation Poseidon Archer: US and UK conducted airstrikes against Houthi (Ansar Allah) military targets in Yemen in response to Houthi attacks on Red Sea commercial shipping. Houthis targeted ships claiming solidarity with Gaza. The Red Sea disruptions cost global shipping tens of billions in additional costs (rerouting via Cape of Good Hope).

question_text: The IRGC (Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps) is Iran's elite military force. Which component specifically manages Iran's missile and drone programs?
explanation: IRGC Aerospace Force manages Iran's ballistic missile and drone programs — including the Shahed-136 suicide drones and Fateh/Zulfiqar ballistic missiles. IRGC Aerospace Force Commander Amir Ali Hajizadeh was killed in the Twelve-Day War (June 2025). Quds Force (external operations) is a separate IRGC branch. IRGC is designated a terrorist organization by USA.

question_text: Which of the following is the correct IRGC component that conducts Iran's foreign proxy operations?
explanation: IRGC Quds Force conducts Iran's external operations — supporting proxies including Hezbollah (Lebanon), Hamas (Gaza), Houthis (Yemen), and PMF (Iraq). Qasem Soleimani, legendary Quds Force commander, was killed by US drone strike on January 3, 2020 at Baghdad airport. His successor, Esmail Qaani, became Quds Force commander.

question_text: Which country in the Middle East hosts the largest US air base (Al Udeid) that was struck by Iran during the 2026 Iran War?
explanation: Al Udeid Air Base — the US's largest Middle East air base — is in Qatar, hosting ~10,000 US personnel and the US Air Forces Central Command (AFCENT). Qatar also hosts the HQ of Hamas political bureau. Iran struck Al Udeid during both the Twelve-Day War (June 2025) and the 2026 Iran War. Qatar also mediated the Gaza ceasefire.

question_text: The 'Axis of Resistance' — Iran's network of regional proxies — includes which of the following groups?
option_a: Hezbollah, Hamas, Houthis, and PMF (Iraqi militias)
explanation: Iran's 'Axis of Resistance': Hezbollah (Lebanon), Hamas (Gaza), Houthis/Ansar Allah (Yemen), and PMF (Popular Mobilization Forces) in Iraq. These groups receive funding, weapons, and training from Iran's IRGC Quds Force. The 2026 Iran War significantly degraded the Axis of Resistance as Iran's own military was severely weakened.

question_text: Iran's Natanz nuclear facility is located in which Iranian province?
explanation: Natanz uranium enrichment facility is in Isfahan Province, Iran — about 250 km south of Tehran. It is Iran's main uranium enrichment site with thousands of centrifuges. Isfahan also hosts the UCF (Uranium Conversion Facility). Both Natanz and Isfahan were targeted by Israel in the Twelve-Day War (June 2025). Fordow is in Qom Province.

question_text: India's strategic interest in the 2026 Iran War context involves which Iranian port under India's development?
explanation: Chabahar Port (Sistan-Baluchistan Province, southeastern Iran, 600 km from Hormuz Strait on the Gulf of Oman) is India's strategic infrastructure investment—India has invested $500+ million in developing it (Phase 1: 2016-2022 completion; Phase 2: 2023-2030 expansion). Chabahar's strategic value: (a) provides India access to Afghanistan (Zaranj-Delaram highway) and Central Asia (bypassing Pakistan's blockade); (b) reduces India's Malacca Strait dependency (via Cape, around Malacca takes 40 days); (c) enables Indian maritime presence in Arabian Sea; (d) facilitates India-Iran-Afghanistan trade corridor (IIAC). During the 2026 Iran War (Feb-April 2026), India maintained strict neutrality—refusing to condemn Operation Epic Fury or support sanctions—partly to protect Chabahar from collateral war damage or Iranian retaliation. Indian Navy vessels at Chabahar were mobilized to: (a) prevent Chabahar's military targeting (de facto protection); (b) maintain supply lines to Indian nationals evacuated via Operation Swadesh; (c) monitor Hormuz closure impacts on Indian shipping. Diplomatically, External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar met Iranian FM Araghchi on May 15, 2026 (post-ceasefire), reaffirming India's commitment to Chabahar despite war disruptions. Operationally, the 2026 war forced Chabahar into partial shutdown (3-week closure, restarted at 40% capacity by May). For India's strategic autonomy: Chabahar represents India's independent infrastructure corridor outside China's Belt-and-Road Initiative (BRI) and US sanctions architecture—a counterweight to Gwadar Port (Pakistan-China). India's 8 million nationals in Gulf region faced evacuation risks during the war; Chabahar remained India's principal evacuation hub alongside Bandar Abbas. The port's disruption threatened India's $2.5 billion annual Afghanistan trade and 2,000+ Indian workers' employment.

question_text: The Samson Option refers to Israel's:
option_a: Conventional military doctrine of preemptive strikes
explanation: The Samson Option is Israel's undeclared nuclear deterrence strategy — the threat of massive nuclear retaliation if Israel's existence is threatened (named after the biblical Samson who destroyed himself and his enemies). Israel maintains a policy of 'nuclear ambiguity' (neither confirming nor denying nuclear weapons). SIPRI estimates Israel has ~90 nuclear warheads.

question_text: Which country has the 'Iron Dome,' 'Arrow,' and 'David's Sling' missile defense systems — all activated during the Twelve-Day War 2025?
explanation: Israel operates a multi-layer missile defense: Iron Dome (short-range, 4-70 km rockets/mortars), David's Sling (medium-range, 40-300 km), and Arrow 2/3 (long-range, 100-2,400 km, ballistic missiles). During the Twelve-Day War (June 2025), all three layers were activated against Iran's Operation True Promise III (550+ ballistic missiles + 1,000+ drones). US also provided Patriot interceptors.

question_text: Which statement about India-Pakistan 2025 conflict is CORRECT?
option_a: India attacked Pakistan's regular army bases
option_b: Operation Sindoor targeted only JeM and LeT terrorist infrastructure
option_c: The ceasefire was mediated by China
option_d: Pakistan launched its operation before India did
explanation: Operation Sindoor (May 7, 2025) specifically targeted terrorist infrastructure of JeM and LeT — NOT Pakistani military or civilian targets. India emphasized this distinction. Pakistan's Operation Bunyan-um-Marsoos was a retaliation AFTER India's Sindoor. The ceasefire was reached on May 10, 2025, with US Secretary of State Rubio involved diplomatically.

question_text: Which of the following chronological sequences of Iran-related conflicts is CORRECT?
option_a: True Promise I → Twelve-Day War → True Promise III → 2026 Iran War
option_b: True Promise I (Apr 2024) → True Promise II (Oct 2024) → Twelve-Day War (Jun 2025) → 2026 Iran War (Feb 2026)
option_c: Twelve-Day War → True Promise III → True Promise I → 2026 Iran War
option_d: True Promise I → True Promise III → Twelve-Day War → 2026 Iran War
explanation: Correct sequence: Operation True Promise I (Iran's first direct attack on Israel, April 13-14, 2024) → Operation True Promise II (Iran's second attack, October 2024) → Twelve-Day War / Operation True Promise III (June 13-24, 2025) → 2026 Iran War (February 28, 2026 - ongoing with Pakistan-mediated ceasefire April 8, 2026).

question_text: The JCPOA (Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action) — Iran nuclear deal — was signed in 2015. When did the USA withdraw?
explanation: The JCPOA (Iran nuclear deal, P5+1 + EU + Iran) was signed in 2015 under Obama. Trump withdrew the USA in 2018 ('maximum pressure' policy). Iran then gradually exceeded JCPOA limits — enriching to 60% uranium purity (near weapons-grade of 90%). Biden tried but failed to revive JCPOA. JCPOA collapse led to escalation culminating in the Twelve-Day War (2025) and 2026 Iran War.

question_text: Which Swiss think tank assessed India's air superiority in Operation Sindoor forced Pakistan to seek ceasefire — and which institution tracks global nuclear arsenals?
option_a: CSS ETH Zürich (air superiority); SIPRI (nuclear arsenals)
explanation: CSS ETH Zürich (Center for Security Studies at Swiss Federal Institute of Technology) assessed India's air superiority in Operation Sindoor. SIPRI (Stockholm International Peace Research Institute) tracks global nuclear arsenals — as of 2025: Russia 5,459 warheads, USA 5,177, China ~500, Pakistan ~170, India ~172, Israel ~90, North Korea ~50.

question_text: The 2026 Iran War (started Feb 28, 2026) was described as starting DURING which process?
explanation: The 2026 Iran War notably began on February 28, 2026 DURING active Iran-US nuclear negotiations — making the timing highly controversial. Critics argued the attack violated diplomatic norms. The US and Israel launched coordinated strikes killing Supreme Leader Khamenei and multiple senior officials. Iran accused the US of 'bad faith' in negotiations.

question_text: India's stance during the Iran-US-Israel conflict was characterized as:
option_a: Strong support for USA and Israel
option_c: Neutral — engaging diplomatically with both sides
explanation: India maintained a neutral stance during the Iran-US-Israel conflict — using diplomacy to engage both sides. EAM Jaishankar met Iranian FM Araghchi in New Delhi (May 15, 2026) while India also maintained defense cooperation with Israel. India's interests: Chabahar Port (Iran), 8 million Indian diaspora in Gulf, energy imports. India abstained from UN votes on the conflict.

question_text: Which is the CORRECT match of military operation → date?
explanation: Correct: Twelve-Day War → June 13-24, 2025 ✓. Incorrect: Operation Sindoor → May 7, 2025 (not April 22 which was the Pahalgam attack), 2026 Iran War → February 28, 2026 (not March), Gaza Phase 1 ceasefire → January 15, 2025 (not March). Key dates to remember for AP HC exam.

question_text: Pakistan mediated the April 8, 2026 Iran-US ceasefire. What motivated Pakistan to take this role despite being under nuclear tension with India?
option_b: Pakistan has historically mediated all Middle East conflicts
option_c: Pakistan shares borders with Iran and has common Muslim identity plus interest in regional stability
explanation: Pakistan mediated the Iran-US ceasefire partly because: Pakistan shares a 900 km border with Iran, has common Muslim identity and historical ties, and benefits from regional stability (energy imports, trade). Pakistan also sought to project global diplomatic relevance after the India-Pakistan standoff of May 2025 weakened its international image.

question_text: Sudan's civil war (SAF vs RSF): Which major city fell to the RSF on October 27, 2025, after an 18-month siege?
explanation: El Fasher — capital of North Darfur state and the last major city under government (SAF) control in Darfur — fell to the RSF (Rapid Support Forces) on October 27, 2025, after an 18-month siege. This was a major RSF victory, extending their control over most of Darfur. ICG rated Sudan as the most likely conflict to escalate in 2026.

question_text: The Ukraine war saw Trump broker a 3-day ceasefire (May 9-11, 2026). US Secretary of State Rubio described the peace process as having:
option_a: Made significant progress with a permanent deal imminent
option_b: Stagnated — US mediation has not led to a fruitful outcome
option_d: Resulted in China joining as co-mediator
explanation: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said US mediation efforts on Ukraine have 'stagnated' and have not led to a 'fruitful outcome.' This contrasted with Trump's optimism ('the beginning of the end'). Putin suggested the war was 'coming to an end' (May 2026). The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) noted that ceasefires without enforcement mechanisms are unlikely to hold.

question_text: Russia officially recognized the Taliban government in Afghanistan on July 3, 2025 — becoming the first country to do so. What was Russia's strategic motivation?
option_b: Countering US influence and expanding Russian influence in Central Asia
option_d: Russian Orthodox Church expansion in Afghanistan
explanation: Russia recognized the Taliban (July 3, 2025) primarily to expand Russian influence in Central Asia and counter US interests. Russia sees Afghanistan as key to Central Asian geopolitics. Russia also wanted to prevent Afghanistan from becoming a safe haven for anti-Russian groups, and sought economic benefits including trade routes and energy projects.

question_text: Israel's PM during the Twelve-Day War (2025) and 2026 Iran War was:
explanation: Benjamin Netanyahu was Israel's PM during both the Twelve-Day War (June 2025) and the 2026 Iran War. Israel's key leaders: Netanyahu (PM), Israel Katz (Defense Minister), Eyal Zamir (IDF Chief of Staff). Netanyahu had been indicted by ICC in November 2024 for alleged war crimes in Gaza. He remained in office despite legal challenges.

question_text: The CENTCOM (US Central Command) commander during the 2026 Iran War was:
explanation: General Michael Kurilla commanded CENTCOM (US Central Command — responsible for Middle East, Central Asia, South Asia) during the 2026 Iran War. US chain of command: Pete Hegseth (Defense Secretary) → Dan Caine (Joint Chiefs Chairman) → Michael Kurilla (CENTCOM). CENTCOM HQ: Tampa, Florida with forward HQ at Al Udeid, Qatar.

question_text: The Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping (2023-2025) primarily targeted ships going through which waterway, disrupting global trade? [2025-2026 Rewrite v2]
option_b: Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait
explanation: Houthis targeted commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait — between Yemen (Africa-Arabian Peninsula) — disrupting 12-15% of global trade. Ships rerouted around Africa's Cape of Good Hope, adding 10-14 days and $1M+ per voyage. The Red Sea connects Suez Canal to Indian Ocean. Operation Poseidon Archer (US-UK) struck Houthi targets in Yemen in response.

question_text: What was the official US-Israel codename for the February 28, 2026 coordinated strike on Iran that killed Supreme Leader Khamenei?
explanation: Operation Epic Fury — coordinated US-Israel strike launched February 28, 2026 on Iran's leadership, nuclear, and missile infrastructure. Ayatollah Ali Khamenei (Supreme Leader since June 4, 1989) was killed on Day 1; former Majlis Speaker Ali Larijani also killed. The strike occurred DURING active US-Iran nuclear negotiations, generating diplomatic controversy. Followed by the Pakistan-mediated April 8 conditional ceasefire and failed Islamabad talks (Apr 11-12).

question_text: Just before Operation Epic Fury, India launched 'Operation Swadesh' to evacuate ~10,000 Indians from Iran. What primarily triggered the evacuation?
option_b: Mass civil unrest + economic collapse (rial at 42,000/USD, inflation 42%) from Dec 28, 2025
explanation: Operation Swadesh (Dec 2025-Jan 2026) was triggered by Iran's economic implosion — rial in free-fall (~42,000/USD), inflation breaching 42%, mass unrest erupting Dec 28, 2025. ~10,000 Indian nationals were airlifted via IAF C-17 Globemaster & C-130J Super Hercules plus Indian Navy ships from Chabahar/Bandar Abbas. It preceded the Feb 28, 2026 US-Israel Operation Epic Fury.

question_text: Ali Larijani, killed in Operation Epic Fury (Feb 28, 2026), held which prior position in Iran's political system?
explanation: Ali Larijani was a former Speaker of the Majlis (Iranian Parliament, 2008-2020) and a powerful conservative voice in the Islamic Republic. He was killed alongside Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei on Day 1 of Operation Epic Fury (Feb 28, 2026). The strike effectively decapitated Iran's senior political-religious leadership, on top of the military commanders already killed in the June 2025 Twelve-Day War.

question_text: The Pakistan-hosted US-Iran talks at Islamabad (April 11-12, 2026) collapsed primarily over which set of disputes?
option_b: US bases withdrawal demand, permanent nuclear dismantlement, $270B-$1T Iran reparations claim
explanation: The Islamabad talks (April 11-12, 2026) — convened after the April 8 conditional ceasefire — collapsed over three issues: (a) Iran's demand for full US withdrawal from Persian Gulf bases; (b) US insistence on permanent dismantlement of Iran's nuclear program; (c) Iran's $270 billion to $1 trillion reparations/damages claim from Operation Epic Fury destruction. Pakistan-mediated.

question_text: The Israel-Hezbollah War 2026 (parallel to the Iran War) erupted on which date?
explanation: The Israel-Hezbollah / Israel-Lebanon War 2026 erupted on March 2, 2026 — concurrent with the Iran War (Operation Epic Fury, Feb 28). 2,000+ killed in Lebanon; 1,000-1,900 Hezbollah fighters killed. Washington DC talks held April 14-15, 2026 leading to a 10-day ceasefire announced April 17, 2026. Israel struck Beirut again on May 7, 2026 killing the then-current Hezbollah leader.

question_text: The Israel-Lebanon 10-day ceasefire was announced on April 17, 2026 after talks held in which city?
explanation: The Israel-Lebanon ceasefire talks were held in Washington DC on April 14-15, 2026, leading to a 10-day ceasefire announced on April 17, 2026. The talks ran in parallel with the Pakistan-mediated Iran-US Islamabad talks (Apr 11-12 — which collapsed). Both arose from the same Feb 28, 2026 Israel-Iran escalation that engulfed Lebanon from March 2, 2026.

question_text: The Gaza Peace Council was inaugurated on January 22, 2026 at WEF Davos. Who chairs it?
option_c: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman
explanation: The Gaza Peace Council was inaugurated on January 22, 2026 at the 56th WEF Davos by US President Donald Trump, who chairs it. UNSC had authorised it on November 17, 2025. Director-General: Nickolay Mladenov (former UN Special Coordinator for Middle East Peace). Members include UAE, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan. India, China and Russia abstained, citing the lack of direct Palestinian Authority participation.

question_text: Which countries notably abstained from joining the Gaza Peace Council (inaugurated Jan 22, 2026)?
explanation: India, China and Russia abstained from joining the Gaza Peace Council, citing sovereignty concerns and the need for direct Palestinian Authority participation. India's abstention reflected its long-standing two-state stance and its 1974 status as the first non-Arab country to recognise the PLO. UAE, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and other US-aligned Sunni-Arab states joined.

question_text: On March 30, 2026, Israel's Knesset passed which controversial law targeting Palestinian convicts?
option_a: Lifetime exile to a third country
option_b: Mandatory death penalty for Palestinians convicted of attacks on Israeli citizens
explanation: On March 30, 2026, the Knesset passed a law imposing the MANDATORY death penalty on Palestinians convicted of attacking Israeli citizens — a sharp escalation from Israel's earlier discretionary use of capital punishment. The law came amid the Israel-Lebanon War and faced strong international criticism. Israel had also demolished the UNRWA HQ in East Jerusalem's Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood in February 2026.

question_text: On December 26, 2025, Israel became the FIRST country in the world to recognise which long-unrecognised African breakaway state?
explanation: On December 26, 2025, Israel became the first country to officially recognise Somaliland — which had declared independence from Somalia on May 18, 1991 (after fall of Siad Barre) but had spent 35 years unrecognised. Strategic rationale: Berbera Port on the Gulf of Aden / Red Sea — countering Houthi maritime threats and Bab el-Mandeb security. Ethiopia had earlier signed a 2024 MoU for Berbera sea access.

question_text: 'Operation Hunter' (January 10, 2026) was a US military operation in which country, conducted in cooperation with that country's new post-Assad government?
explanation: Operation Hunter (Jan 10, 2026) — US strikes on ISIS strongholds in Syria, conducted in cooperation with the new Syrian government of President Ahmed al-Shara (HTS-led, in power since Bashar al-Assad's ouster in December 2024). It was part of a Trump 2.0 'hard power before diplomacy' sequence: Dec 25-26 Nigeria/Sokoto strikes vs Boko Haram + ISIS-WA; Dec 30 Saudi strikes on Mukulla port (Yemen); Jan 3 Operation Absolute Strike (Venezuela); Jan 10 Operation Hunter (Syria).

question_text: Saudi Arabia's December 30, 2025 air strikes on which Yemeni port targeted the Southern Transitional Council (STC) forces?
explanation: On December 30, 2025, Saudi Arabia conducted air strikes on Mukulla port (Yemen) against Southern Transitional Council (STC) forces — a Houthi-related escalation in Yemen's long-running multi-sided civil war. The Saudi action came alongside US-UK Operation Poseidon Archer (against Houthis in north-west Yemen) and reflected the fragmentation of Yemeni anti-Houthi forces.

question_text: On January 7, 2026, President Trump signed an executive order withdrawing the US from how many international bodies in a single day — the largest such withdrawal in US history?
explanation: On January 7, 2026, Trump's executive order withdrew the US from 66 international bodies simultaneously — the largest single-day multilateral withdrawal in US history. Notable exits: International Solar Alliance (ISA, India-France led), IPCC, UN ECOSOC, UNFPA. Earlier exits (since Jan 20, 2025): WHO and Paris Agreement (Day 1), UNHRC, UNESCO. This dismantled US presence in global climate and development governance.

question_text: Trump's January 2026 Greenland annexation overtures provoked a joint condemnation from how many EU countries plus the UK?
explanation: Trump's January 2026 push to annex Greenland (a Danish autonomous territory of strategic Arctic value — minerals + sea routes) drew a joint condemnation from 8 EU countries plus the UK. Trump retaliated with a 10% additional tariff on countries opposing the annexation talks. The Trans-Atlantic deal froze on Jan 13, 2026 after a 25-minister meeting failed.

question_text: The 'Coalition of the Willing' on Ukraine security guarantees was convened in Paris on January 6, 2026 — led by which leader, after Trump tilted toward bilateral Russia talks?
explanation: French President Emmanuel Macron led the Paris 'Coalition of the Willing' on January 6, 2026 to provide security guarantees to Ukraine — building an alternative architecture as the US under Trump pursued a bilateral track with Russia. Participants: France, UK, Germany, Italy, Poland, Nordics, Baltics, Canada, Australia. Absent: USA, Hungary (Orbán still PM at the time), Slovakia.

question_text: The New START treaty — the last US-Russia nuclear arms control treaty — expired on which date in 2026, leaving no binding strategic arms cap for the first time since 1972?
explanation: New START expired on February 5, 2026 — for the first time since 1972 (SALT-I era), no binding US-Russia strategic arms control treaty exists. Signed at Prague (April 2010) by Obama and Medvedev, it had capped each side at 1,550 deployed strategic warheads + 700 deployed delivery systems. Russia had suspended participation in Feb 2023. Restart talks held in Abu Dhabi (UAE-mediated) produced no breakthrough.

question_text: Bangladesh held its first general election after Sheikh Hasina's August 2024 ouster on February 18, 2026. Which party won, and how many of 300 seats?
explanation: Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) won a landslide victory of 209 of 300 seats (70% majority) in the February 18, 2026 general election—Bangladesh's first election after the August 5, 2024 ouster of PM Sheikh Hasina (after 16 years in office). Awami League (AL) was BANNED from contesting—the first exclusion of a major party from elections since Bangladesh's 1971 independence—citing AL's responsibility for the July 2024 Gen-Z-led mass uprising that killed ~1,400 protesters in police crackdowns (July 16-August 5). The interim government, led by Muhammad Yunus (Nobel Prize 2006, microfinance pioneer), managed 6-month democratic transition. BNP's victory reflected: (a) anti-Hasina backlash (corruption allegations, 16 years authoritarian rule, extrajudicial killings); (b) pro-Islamic voter sentiment (BNP's Jamaat-e-Islami ally received ministerial positions); (c) younger generation's demand for democratic accountability. For India: the BNP victory raised concerns—BNP historically tilt pro-Pakistan, advocate closer Islamic ties, and oppose India-centric policies. Key India-Bangladesh issues: (a) Hindu minority protection (Hindus 8% of population, ~2,600 documented attacks post-Hasina ouster); (b) Teesta water-sharing treaty (pending 20+ years); (c) border terrorism via Rohingya camps; (d) maritime boundary disputes (Saint Martin Island). BNP's coalition with Jamaat-e-Islami (designated terrorist by India for 2008 Mumbai attack links) alarmed New Delhi. India's response: cautious engagement, monitoring minority rights, securing maritime boundaries. Bangladesh's transition from Hasina's quasi-authoritarian rule to BNP's Islamic-tilted democracy represented a significant shift in South Asian geopolitics.

question_text: Who was sworn in as Bangladesh's new Prime Minister on February 17, 2026 — the son of late PM Khaleda Zia and BNP founder Ziaur Rahman?
explanation: Tarek Rahman was sworn in as Bangladesh's new PM on February 17, 2026 by President Mohammed Shahabuddin. Son of Khaleda Zia (late former PM) and Ziaur Rahman (BNP founder & former President), he had been in UK exile since 2008. His prior in-absentia convictions were overturned by the Yunus interim government. India's concerns: Hindu minorities (~8% pop., 2,600+ documented attacks since Aug 2024), BNP's traditional pro-Pakistan tilt, Teesta water-sharing agreement.

question_text: Min Aung Hlaing was elected President of Myanmar on April 9, 2026 in a junta-managed election. How many votes did he secure out of 584?
explanation: Min Aung Hlaing—the junta chief (Senior General) who orchestrated Myanmar's February 1, 2021 coup (claiming election fraud despite Aung San Suu Kyi's NLD's landslide 2020 victory)—was 'elected' President with 429 of 584 votes in a heavily controlled April 9, 2026 'election.' Yi Win was appointed new Army Chief, consolidating junta succession. The election was widely condemned as illegitimate: (a) Parliament dominated by military-appointed members (25% reserved seats) and Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP, military's civilian façade); (b) opposition parties (NLD) banned; (c) no international observers; (d) opposition leaders (Aung San Suu Kyi, Win Myint) imprisoned for politically-motivated charges; (e) voting in war zones under military control impossible due to active combat. Myanmar's civil war (Feb 2021-May 2026): 90,000+ battle deaths, 3+ million internally displaced, 1+ million fled abroad. Opposing forces: Tatmadaw (junta military, 400,000+ troops), PDF (People's Defence Force, anti-junta militia, 100,000+ fighters), 150+ ethnic armed organizations. For India: Myanmar's junta 'election' indicated consolidation of Beijing-backed authoritarian rule (Min Aung Hlaing visiting Beijing multiple times since 2021), exclusion of India from Myanmar's strategic calculus, and deterioration of India-Myanmar relations post-coup. India's BIMSTEC coordination collapsed. Northeast India border security threats persisted due to rebel bases in Myanmar. The 2026 'election' formally ended any international pretense of legitimate governance transition—Myanmar joined authoritarian axis (Russia, Belarus, North Korea). International sanctions (US, EU, UK, Canada) remained ineffective; Myanmar's isolation deepened, pushing it fully into Chinese orbit (BRI, strategic dependence).

question_text: Nepal's 47th Prime Minister Balendra Shah ('Balen') was sworn in on March 27, 2026 at age 35 — Nepal's youngest ever PM. The previous day's protests against KP Sharma Oli's September 2025 crackdown reportedly killed how many?
explanation: Balen Shah — civil engineer + rapper + former Kathmandu Mayor — sworn in as Nepal's 47th PM on March 27, 2026 at 35 (youngest ever). The September 2025 Gen-Z protests (sparked by a social media ban and economic stagnation) faced lethal force authorised by then-PM KP Sharma Oli; 76 were killed in the crackdown. Oli was arrested on March 28, 2026 (the day after Balen's swearing-in).

question_text: India formally objected on January 9, 2026 to Chinese infrastructure construction in which Pakistan-Occupied territory ceded by Pakistan to China under the 1963 Sino-Pakistan Boundary Agreement?
explanation: India formally objected on January 9, 2026 to Beijing's infrastructure construction in the Shaksgam Valley (Trans-Karakoram Tract)—5,180 sq km of erstwhile Jammu & Kashmir territory that Pakistan illegally ceded to China under the March 2, 1963 Sino-Pakistan Boundary Agreement (signed between Chinese Foreign Minister Zhou Enlai and Pakistani FM Z.A. Bhutto). India rejects the 1963 agreement as null and void—same legal position applied to China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) infrastructure in Gilgit-Baltistan. The 1963 agreement was signed without India's consent despite J&K's legal sovereignty (India-China war 1962 context prevented India's participation). Shaksgam's cession involved 5,180 sq km of high-altitude trans-Himalayan plateau (3,600+ m elevation, uninhabited, glaciated) connecting Xinjiang to Gilgit. China's infrastructure projects (post-2024 LAC disengagement accord) included: roads, surveillance posts, communication networks, suggesting Beijing's preparation for long-term occupation consolidation. India's January 2026 objection reaffirmed: (a) India's constitutional claim to J&K (Constitution Article 370); (b) rejection of unilateral territorial cession by Pakistan (which India treats as incomplete/provisional); (c) India's commitment to resolving territorial disputes bilaterally via Simla Agreement (1972) framework, not third-party involvement. The objection occurred despite India-China October 2024 LAC disengagement (Depsang, Demchok) and 2025 Modi-Xi handshake at Kazan BRICS Summit—indicating India's strategic differentiation: LAC peace vs. broader territorial claim maintenance. Pakistan's 1963 cession was Pakistan's attempt to resolve Sino-Pakistani disputes (similar to 1949 Karachi Agreement with China on border) while facing India's superior claims under UN's decolonization principle (India's J&K inheritance from British-era princely states).

question_text: India-China border trade resumed via the Lipulekh Pass (Uttarakhand) in April 2026 — ending a freeze that had lasted how many years?
explanation: India-China border trade via the Lipulekh Pass (Uttarakhand, 3,680 m elevation, Kumaon Himalayas) resumed in April 2026—ending a 64-year freeze dating back to the October-November 1962 Sino-Indian War (NEFA campaign, Ladakh front). The Lipulekh trade route historically connected Garhwal (India) to Tibet (Kailas, Mansarovar region) via ancient salt/wool caravan networks; closure following the 1962 war represented the most prolonged closure of India-China border trade in modern history. The April 2026 resumption was symbolic reconstruction of diplomatic normalization following: (a) October 2024 LAC (Line of Actual Control) disengagement agreement on Depsang and Demchok sectors (de-escalation of forward positions, disputed since 2020 Galwan clash); (b) May 2025 Modi-Xi handshake at Kazan BRICS Summit (first positive engagement post-2020); (c) Resolution of bilateral military tensions (withdrawal of force concentrations, de-escalation protocols). The trade resumption was accompanied by: (a) reopening of Kailash Mansarovar Yatra (pilgrimage route via Lipulekh, suspended 2020-2024, ~5,000 annual pilgrims); (b) institutional frameworks (Joint Working Group on borders, confidence-building measures); (c) economic spillovers (limited, ~USD 136B bilateral trade remains far below potential due to persistent border disputes). Operationally, the April 2026 opening involved: reconstruction of 40 km of trade route via Lipulekh, establishment of border customs posts, and phased merchant traffic (initial 100 traders/month). Politically, the resumption signaled India-China's managed rivalry model—compartmentalizing economic cooperation while maintaining security standoff on disputed borders (Arunachal Pradesh, Ladakh, Sikkim). The Kailash Mansarovar resumption particularly held religious-cultural significance: the Mansarovar lake sacred in Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism; pilgrimage cessation had angered Indian Hindu constituencies. The trade's symbolic and economic insignificance (compared to 2020-2024 military tensions) suggested border normalization remained fragile—contingent on sustained diplomatic management.

question_text: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2025 was awarded for which discovery foundational to quantum computing?
option_a: Detection of gravitational waves using LIGO
option_b: Macroscopic quantum mechanical tunnelling and energy quantisation in electric circuits
option_c: Observation of the Higgs boson at CERN
explanation: Nobel Physics 2025: John Clarke, Michel H. Devoret, and John M. Martinis — for macroscopic quantum mechanical tunnelling and energy quantisation in electric circuits. This foundational work enabled superconducting qubit-based quantum computers, the most practical approach to quantum computing today. Martinis led Google's quantum team that achieved 'quantum supremacy' in 2019 using the Sycamore processor — performing calculations in 200 seconds that would take classical computers ~10,000 years. This award reflects the global race in quantum computing where nations like India are investing heavily (IIT Delhi, CSIR labs launching quantum research centres by 2026). The 2025 Physics Nobel underscores how quantum technology will shape 21st-century computing globally. Nobel Physics 2024: Hopfield & Hinton (AI/neural networks).

question_text: Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2025 was awarded for the development of which ultra-porous crystalline materials?
explanation: Nobel Chemistry 2025: Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson, and Omar M. Yaghi — for developing metal-organic frameworks (MOFs). MOFs represent a breakthrough in materials science with the highest surface area per gram of any known material (~7,000 m²/g — larger than a football field in a single gram). Applications span critical global challenges: CO2 capture for climate action, hydrogen storage for clean fuel cells, water harvesting from desert air (particularly relevant for India's water security challenges), medical drug delivery, and environmental remediation. Omar Yaghi (UC Berkeley, Syrian-American) coined 'reticular chemistry' — the science of linking molecular building blocks into extended frameworks. India's Institute of Technology Delhi (IIT Delhi) and other research centres are developing MOF applications for air purification and water treatment in urban areas. This chemistry award exemplifies how fundamental science drives solutions to planetary challenges. Yaghi's work bridges continents — Kitagawa (Kyoto University, Japan) and Robson (University of Melbourne, Australia) represent Asia-Pacific's role in materials science.

question_text: Nobel Prize in Physiology/Medicine 2025 was awarded for the discovery of which immune cells that prevent autoimmune diseases?
explanation: Nobel Medicine 2025: Mary E. Brunkow, Fred Ramsdell, and Shimon Sakaguchi — for discovering regulatory T cells (Tregs) and their critical role in preventing autoimmune diseases. Tregs express the FOXP3 transcription factor and act as 'immune brakes' to prevent the body's immune system from attacking its own tissues. Mutations in FOXP3 cause IPEX (Immune dysregulation, Polyendocrinopathy, Enteropathy, X-linked) syndrome — a severe condition. This discovery opened new therapeutic avenues for treating autoimmune diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, Type 1 diabetes) — significant health concerns in India affecting millions. Treg-targeted therapies are now in clinical trials globally. Sakaguchi's work (Osaka University) demonstrated that depleting Tregs leads to autoimmunity, while boosting Tregs prevents it. This Nobel recognises how fundamental immunology discoveries translate to treating chronic inflammatory conditions. The recognition also highlights Japan's leadership in immunology research alongside American and international contributions. Nobel Medicine 2024: Ambros & Ruvkun (microRNA discovery in gene regulation).

question_text: Which Hungarian author won the Nobel Prize in Literature 2025 for 'compelling and visionary oeuvre that reaffirms the power of art amid apocalyptic terror'?
explanation: Nobel Literature 2025: László Krasznahorkai (Hungary) — for his 'compelling and visionary oeuvre that, in the midst of apocalyptic terror, reaffirms the power of art.' His masterpiece 'Satantango' (1985) uses innovative 12-chapter structure mimicking Argentine tango (6 steps forward + 6 back), set in a decaying Hungarian collective farm post-communism. The novel explores despair, salvation, and human ambition through long, hypnotic prose. Director Béla Tarr adapted it into a monumental 7.5-hour film (1994) considered one of cinema's greatest achievements. Krasznahorkai's work reflects Central European existential philosophy — themes of state collapse, individual powerlessness, and art's redemptive potential resonate globally. His 2025 Nobel recognition celebrates Hungarian literature's global significance alongside the same year's Booker Prize winner David Szalay (Hungarian-British), making 2025 a banner year for Hungarian letters. Krasznahorkai's themes of institutional breakdown and moral uncertainty are studied in universities worldwide, influencing contemporary writers beyond Europe. His recognition affirms how Eastern European voices challenge Western literary dominance. Nobel Literature 2024: Han Kang (South Korea, first Korean to win).

question_text: The Nobel Peace Prize 2025 was awarded to Maria Corina Machado for her democratic struggle in which country?
explanation: Nobel Peace Prize 2025: Maria Corina Machado (Venezuela) — for 'tireless work promoting democratic rights for the people of Venezuela and her struggle to achieve a just and peaceful transition from dictatorship to democracy.' Machado is the face of Venezuelan opposition against Nicolás Maduro's 25-year authoritarian rule. Despite winning the 2024 opposition presidential primary with overwhelming support, she was barred from candidacy by Maduro's regime using arbitrary legal disqualifications — a hallmark of autocratic suppression. She continues leading her 'Vente Venezuela' movement from exile while maintaining communications with supporters inside the country. Venezuela's humanitarian crisis has displaced over 7.7 million refugees globally, including to India and other South Asian nations. The Nobel award recognises her non-violent resistance and commitment to restoring democratic institutions. Her struggle exemplifies global democracy defenders facing authoritarian oppression — similar to contemporary challenges in Myanmar, Iran, and elsewhere. The award validates civil society resistance and international solidarity with democratic movements. Nobel Peace Prize 2024: Nihon Hidankyo (Japanese atomic bomb survivors advocacy). Nobel Peace Prize 2023: Narges Mohammadi (Iran's women's rights, jailed).

question_text: Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences 2025 was awarded for research on innovation-driven growth and 'creative destruction.' Who were the laureates?
option_a: Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson, James Robinson
option_b: Claudia Goldin, Lawrence Katz, Lawrence Summers
option_c: Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion, Peter Howitt
option_d: Paul Romer, Robert Lucas, Robert Barro
explanation: Nobel Economics 2025: Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion, and Peter Howitt — for explaining how technological innovation drives long-term economic growth. Mokyr (Northwestern University) conducted historical analysis tracing technological breakthroughs and institutional conditions enabling innovation across centuries — showing how the Industrial Revolution emerged from specific social structures. Aghion & Howitt developed 'endogenous growth' theory with 'creative destruction' — new innovations render older products/technologies obsolete while creating new markets and employment, driving sustained GDP growth. This framework explains why countries investing in R&D (like India's increasing CSIR and startup ecosystem investments) experience higher long-term productivity. The award underscores innovation's centrality to development economics — relevant to India's tech startup boom, IT services sector, and emerging manufacturing. Their work validates public investment in education and research infrastructure as drivers of prosperity. Nobel Economics 2024: Acemoglu, Johnson, Robinson (institutions & prosperity). The 2025 award celebrates how innovation systems shape national development trajectories.

question_text: Nobel Chemistry 2025 laureate Omar M. Yaghi is known as the father of which branch of chemistry?
explanation: Omar M. Yaghi (UC Berkeley) pioneered and named 'reticular chemistry' — the science of linking organic and inorganic molecular building blocks (linkers and nodes) into extended crystalline porous frameworks via strong chemical bonds. This controlled-architecture approach creates materials with unprecedented properties. His metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) can hold 200 times more hydrogen than steel cylinders at identical pressure — critical for hydrogen fuel storage in vehicles. Yaghi's reticular chemistry has enabled MOFs to capture CO2 from industrial emissions and even directly from ambient air — urgent climate change applications. His work demonstrates how fundamental chemistry discoveries translate to solving global challenges. Yaghi's Nobel win (shared with Kitagawa, Kyoto University; Robson, University of Melbourne) represents international scientific collaboration. The award recognises how 'molecular engineering' creates designer materials with precisely controlled pore sizes, chemical affinities, and functionalities for applications from water purification to pharmaceutical manufacturing. His recognition elevates reticular chemistry as a defining 21st-century materials science field. The 2025 Chemistry Nobel celebrates how human-designed porous materials outperform nature in specific applications.

question_text: László Krasznahorkai's Nobel-winning novel 'Satantango' has a unique structure. What is distinctive about its 12 chapters?
option_b: 6 forward + 6 backward chapters mimicking tango steps
option_c: 12 chapters each told by a different character
option_d: Alternates between past and future timelines
explanation: Krasznahorkai's 'Satantango' (1985) features an ingenious structural mirror: 12 chapters composed as 6 forward + 6 backward — directly mirroring the Argentine tango's choreographic pattern of six steps forward followed by six steps backward. This structural parallelism between dance movement and narrative structure creates a unique reading experience — the second half reverses and recontextualises earlier scenes. Set in a decaying Hungarian collective farm in the post-communist 1980s, the novel captures societal collapse, moral corruption, and individual desperation through this dance-like narrative rhythm. Director Béla Tarr's acclaimed film adaptation (1994) stretches to 7.5 hours, becoming a cinema landmark through its static camera shots and deliberate pacing that mirrors the novel's meditative density. The tango structure symbolises how history repeats in cycles — forward progress inevitably followed by retreat, mirroring Hungary's 20th-century oscillations between authoritarian regimes. Krasznahorkai's formal innovation demonstrates how narrative structure embodies philosophical content — a signature of contemporary literary excellence. The Nobel Literature 2025 recognition affirmed how Eastern European experimental fiction challenges conventional storytelling globally. The novel's structure influenced contemporary authors exploring cyclical and non-linear narratives.

question_text: The Nobel Peace Prize is uniquely awarded in which city, unlike the other Nobel Prizes given in Stockholm?
explanation: The Nobel Peace Prize is uniquely awarded in Oslo, Norway by the Norwegian Nobel Committee — the only Nobel Prize distinguished by its geographic separation. All other Nobel Prizes (Physics, Chemistry, Medicine/Physiology, Literature, Economics) are awarded in Stockholm, Sweden by Swedish institutions. This geopolitical distinction reflects Alfred Nobel's 1895 will and his deliberate choice to award peace separately through Norwegian governance — reflecting Scandinavia's historical commitment to arbitration and conflict resolution. The ceremony at Oslo's Oslo City Hall represents Norway's soft power projection and emphasises that peace-making is a distinct endeavour from scientific/literary achievement. Recipients are invited to deliver the Nobel Peace Lecture — a global platform amplifying their causes and message. The Oslo setting symbolises Scandinavian neutrality and international cooperation. This institutional separation has given the Peace Prize unique gravitas and symbolic weight in international diplomacy. Nobel Peace 2025: Maria Corina Machado (Venezuela, democratic opposition). Nobel Peace 2024: Nihon Hidankyo (Japanese atomic bomb survivors' peace advocacy). India has produced Peace Prize winners: Kailash Satyarthi (2014, child labour), Rabindranath Tagore (1913, poet/philosopher), Motilal Nehru and Gandhi (nominated multiple times, Gandhi controversially never won). The Peace Prize's Oslo location emphasises universal values transcending national boundaries.

question_text: Nobel Physics 2025 laureate John M. Martinis led which tech company's team to claim 'quantum supremacy' in 2019?
explanation: John M. Martinis led Google's quantum computing division whose Sycamore processor claimed 'quantum supremacy' in 2019 — a watershed moment when a quantum computer performed a specific calculation in 200 seconds that leading classical supercomputers would require ~10,000 years to solve. This demonstrated quantum computing's potential advantage over classical computing for certain problem classes. Martinis' foundational work on superconducting qubits (quantum bits) and their energy quantisation made this breakthrough possible. His Nobel Physics 2025 recognition (shared with John Clarke and Michel H. Devoret) honours the theoretical underpinnings enabling practical quantum computers. Superconducting qubits operate at near absolute zero (millikelvins), exploiting quantum tunnelling — particles passing through energy barriers classically forbidden. This quantum advantage has profound implications for cryptography, drug discovery, materials science, and optimisation problems. India is rapidly building quantum computing capabilities (IIT Delhi, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research launching quantum centres) recognising that quantum technology will reshape global computing and cybersecurity. Google's quantum leadership represents American tech dominance in next-generation computing, while other nations (China with Jiuzhang, IBM with quantum services) pursue parallel approaches. The 2025 Physics Nobel affirms quantum computing's transition from theoretical physics to practical engineering.

question_text: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) — subject of Nobel Chemistry 2025 — are being tested for which crucial climate application?
explanation: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), honoured in Nobel Chemistry 2025, represent a transformative solution for CO2 capture — a critical climate change mitigation technology. MOFs' exceptional properties make them ideal for this application: their ultra-high surface area (up to 7,000 m²/g, equivalent to an American football field compressed into a gram) can adsorb vast amounts of CO2 from industrial flue gases and directly from ambient air. Point-source capture (factory emissions) and direct air capture (DAC) are both viable pathways. Several MOF-based CO2 capture systems are transitioning from laboratories to pilot plants worldwide. Beyond climate applications, MOFs excel in complementary challenges: water harvesting from desert and arid air (relevant to India's water security in drought-prone regions), hydrogen storage for clean fuel cells in transport decarbonisation, pharmaceutical drug delivery optimising bioavailability, and environmental remediation of contaminated water. The 2025 Nobel Chemistry recognition validates MOFs as foundational to climate solutions. India's CSIR laboratories are exploring MOF applications for air purification and water treatment in urban areas. The award signifies how fundamental materials science directly addresses planetary challenges — climate change, water scarcity, energy transition. MOF technologies represent humanity's technological response to existential environmental threats.

question_text: The 2025 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences was the Sveriges Riksbank Prize. How does it differ from the original Nobel Prizes?
option_a: It is awarded only to European economists
option_b: It was established in 1968 in memory of Alfred Nobel, not part of original 1895 will
option_d: It is awarded every two years
explanation: The Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences (formally 'Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel') was established in 1968 by Sweden's Riksbank (central bank) — significantly, it was NOT part of Alfred Nobel's original 1895 will. The original five Nobel Prizes (Physics, Chemistry, Medicine/Physiology, Literature, Peace) were endowed by Alfred Nobel's testament. The Economics Prize was added later, reflecting 20th-century recognition of economics' importance to human society. The first Economics Prize was awarded in 1969 to Ragnar Frisch (Norway) and Jan Tinbergen (Netherlands) for developing econometric models. By 2025, the Economics Prize carries equal prestige and monetary value (~10 million SEK) as other Nobels, though technically it remains a separate institution. This historical distinction highlights how awards evolve to reflect changing disciplinary prominence. India has produced Economics laureates: Amartya Sen (1998, development economics and poverty), Abhijit Banerjee (2019, poverty alleviation), and Esther Duflo (2019 co-winner, from MIT). The 2025 Economics Prize honouring Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion, and Peter Howitt recognised innovation-driven growth — relevant to India's development trajectory and STEM innovation investment. The prize's evolution demonstrates how international recognition adapts to emerging knowledge domains.

question_text: Beyoncé won Album of the Year at the 67th Grammy Awards (February 2025) for which album — her first ever AOTY win?
explanation: 67th Grammy Awards (February 2, 2025, Crypto.com Arena, Los Angeles): Beyoncé achieved a long-overdue milestone winning Album of the Year for 'Cowboy Carter' — a country-crossover album and her FIRST Grammy Album of the Year award despite receiving a record number of nominations throughout her career. The win ended decades of speculation about whether the Grammys would finally give her the industry's highest honour. She also won Best Country Album and Best Country Duo/Group Performance, cementing her crossover into country music. 'Cowboy Carter' (2024) represents Beyoncé's artistic evolution, drawing on country music traditions often historically excluded from by African American artists. The album reclaims country music heritage and includes production innovation. This win carried cultural significance beyond music — recognition of Black artists in traditionally white-dominated country genre. The ceremony was delayed one day (from Feb 1) due to devastating Los Angeles wildfires of January 2025, showcasing the event's adaptability during crises. Beyoncé holds the all-time record for most Grammy nominations by any artist (32+ nominations). Her AOTY win validated decades of creative excellence and cultural impact. The award demonstrated Grammy recognition evolving toward historic correction — acknowledging overlooked achievements by one of music's greatest artists.

question_text: Kendrick Lamar won 5 out of 5 nominations at the 67th Grammys 2025, sweeping with which diss track targeting Drake?
explanation: 67th Grammy Awards (February 2025): Kendrick Lamar executed a historic clean sweep, winning ALL 5 nominations with 'Not Like Us' — a diss track in the highly publicised rap feud targeting Drake. The five Grammy wins were: Record of the Year, Song of the Year, Best Rap Song, Best Rap Performance, and Best Music Video. This perfect sweep demonstrated critical and commercial validation of Lamar's artistry and competitive prowess in hip-hop. 'Not Like Us' became a cultural phenomenon and streaming mega-hit, dominating charts globally. Lamar's Grammy dominance reflected his standing as hip-hop's preeminent artist of the 2020s. He subsequently performed 'Not Like Us' at the Super Bowl LIX halftime show (February 9, 2025) in New Orleans — amplifying the track before a 100+ million global audience. Serena Williams appeared in the halftime audience, underscoring celebrity-calibre draw.
