For India: (1) QUAD coordination — Lee's Democratic Party is traditionally less hawkish on North Korea than conservatives; Lee's inauguration (May 10, 2025) meant the first Democratic president in QUAD in years. However, Lee maintained US alliance and QUAD commitment, (2) Defense cooperation — Lee visited India April 19-21, 2026, launching India-Korea Special Strategic Partnership with $54B bilateral trade target, semiconductor/shipbuilding MoUs, showcasing Lee's commitment to India ties despite his centrist positioning, (3) North Korea policy — Lee's more dialogue-oriented North Korea approach (vs. conservative hawkishness) potentially eases Korean Peninsula tensions, benefiting India's regional stability interests and energy security (Korean Peninsula conflict could disrupt regional supply chains). For India-South Korea partnership, Lee's presidency opened new opportunities in AI, green energy, and defense manufacturing cooperation announced during his India visit.

question_text: In Japan's political system, the PM is selected by both chambers of the National Diet. Sanae Takaichi led which coalition?
explanation: Sanae Takaichi became Japan's PM (October 21, 2025) leading an LDP (Liberal Democratic Party) + Japan Innovation Party coalition. The LDP had traditionally partnered with Komeito (Buddhist-affiliated party) since 1999, but following the 2024 LDP internal elections and funding scandals that weakened LDP discipline, Takaichi shifted coalition strategy. She won the LDP leadership election in 2025 defeating Shinjirō Koizumi. The Japan Innovation Party (Nippon Ishin, known for regional decentralization focus, popular in Kansai region) offered Takaichi stronger legislative support (both chambers) than the declining Komeito. Strategic significance for India: Japan's coalition shift reflects domestic political realignment affecting Indo-Pacific strategy. For India: (1) Coalition stability — Takaichi's LDP-Ishin coalition requires careful management of divergent agendas; this could slow domestic policy changes but strengthen Japan's external commitments (QUAD, India partnerships) as international engagement transcends domestic coalition friction, (2) QUAD stability — Takaichi's hawkish defense posture is aligned across both coalition partners (both favor stronger military), ensuring Japan's QUAD participation remains bipartisan-stable, (3) India-Japan ties — Takaichi visited India January 12-13, 2026 (her first official Asian trip), signing 19 MoUs worth EUR 1.24B under Green and Sustainable Development Partnership (GSDP). The coalition's defense focus strengthens India-Japan defense industrial cooperation. For Japan-India partnership, coalition politics don't undermine India ties — both LDP and Ishin prioritize US alliance, QUAD membership, and China containment, aligning with India's strategic interests.

question_text: The 2026 FIFA World Cup will feature 48 teams for the first time. How many teams played in previous World Cups (since 1998)?
explanation: FIFA World Cups from 1998-2022 featured 32 teams (8 groups of 4). The 2026 World Cup (USA-Canada-Mexico, first 3-nation hosted tournament) expands to 48 teams — restructured as either 16 groups of 3 teams or 12 groups of 4, TBD by FIFA. This represents a 50% expansion intended to include more nations, but critics warn it dilutes tournament quality (more mismatches, weaker teams). Strategic significance for India: Global football expansion affects India's football development strategy. For India: (1) India's football gap — India's national team (FIFA ranking ~117, 1,500+ points) has NEVER qualified for FIFA World Cup finals despite having 1.4B+ population; the 48-team expansion mathematically improves India's qualification chances, (2) Qualifying pathway — For 2026, AFC (Asian Football Confederation) has 8.5 spots (out of 48); India faces 45 Asian teams competing for these spots; with 48-team format creating more predictable group dynamics, India's qualification route becomes feasible if India maintains consistent Elo rating improvement, (3) Youth development — Global World Cup expansion incentivizes youth football investment in emerging nations; India's football academies (Indian Super League, SAI programs) benefit from expanded World Cup pathways, (4) Economic opportunity — World Cup qualification boosts national team revenue, sponsorships, and domestic league growth (see how Morocco's 2022 semi-final run elevated African football investment). For India's football ambitions, 2026 World Cup expansion represents an inflection point: if India qualifies, it catalyzes football's transformation from niche sport to mainstream in India. FIFA World Cup 2022: Qatar hosted (first Middle East, first November-December winter timing); Argentina won (3rd title after 1978, 1986). 2026 will be the first 3-nation hosted World Cup in history, expanding the tournament's global footprint.

question_text: Which Indian city was ranked as the world's most populous urban area in 2025 by the United Nations?
explanation: Delhi National Capital Region (NCR) was ranked the world's most populous urban area in 2025 by UN Habitat — surpassing Tokyo (previous #1). Delhi NCR's metropolitan population: 33+ million in city proper (within Delhi municipal corporation), 35+ million in Greater Delhi NCR (including suburban districts in Haryana, Uttar Pradesh). Tokyo's population declined to ~32M due to Japan's shrinking demographics. Note: Jakarta's measurement at ~42M reflects Greater Jakarta (Jabodetabek) including suburban zones; different methodologies (city proper vs. metropolitan area) produce variations in rankings. Strategic significance for India: Delhi's status as world's most populous urban area reflects India's demographic scale and urbanization pace. For India: (1) Infrastructure pressure — Delhi's 35M+ population strains water supply (Yamuna depletion, groundwater extraction dropping aquifers 2-3m/year), transport (metro expansion ongoing, pollution crises in winter), waste management (landfill crisis), housing (migrant slums proliferating), (2) Climate vulnerability — Delhi faces heat stress intensifying (52°C+ summer peaks by 2025); rapid urbanization in semi-arid region exacerbates heat island effects. Delhi's ranking validates India's climate action urgency — urban heat mitigation becomes critical for 35M people's survival, (3) Development model — Delhi as world's largest metropolitan area by population (not GDP or economic output) reveals India's development challenge: massive population without proportional GDP/job generation. Policy priority shifts to job creation, skills training, livelihood diversification for Delhi's labor-surplus, capital-sparse economy. For India's urbanization strategy, Delhi's #1 global ranking validates investment in metro systems, smart city infrastructure, affordable housing — critical for managing growth humanely. Delhi's ranking also strengthens India's voice in global urban development forums, positioning India as a leader in addressing megacity challenges.

question_text: WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala is from which country and represents which milestone?
option_b: Nigeria, first woman and first African DG of WTO
explanation: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala (Nigeria, born 1957) is WTO Director-General — first woman AND first African to hold this position (appointed March 2021; re-appointed for 2nd term 2025-2029). She previously served as Nigeria's Finance Minister (twice: 2003-06, 2011-15) and World Bank Managing Director (2012-2019). At WTO, she's focused on fisheries subsidy reforms, e-commerce negotiations, TRIPS/vaccine equity, and dispute settlement modernization. WTO (World Trade Organization) HQ: Geneva, Switzerland. Founded: January 1, 1995 (successor to GATT 1947). WTO has 166 member nations (India is a founding member, 1995). Strategic significance for India: WTO leadership diversity affects global trade rules affecting India. For India: (1) Developing nation voice — Okonjo-Iweala, as Africa's first WTO DG, elevated developing nations' concerns (fisheries subsidies disproportionately hurting African/Asian fishers, TRIPS restrictions on vaccine access, climate finance linkage to trade), (2) India-WTO alignment — India (largest WTO developing nation bloc member alongside China, Brazil) found strong advocacy partner in Okonjo-Iweala; India's positions on TRIPS flexibilities for COVID vaccines, climate-trade nexus, and special & differential treatment got WTO leadership backing, (3) Agricultural trade — India's farm exports (rice, sugar, wheat) benefit from Okonjo-Iweala's push for subsidy reductions in developed nations (US, EU), (4) Dispute settlement — Okonjo-Iweala revived WTO's appellate dispute settlement (dysfunctional since US blocked appointments 2017-2020); functioning dispute resolution benefits India's trade litigation against US/EU, (5) Women in global governance — Okonjo-Iweala's appointment validates women's leadership in international institutions, supporting India's advocacy for gender parity in global governance boards. For India's trade strategy, WTO under Okonjo-Iweala provides a more developing-nation-friendly forum compared to the GATT era, though megadeals (CPTPP, RCEP) happen outside formal WTO now.

question_text: Tarique Rahman is set to become Bangladesh's Prime Minister after the February 12, 2026 election. His party (BNP) won how many of the declared seats?
explanation: The BNP (Bangladesh Nationalist Party), led by Tarique Rahman, won 209 of 297 declared seats in the February 12, 2026 election (59.88% turnout) — a landslide. Jamaat-e-Islami was principal opposition (68 seats). It was Bangladesh's first election after the 2024 student uprising removed Sheikh Hasina (Awami League). Tarique returned in Dec 2025 after 17 years of exile in London, succeeding his mother Khaleda Zia (died Dec 2025) as BNP leader. Strategic significance for India: Tarique's BNP represents a pro-Pakistan, anti-India tilt compared to Hasina's Awami League which maintained close India ties. BNP's landslide shifts Bangladesh away from India's sphere — a critical geopolitical loss for India's South Asia dominance. Key concerns for India: (1) Rohingya repatriation — Tarique may coordinate with Pakistan on Rohingya camps (~900K in Cox's Bazar), affecting India's stance; (2) Border disputes — the 1974 Indus Waters Treaty equivalent (Ganges Water Sharing Treaty 1996) may face pressure for renegotiation; (3) China-Bangladesh infrastructure — BNP may accelerate Chinese Belt & Road projects (Padma Bridge, power plants) over India's interests; (4) Terrorism — historically BNP had weak counter-terrorism measures, risking LeT/JeM resurgence affecting India's Northeast security. India's strategic challenge: rebuilding ties with Tarique after supporting Hasina, while managing a fundamental shift in Bangladesh's geopolitical alignment from India toward Pakistan-China partnership.

question_text: Senior General Min Aung Hlaing was sworn in as Myanmar's 11th President on April 10, 2026. He was elected by parliament with how many votes?
explanation: Min Aung Hlaing — Myanmar's military coup leader since Feb 1, 2021 — was elected the country's 11th President on April 3, 2026 with 429 of 584 votes from the pro-military parliament. Inaugurated April 10, 2026 in Naypyidaw. He stepped down as Tatmadaw Commander-in-Chief on March 30, 2026 to qualify constitutionally. Vice Presidents: Nyo Saw and Nan Ni Ni Aye. Aung San Suu Kyi (NLD) remains imprisoned. Democracy watchdogs decried the election as a farce. Strategic significance for India: Min Aung Hlaing's consolidation of military rule (coup in Feb 2021, now presidency in Apr 2026) represents a setback for India's democratic partnerships in Southeast Asia. Myanmar is critical for India's Act East policy — it borders India (Assam, Manipur, Mizoram: 1,468 km), hosts 30K+ Indian diaspora, and controls the Strait of Malacca gateway. Min Aung Hlaing's military regime: (1) Has deepened Myanmar-China military ties (Chinese weapons, training), risking Indian influence in the region; (2) Created Rohingya refugee crisis (~1M in Bangladesh, 100K+ in India's Northeast), destabilizing India's border regions and fueling insurgency; (3) Has weakened India-Myanmar defense cooperation (joint exercises limited, joint patrols reduced). India's policy challenges: maintaining military engagement while critiquing democratic backsliding, ensuring Myanmar's Strategic autonomy isn't entirely captured by China. Myanmar's Chinse-linked economic projects (Kyaukpyu Deep Seaport, infrastructure) threaten India's Indo-Pacific presence. India balances its 'Act East' policy with pragmatic engagement on border security, counter-insurgency, and non-aligned positioning.

question_text: Khaled El-Enany, who took oath as UNESCO Director-General on November 15, 2025, represents which historic milestone?
option_b: First DG from an Arab country
explanation: Khaled El-Enany (Egypt) was elected UNESCO's 12th Director-General on November 6, 2025 with 172 of 174 votes; took oath November 15, 2025. He is the FIRST DG FROM AN ARAB COUNTRY, and the second from Africa (after Senegal's Amadou Mahtar Mbow, 1974-87). An Egyptologist and Helwan University professor, he served as Egypt's Antiquities/Tourism Minister and led the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization. He succeeded Audrey Azoulay (France). Strategic significance for India: El-Enany's appointment as UNESCO DG signals Global South reassertion in multilateral institutions — aligned with India's broader push for UN reforms and inclusive governance. Egypt's election of El-Enany reflects Arab world's growing soft-power influence in international institutions, challenging Western dominance. For India's cultural diplomacy: El-Enany's UNESCO tenure (2025-2029) creates opportunities for India's heritage agenda — UNESCO World Heritage sites in India (42 sites), intangible cultural heritage (yoga, Ayurveda, Indian classical arts), and knowledge-sharing on ancient civilizations. India-Egypt cultural ties (Pharaonic studies partnerships, archaeological collaborations at Aswan High Dam region) are strengthened. Egypt also holds critical geographic position for India's connectivity — Suez Canal routes, Red Sea shipping (10% of India's trade). El-Enany's focus on inclusive cultural preservation (following his Egyptology expertise) aligns with India's advocacy for protecting global heritage sites threatened by terrorism and climate change in developing nations. India can leverage El-Enany's tenure to advance its agenda on protecting Himalayan heritage sites and cultural preservation in conflict-affected South Asian regions.

question_text: Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey became Commonwealth Secretary-General on April 1, 2025. Which country and earlier role does she represent?
explanation: Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey (Ghana) became the 7th Commonwealth Secretary-General on April 1, 2025 — the FIRST AFRICAN WOMAN to hold this office. She was Ghana's Minister for Foreign Affairs and Regional Integration (Jan 2017 - Jan 2024) and a member of Ghana's National Security Council. Appointed by Commonwealth Heads of Government at CHOGM Apia, Samoa (2024). Priorities: youth/women empowerment, Commonwealth trade revival, climate emergency. She succeeded Patricia Scotland (UK). Strategic significance for India: Botchwey's appointment reshapes Commonwealth leadership toward Africa and gender representation — both priorities for India's multilateral engagement. The Commonwealth comprises 56 nations (2.6B people), including 20 African members; India is a core founding member and chair of CHOGM next (2026). Botchwey's focus on Commonwealth trade revival directly benefits India: (1) India-Commonwealth trade potential — India-UK FTA (2025), India-CARICOM partnerships, India-Africa EXIM Bank cooperation; (2) Youth/women empowerment — India's demographic dividend (median age 28) creates opportunities for skills-sharing through Commonwealth platforms; (3) Climate emergency — Botchwey's climate focus aligns with India's Climate Action leadership (G20 chair 2025, COP29 hosting). India can leverage Botchwey's tenure to advance Commonwealth cooperation on: renewable energy (India's 500GW solar target), tech entrepreneurship (India's startup ecosystem), and shared democratic values. Ghana is strategically important for India's West African engagement (Indian diaspora ~15K, trade potential ~$500M+ with deepening).

question_text: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf was elected Chairperson of the African Union Commission on February 15-16, 2025. He is from which country?
explanation: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf (Djibouti) was elected AU Commission Chairperson on Feb 15-16, 2025 at the 38th AU Summit in Addis Ababa, after 7 rounds of voting. He defeated Madagascar's Richard Randriamandranto and Kenya's Raila Odinga. Youssouf was Djibouti's Foreign Affairs Minister (2005-2025) — a career diplomat fluent in French, English, Arabic. He succeeded Moussa Faki Mahamat (Chad). Deputy: Selma Malika Haddadi (Algeria). 4-year renewable term. Strategic significance for India: Youssouf's election signals Djibouti's rising influence in African affairs — strategically significant for India as Djibouti controls Bab el-Mandeb Strait (12% of global shipping). His 20-year diplomatic career positions him to advance Africa's integration agenda. For India-Africa relations: (1) India-AU partnership deepens (India maintains Comprehensive Africa Policy); (2) Africa's voice in BRICS, G20, UN expands — India chairs BRICS and collaborated with AU on Security Council reform; (3) Regional connectivity aligns with India's maritime security initiatives. Djibouti hosts Indian naval presence (logistical support for Indian Navy operations in Gulf of Aden) — Youssouf's tenure enables stronger India-Djibouti defense cooperation through AU platforms.

question_text: Yuji Iwasawa (Japan) was elected President of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) on March 3, 2025. He succeeded which previous President?
explanation: Judge Yuji Iwasawa (Japan) became ICJ President on March 3, 2025, succeeding Nawaf Salam (Lebanon) who resigned to become Lebanon's PM. Iwasawa, ICJ judge since June 2018, was earlier professor of international law at University of Tokyo and chair of the UN Human Rights Committee. His ICJ presidency runs to February 5, 2027. ICJ HQ: Peace Palace, The Hague, Netherlands. Established 1945. Strategic significance for India: Japan's representation at the ICJ's highest office strengthens India-Japan strategic partnership — both nations champion rules-based international order. Iwasawa's presidency is significant for India-Japan cooperation on: (1) Maritime law — both nations advocate freedom of navigation in South China Sea against Chinese expansionism; (2) UN reforms — Japan and India jointly push for Security Council expansion; (3) International justice — India uses ICJ for disputes with Pakistan (Indus Waters), terrorism advocacy. Iwasawa's human rights background aligns with India's positions on humanitarian intervention and refugee protections in multilateral forums.

question_text: Antonio Costa (Portugal) became President of the European Council on December 1, 2024. He succeeded which Belgian politician?
explanation: Antonio Costa (Portugal, former PM 2015-2024) became President of the European Council on Dec 1, 2024 — succeeding Charles Michel (Belgium, 2019-2024). The European Council represents EU heads of state/government. Other EU 'top jobs' renewed in 2024: Ursula von der Leyen (Germany) — re-elected Commission President for 2nd term; Kaja Kallas (Estonia) — EU High Representative. Costa's term: 2.5 years. Strategic significance for India: Costa's European Council presidency (2024-26) is significant for India's EU engagement. Costa, a moderate socialist, prioritizes EU integration, economic recovery, and NATO 2% defense spending. For India: (1) EU-India FTA negotiations accelerate under Costa's leadership; (2) Defense partnerships — India-EU cooperation on cyber security, space, counter-terrorism expand; (3) Strategic autonomy — Costa's emphasis on European autonomy aligns with India's call for multipolarity and reduced Western hegemony in global governance.

question_text: Mark Rutte became NATO Secretary-General on October 1, 2024. He was previously Prime Minister of which country (longest-serving PM in its history)?
explanation: Mark Rutte (Netherlands) — Dutch PM 2010-2024 (~14 years) — became NATO's 14th Secretary-General on Oct 1, 2024, succeeding Jens Stoltenberg. NATO HQ: Brussels. Founded 1949. Has 32 members (Finland 2023, Sweden Mar 2024). Rutte's main challenges: Russia-Ukraine, US burden-sharing under Trump. Strategic significance for India: Rutte's NATO leadership (2024-28) impacts India's strategic positioning. NATO's focus on Russia containment directly affects: (1) NATO's expansion toward Indo-Pacific (partnerships with Japan, South Korea, Australia); (2) European arms supply to India and Indo-Pacific partners (artillery, air defense systems for Taiwan, Philippines); (3) NATO's cyber security standards influence India's defense modernization. Rutte's pragmatic approach to US burden-sharing aligns with India's appeals for burden-sharing in regional security — particularly in Indo-Pacific where India faces dual challenges from China and Pakistan. NATO's Indo-Pacific focus (through India partnerships) supports India's multipolarity narrative against Chinese hegemony.

question_text: Mathias Cormann was re-elected OECD Secretary-General for a 2nd 5-year term (2026-2031). He is a former Finance Minister of which country?
explanation: Mathias Cormann (Australia) — Australia's former Finance Minister (2013-2020) — was re-elected OECD Secretary-General for his 2nd term (June 1, 2026 - May 31, 2031). First took office June 1, 2021. OECD HQ: Paris. Founded 1961. 38 member countries. Belgium-born, migrated to Australia. India is an OECD 'Key Partner'. Strategic significance for India: Cormann's re-election for a second term ensures continuity in OECD's economic governance (2026-31). For India: (1) OECD 'Key Partner' status — India participates in OECD projects on taxation, digital economy, trade; Cormann's leadership affects policy direction; (2) Tax cooperation — OECD's global minimum tax (15%) and BEPS initiatives impact India's tax revenues (India's tech sector, global companies' tax planning); (3) Economic standards — India seeks OECD membership as symbol of development progress. Cormann's Australian background strengthens India-Australia-OECD coordination on Indo-Pacific economic governance and supply chain resilience.

question_text: Claudia Sheinbaum was sworn in as Mexico's President on October 1, 2024. Which historic milestone does she represent?
option_b: First woman President of Mexico (and first of Jewish descent)
option_d: First President to serve a 4-year term
explanation: Claudia Sheinbaum (Morena party) was sworn in as Mexico's first female President on October 1, 2024 — also Mexico's first president of Jewish descent. A climate scientist (PhD), she was former Head of Mexico City (2018-2023). Key challenge in 2025-26: managing Trump's tariffs. Strategic significance for India: Sheinbaum's presidency represents Latin America's democratic evolution toward gender representation — a trend that strengthens India's advocacy for women in global governance. For India-Mexico relations: (1) Climate cooperation — Sheinbaum's expertise aligns with India's climate leadership (India chairs COP29, UN climate initiatives); (2) Tech and renewable energy — Mexico-India partnerships on solar manufacturing and lithium mining (critical for EV batteries) expand; (3) Geopolitical significance — Mexico's position in the US-China-India competition affects Indian tech exports through USMCA. Sheinbaum's independence from Trump's tariff pressures signals Latin America's strategic autonomy, supporting India's multipolarity narrative.

question_text: Prabowo Subianto was sworn in as Indonesia's 8th President on October 20, 2024. He was previously Defence Minister and the running mate in 2024 was the son of the previous president. Who?
explanation: Prabowo Subianto (Gerindra party) was sworn in as Indonesia's 8th President on October 20, 2024. VP: Gibran Rakabuming Raka (Jokowi's eldest son). Court ruling lowered age requirement for 36-year-old Gibran. Prabowo, ex-Defence Minister (2019-2024) and ex-general, oversaw Indonesia's January 2025 entry into BRICS as 11th full member. Strategic significance for India: Prabowo's presidency (2024-29) marks critical shift in Indonesia's positioning — from Jokowi's balancing act to more nationalist, military-influenced approach. For India: (1) BRICS membership — Indonesia's accession on Prabowo's watch strengthens India-Indonesia-BRICS alignment on multipolarism, de-dollarization; (2) Defence cooperation — Prabowo prioritizes defense modernization — India-Indonesia defense partnerships deepen (ship-building, defense manufacturing; $1B trade target); (3) South China Sea — Prabowo's military background signals firm stance against Chinese assertiveness, supporting India's FOIP strategy; (4) ASEAN coordination — Indonesia, ASEAN chair 2024, works with India on counter-terrorism, maritime security, supply chain resilience in Indo-Pacific.

question_text: Anura Kumara Dissanayake (AKD) became Sri Lanka's President in September 2024. His party-coalition NPP won a parliamentary supermajority. NPP stands for:
explanation: Anura Kumara Dissanayake (AKD) of the JVP-led NPP coalition was elected Sri Lanka's 9th President on September 21, 2024. In November 14, 2024 snap parliamentary election, NPP won 2/3 supermajority (159/225 seats) — first true leftist supermajority in Sri Lanka's history. Pursued anti-corruption reforms, IMF continuation, and balanced India-China ties. Visited India (Dec 2024) — first foreign visit. Strategic significance for India: AKD's NPP landslide represents historic political realignment in Sri Lanka — from family dynasties to left-leaning anti-corruption coalition. For India: (1) Anti-corruption agenda — AKD's reforms target corruption that earlier weakened India's projects (ports, railways); (2) Debt restructuring — Sri Lanka's IMF program (post-April 2022 bankruptcy) affects India's BD port stakes (Colombo Port); (3) Strategic autonomy — AKD balances India-China ties (rejects Chinese debt-trap accusations, maintains Chinese investment) while strengthening India ties; (4) India-Sri Lanka relations — AKD's Dec 2024 India visit signaled commitment to regional partnership (fisheries, Tamil minority concerns, religious harmony). India navigates NPP's socialist leanings while securing Sri Lankan waters (critical for Indian Ocean naval operations).

question_text: Friedrich Merz visited India on January 12-13, 2026 — his first official Asian visit. How many MoUs/pacts were signed and what was Germany's GSDP funding announcement?
option_b: 19 MoUs, EUR 1.24 billion fresh under GSDP
explanation: Chancellor Friedrich Merz's India visit (Jan 12-13, 2026) saw 19 MoUs signed, including Defence Industrial Cooperation, semiconductors, critical minerals, and green-ammonia (AM Green - Uniper). Germany announced EUR 1.24 billion fresh under GSDP as part of EUR 10 billion commitment. Also: visa-free airport transit for Indians, battery storage working group, India-Germany skilling centre at Hyderabad NSTI. Strategic significance for India: Merz's Jan 2026 India visit — his first official Asian visit as Chancellor — signals Germany's strategic pivot toward India and Asia. The 19 MoUs signify comprehensive deepening: (1) Defense industrial partnership — critical for India's military modernization amid China threat; semiconductors crucial for tech sovereignty; (2) Green energy — EUR 1.24B under GSDP targets India's renewable (500GW target), battery storage, green ammonia (reducing fertilizer import dependence); (3) Talent mobility — India-Germany skilling center strengthens bilateral ties; (4) Strategic autonomy — Germany's emphasis on India partnership reflects EU strategy to diversify away from US-China duopoly, aligning with India's multipolarity vision. Merz's visit marks Germany's elevation of India as strategic technology and defense partner in Indo-Pacific strategy.

question_text: Lee Jae-myung made a State Visit to India on April 19-21, 2026 as the first South Korean President to visit since taking office in June 2025. Which major agreement was a centerpiece?
option_b: Joint Strategic Vision for the India-Republic of Korea Special Strategic Partnership
explanation: President Lee Jae-myung's India State Visit (April 19-21, 2026) produced Joint Strategic Vision for India-Korea Special Strategic Partnership covering shipbuilding, semiconductors, AI, arms co-production. Key: HD Korea Shipbuilding MoU for greenfield Tamil Nadu shipyard; Digital Bridge launched; CEPA upgrade talks; target $54B trade by 2030. Strategic significance for India: Lee's April 2026 India visit — only 10 months after assuming office — signals South Korea's elevation of India as core strategic partner. Joint Strategic Vision framework significance: (1) Shipbuilding partnership — HD Korea's Tamil Nadu yard supports India's 'Make in India' naval modernization (target 200 warships by 2050); (2) Semiconductor cooperation — South Korea's chip expertise (Samsung, SK Hynix) addresses India's chip sovereignty; (3) AI and tech — India-Korea Digital Bridge fosters collaboration in AI, 5G, fintech; (4) Defense co-production — joint arms manufacturing reduces India's import dependence on US/Russia; (5) Economic target $54B by 2030. Lee's visit marks South Korea's commitment to QUAD-adjacent partnerships with India in Indo-Pacific security amid North Korea threats and China's rise.

question_text: Cyril Ramaphosa retained South Africa's presidency in 2024-2026 by forming a 'Government of National Unity' (GNU). Which party became ANC's key coalition partner after ANC lost its majority for first time since 1994?
explanation: After May 29, 2024 elections — ANC won only 40% (down from 57%), losing outright majority for first time since 1994. Cyril Ramaphosa formed GNU with Democratic Alliance (DA, Steenhuisen) as key partner. GNU also included IFP, Patriotic Alliance. EFF (Malema) and MK Party (Zuma) remained in opposition. South Africa chaired G20 in 2025. Strategic significance for India: Ramaphosa's GNU (2024-29) represents democratic consolidation amid South Africa's political fragmentation — significant for India's BRICS-plus-Africa strategy. GNU's significance for India: (1) Stable governance — Ramaphosa's coalition averts collapse and ensures South Africa's G20 leadership continuity (2025 Johannesburg Summit succeeded); (2) BRICS stability — South Africa's political stability is critical for BRICS cohesion as India takes BRICS chair 2025-26; (3) ANC-DA coalition — brings pro-business (DA) perspective alongside ANC's development agenda, supporting India-South Africa trade; (4) Regional leadership — stable South Africa enhances Southern Africa security (SADC), benefits India's Indian Ocean presence. India navigates GNU's internal contradictions (DA's Western ties vs. ANC's BRICS alignment) while advancing India-South Africa strategic partnership.

question_text: PM Modi visited Washington DC on February 12-13, 2025 — meeting President Trump in Trump's 2nd term. Which initiative for India-US relations was launched at this summit?
option_b: COMPACT — Catalyzing Opportunities for Military Partnership, Accelerated Commerce & Technology
explanation: At Modi-Trump summit in Washington DC (Feb 12-13, 2025), 'COMPACT' (Catalyzing Opportunities for Military Partnership, Accelerated Commerce & Technology) was launched as new framework replacing iCET. Joint statement included: India to import more US oil/LNG, F-35 fighter jets, target $500B trade by 2030 ('Mission 500'), TRUST initiative (Tech for Strategic Trade), and extradition of 26/11 accused Tahawwur Rana. Strategic significance for India: Modi's Feb 2025 Washington visit during Trump's 2nd term marked a reset of India-US ties through COMPACT — replacing narrower iCET. COMPACT significance: (1) Military partnership — F-35s, defense co-production, Indo-Pacific naval coordination against China; (2) Trade expansion — 'Mission 500' ($500B by 2030) requires India to address Trump's tariff concerns (Russian oil, trade barriers); (3) Technology competition — TRUST initiative positions India-US as counter to China's tech dominance in AI, semiconductors, 5G; (4) Strategic autonomy — India's balancing act: accepting US security partnership while maintaining Russian energy ties (35-40% of crude) and non-aligned positioning. Modi-Trump chemistry (personal rapport) enabled COMPACT despite Trump's August 2025 tariff threat — demonstrating India's diplomatic skill in managing transactional US relations.

question_text: UAE Vice President and PM Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum made a state visit to India in January 2026. He is also the ruler of which emirate?
explanation: Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum is Vice President & PM of UAE (since 2006) AND Ruler of Dubai (since 2006). Visited India January 2026 to deepen India-UAE Comprehensive Strategic Partnership (CEPA in force since May 2022). UAE President: Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan (MBZ). UAE chief guest at India's 2024 Republic Day. India's 3rd largest trade partner (~$85B). Strategic significance for India: Sheikh Mohammed's Jan 2026 India visit reinforced India-UAE partnership as cornerstone of India's West Asia strategy. Significance: (1) Economic cornerstone — UAE is India's 3rd largest trade partner ($85B), major FDI source, home to 3.5M Indians (largest diaspora outside SAARC); (2) CEPA deepening — UAE-India trade target $200B by 2030; (3) Strategic alliance — UAE-India cooperation on counter-terrorism, maritime security, regional stability in volatile West Asia; (4) Geopolitical positioning — UAE's Jan 2026 visit signals continued India alliance despite potential US-Iran normalization, Chinese investment, Israeli alignment. Visit demonstrated India's critical importance to UAE's 2030 diversification vision (beyond oil to tech, finance, logistics). Sheikh Mohammed's engagement with Modi personally strengthened bilateral ties amid regional instability (Syria crisis, Yemen, Iran tensions).

question_text: Ajay Banga continued as President of the World Bank Group through 2025-2026. He is the first person of Indian origin to head the World Bank. He took office in:
explanation: Ajay Banga (Indian-American) became World Bank's 14th President on June 2, 2023 — first Indian-origin and first naturalized American (Sikh) to lead. Former Mastercard CEO. 5-year term runs to 2028. HQ: Washington DC. India is World Bank's largest cumulative borrower. Compare: Kristalina Georgieva (Bulgaria) — IMF MD (re-elected 2024-2029). Strategic significance for India: Banga's World Bank presidency (2023-28) represents historic moment — first Indian-origin leader of Bretton Woods institution. Significance: (1) India's voice in global economic governance — Banga advocates for Global South priorities (debt relief, climate finance, development); (2) World Bank lending to India — India remains largest cumulative borrower (~$150B outstanding); Banga's prioritization of climate finance, renewable energy benefits India's green transition; (3) Sikh representation — Banga's leadership in global institutions symbolizes India's secular, inclusive democracy; (4) Development agenda — Banga's focus on inclusive development, gender equality, inequality fighting aligns with India's SDG priorities. Banga's leadership strengthens India's claims for UN Security Council permanent seat and multilateral institution reforms advocating for Global South representation.

question_text: In a major Aug 2025 Trump executive action, the US imposed a 50% reciprocal tariff on Indian goods citing two specific grievances. Which were they?
option_a: India's currency manipulation and farm subsidies
option_b: India's Russian oil purchases and trade barriers
option_c: India's data localization and tech regulations
explanation: Trump's executive order (Aug 6, 2025) imposed 50% reciprocal tariffs on Indian goods, citing: (1) India's Russian crude oil purchases (~35-40% of imports post-Ukraine war) and (2) India's perceived 'high tariff barriers' against US goods. Effective Aug 27, 2025. India responded with diplomatic engagement; trade deal negotiations in 2025-26 alongside Mission 500 ($500B by 2030). Strategic significance for India: Trump's Aug 2025 tariff action exposed cracks in Modi-Trump COMPACT despite Feb 2025 summit bonhomie. Significance: (1) Strategic autonomy under pressure — Trump demanded India abandon Russian oil (violates non-aligned principle) to conform to US sanctions; (2) Energy security dilemma — India's 35-40% crude from Russia reflects post-Ukraine diversification away from Middle East; reducing Russian imports risks energy inflation; (3) Trade negotiation leverage — Aug tariffs were pressure tactic for India-US trade deal negotiations (resolved by Nov 2025 with concessions); (4) QUAD implications — Trump's India tariffs exposed limits of QUAD cohesion when bilateral trade interests clash. Tariff episode demonstrated that despite strategic partnership language, India must balance US demands with strategic autonomy on energy, trade, and non-alignment principles. India's diplomatic skill in negotiating tariff reduction without abandoning Russian oil showed pragmatic geopolitics.

question_text: Match: Which combination of 2025-2026 multilateral appointments is FULLY CORRECT?
option_a: UNESCO DG = El-Enany (Egypt); NATO SG = Rutte (Netherlands); AU Commission = Youssouf (Djibouti); Commonwealth SG = Botchwey (Ghana)
option_b: UNESCO DG = Azoulay (France); NATO SG = Stoltenberg (Norway); AU = Faki (Chad); Commonwealth = Scotland (UK)
option_c: UNESCO DG = Botchwey (Ghana); NATO SG = Costa (Portugal); AU = Rutte; Commonwealth = El-Enany
option_d: UNESCO DG = El-Enany; NATO SG = Costa; AU = Botchwey; Commonwealth = Rutte
explanation: Correct (Option A): UNESCO DG = Khaled El-Enany (Egypt, since Nov 15, 2025) — FIRST DG from Arab country; NATO SG = Mark Rutte (Netherlands, since Oct 1, 2024) — longest-serving Dutch PM; AU Commission Chair = Mahmoud Ali Youssouf (Djibouti, since Feb 2025) — East Africa diplomat; Commonwealth SG = Shirley Botchwey (Ghana, since Apr 1, 2025) — FIRST African woman in office. Option B lists outgoing predecessors (Azoulay/France, Stoltenberg/Norway, Faki/Chad, Scotland/UK). Strategic significance for India: This cohort of 2024-2026 appointments represents Global South's rising voice in multilateral institutions — all four new leaders prioritize: (1) Development/equity (El-Enany's heritage preservation, Botchwey's trade revival, Youssouf's African integration, Rutte's burden-sharing fairness); (2) India partnerships — Egypt (UNESCO cultural agenda), Ghana (Commonwealth youth/tech), Djibouti (AU-India strategic ties), Netherlands (NATO-India defense cooperation). These appointments align with India's advocacy for inclusive multilateralism, non-aligned positioning, and Global South empowerment in global governance reform.

question_text: The Twelve-Day War between Israel and Iran lasted from:
explanation: The Twelve-Day War lasted from June 13 to June 24, 2025. It began when Israel launched a surprise attack on Iran's nuclear and military facilities and ended with a ceasefire brokered under US pressure.

question_text: Which country launched the surprise attack that started the Twelve-Day War in June 2025?
explanation: Israel launched the surprise attack on June 13, 2025, targeting Iran's nuclear facilities (Natanz, Isfahan, Fordow), military bases, and assassinating key IRGC generals and nuclear scientists.

question_text: Which three Iranian nuclear facilities were targeted during the Twelve-Day War?
explanation: Israel (and later the US on June 22) targeted Iran's key nuclear facilities: Natanz (main enrichment plant), Isfahan (research centre), and Fordow (underground plant near Qom). All three were extensively damaged.

question_text: What was Iran's retaliatory operation name during the Twelve-Day War against Israel?
explanation: Iran's retaliation in the Twelve-Day War was called 'Operation True Promise III' — involving 550+ ballistic missiles and 1,000+ suicide drones targeting Israeli cities, military bases, energy infrastructure, and government sites.

question_text: How many ballistic missiles did Iran fire during the Twelve-Day War?
explanation: Iran retaliated with over 550 ballistic missiles and over 1,000 suicide drones during the Twelve-Day War (June 2025), hitting civilian population centres, hospitals, and military/energy/government sites in Israel.

question_text: The US strikes on Iran's nuclear sites (Natanz, Fordow, Isfahan) on June 21-22, 2025 were codenamed:
explanation: 'Operation Midnight Hammer' was the US codename for the June 21-22, 2025 strikes during the Twelve-Day War. It involved 7 B-2 Spirit stealth bombers flying 37 hours from Missouri, dropping GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator bunker-busters on Fordow — the first operational use of the GBU-57. Over 125 aircraft participated. Iran retaliated by striking Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar.

question_text: After the US bombed its nuclear sites on June 22, 2025, Iran retaliated by striking which US military base?
explanation: Iran fired missiles at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar — the largest US military base in the Middle East — in retaliation for the US strikes on its nuclear facilities on June 22, 2025.

question_text: Which IRGC commander (Chief of IRGC) was killed during the Twelve-Day War?
explanation: Hossein Salami, the Commander-in-Chief of the IRGC (Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps), was killed during Israel's attacks in the Twelve-Day War (June 2025).

question_text: Which head of Iran's IRGC Aerospace Force was killed in the Twelve-Day War?
explanation: Amir Ali Hajizadeh, Commander of the IRGC Aerospace Force (responsible for Iran's missile and drone programme), was killed during Israel's strikes in the Twelve-Day War.

question_text: Iran's Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces, killed in the Twelve-Day War, was:
explanation: Mohammad Bagheri, Chief of Staff of Iran's Armed Forces, was killed during Israel's attacks in the Twelve-Day War (June 2025). Gholam Ali Rashid (another senior general) was also killed.

question_text: How many leading Iranian nuclear scientists did Israel assassinate during the Twelve-Day War?
explanation: Israel assassinated at least 10 leading Iranian nuclear scientists during the Twelve-Day War, using commandos and Mossad operatives inside Iran.

question_text: What happened to Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian during the Twelve-Day War?
option_a: He was killed in an Israeli airstrike
explanation: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was wounded in action (WIA) during the Twelve-Day War (June 2025). He had been elected President in mid-2024 after Ebrahim Raisi's death.

question_text: On the day before the Twelve-Day War, the IAEA declared Iran non-compliant with nuclear obligations. This resolution was put forward by which four countries?
explanation: On June 12, 2025 (the day before Israel attacked), the IAEA Board passed a resolution declaring Iran non-compliant with its nuclear obligations. The resolution was put forward by USA, UK, France, and Germany (the E3+US group).

question_text: After the Twelve-Day War, Iran took which major step regarding its nuclear oversight?
option_b: Signed new nuclear deal with Russia
explanation: Iran suspended cooperation with the IAEA after the Twelve-Day War, accusing the agency of sharing information about nuclear facility locations with Israel, which Iran said enabled the targeted strikes.

question_text: How many Mossad (Israeli intelligence) agents did Iran claim to arrest during the Twelve-Day War?
explanation: Iran claimed to have arrested over 700 Mossad agents during the Twelve-Day War, and reportedly executed 5 of them. Israel's Mossad was credited with intelligence and commando operations inside Iran.

question_text: Israeli civilian casualties in the Twelve-Day War were:
explanation: Israel suffered 32 civilians and 1 off-duty soldier killed, with 3,238 wounded in the Twelve-Day War. Iran's retaliation with 550+ missiles and 1,000+ drones targeted Israeli cities.

question_text: The ceasefire that ended the Twelve-Day War on June 24, 2025 was brokered by:
explanation: The ceasefire on June 24, 2025 was agreed under US pressure. The US played the role of both a combatant (bombing nuclear sites on June 22) and ceasefire broker — a unique dual role in this conflict.

question_text: During the Twelve-Day War, Iran imposed an internet blackout. The Iranian government did this primarily to:
option_a: Protect government networks from Israeli cyber attacks
option_b: Prevent protests from spreading and restrict flow of information
explanation: The Iranian government imposed internet blackouts during the Twelve-Day War to prevent protests from spreading and to restrict the flow of information about casualties and military losses to both domestic and international audiences.

question_text: Which Iranian aircraft were destroyed by Israel during the Twelve-Day War?
explanation: Israel destroyed 5 F-14 Tomcat fighter jets, 2 F-5 Tiger jets, and 8 AH-1 Cobra helicopters belonging to Iran during the Twelve-Day War. Iran's F-14s are American-era jets supplied before the 1979 revolution.

question_text: The Fordow nuclear plant in Iran is significant because it is:
option_a: Located near Tehran, Iran's largest city
option_b: Built underground inside a mountain near Qom
option_c: A light water reactor given by Russia
option_d: A plutonium reprocessing facility near the sea
explanation: The Fordow Fuel Enrichment Plant is located underground inside a mountain near Qom, making it extremely hardened and difficult to destroy from the air. Despite this, US strikes on June 22, 2025 damaged it.

question_text: The 2026 Iran War officially began on:
explanation: The 2026 Iran War began on February 28, 2026, when the United States and Israel launched coordinated airstrikes on Iran, targeting military and government sites. The surprise attacks were launched while US-Iran nuclear negotiations were ongoing.

question_text: The 2026 Iran War attacks by the USA and Israel were launched while what diplomatic activity was in progress?
option_a: UN Security Council emergency meeting on Iran
explanation: The US-Israel attacks on February 28, 2026 were launched as a surprise during ongoing US-Iran nuclear negotiations — a diplomatic deception that shocked the international community.

question_text: Which major Iranian leader was killed in the US-Israel airstrikes during the 2026 Iran War?
explanation: Ali Khamenei, Iran's Supreme Leader since 1989, was killed in the US-Israel strikes during the 2026 Iran War. He had been Supreme Leader for over 35 years since succeeding Ayatollah Khomeini.

question_text: Ali Larijani, killed in the 2026 Iran War, was notable as:
option_c: Former Speaker of Iran's Parliament and senior official
explanation: Ali Larijani, killed during the 2026 Iran War, was a highly influential Iranian politician — former Speaker of the Islamic Consultative Assembly (Parliament) and a senior advisor to the Supreme Leader.

question_text: In response to the 2026 US-Israel attacks, Iran closed which critical global waterway?
explanation: Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for the US-Israel attacks. This triggered the '2026 Strait of Hormuz Crisis'. Approximately 20% of global oil trade passes through this narrow strait between Iran and Oman.

question_text: The Strait of Hormuz, which Iran closed in 2026, lies between Iran and which country on the opposite shore?
explanation: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway between Iran (to the north) and Oman (to the south). It is the world's most important oil chokepoint — about 20% of global oil and 30% of global LNG passes through it.

question_text: During the 2026 Iran War, Iran fired missiles and drones at US military bases in multiple Arab countries. Which of the following was NOT among those countries?
explanation: Iran targeted US military bases in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and UAE. Egypt was NOT targeted — it does not host a major US military base targeted in this conflict.

question_text: Britain's military base struck by an Iranian drone during the 2026 Iran War is located on which island?
explanation: Britain's Akrotiri military base on Cyprus was struck by an Iranian drone during the 2026 Iran War. The UK Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia are located on the island of Cyprus.

question_text: Iranian missiles fired during the 2026 war were intercepted over which NATO country?
explanation: Iranian ballistic missiles were intercepted over Turkey during the 2026 Iran War. Turkey, a NATO member, cooperated with allied air defences to intercept the missiles despite not being a direct participant in the war.

question_text: How many US soldiers were killed in the 2026 Iran War (as of April 30, 2026)?
explanation: 15 US soldiers were killed in the 2026 Iran War (as of April 30, 2026 report), with 538 military personnel wounded. The US also had 17+ military sites damaged.

question_text: Israel's economic damage from the 2026 Iran War was estimated at approximately:
explanation: Israel's economic damage from the 2026 Iran War was estimated at approximately $50 billion as of April 30, 2026. Israel suffered 18 soldiers and 28 civilians killed, with 8,524 injured.

question_text: According to HRANA (Human Rights Activists News Agency), how many people were killed in Iran in the 2026 Iran War?
explanation: HRANA reported 3,636 killed in Iran (1,221 military personnel, 1,701 civilians, and 714 unclassified) with 26,500 injured, as of the April 30, 2026 report.

question_text: How many Iranian ballistic missile launchers were destroyed in the 2026 Iran War (per US and Israel)?
explanation: According to US and Israel, 190+ ballistic missile launchers were destroyed in the 2026 Iran War, along with 155 naval vessels destroyed or damaged. Iran also lost 6,000+ military personnel per US-Israel estimates.

question_text: Pakistan mediated the Islamabad Talks (April 11-12, 2026) between the US and Iran. The talks ended:
option_b: Without a deal after 21 hours of negotiations
option_c: With Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz
option_d: With the US lifting all sanctions
explanation: The Islamabad Talks (April 11-12, 2026), mediated by Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and FM Ishaq Dar, lasted 21 hours over 3 rounds but ended without a deal. Key disagreements: Iran's nuclear programme, Strait of Hormuz status, and $6 billion in frozen Iranian assets.

question_text: The 2026 Israel-Lebanon War (March 2 – April 16, 2026) was triggered by which event?
option_b: Hezbollah firing rockets at Israel following the US-Israel assassination of Khamenei
option_c: An Israeli ground invasion of southern Lebanon
option_d: A Hezbollah drone strike on Tel Aviv
explanation: The 2026 Israel-Lebanon War erupted on March 2, 2026 when Hezbollah fired rockets at Israel following the US-Israel assassination of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei (Feb 28, 2026 in Operation Epic Fury). A ceasefire was reached on April 16, 2026 after Washington talks.

question_text: On May 15, 2026, after a third round of Washington talks, the porous Israel-Lebanon ceasefire was:
explanation: On May 15, 2026, after a third ambassador-level round of US-hosted Washington talks (following April 14 and April 23 rounds), the US announced a 45-day extension of the porous Israel-Lebanon ceasefire. Hezbollah disarmament remained the key unresolved demand. At least 657 people had been killed by Israeli attacks in Lebanon since the ceasefire began.

question_text: US Defense Secretary during the 2026 Iran War was:
explanation: Pete Hegseth served as US Secretary of Defense during the 2026 Iran War, under President Donald Trump's second administration. He was a former Fox News host who was controversially appointed to the role.

question_text: The 2026 US military buildup in the Middle East was described as the largest since which earlier conflict?
explanation: The Trump administration launched the largest US military buildup in the Middle East since the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq, including deploying two aircraft carrier strike groups to the region.

question_text: How many aircraft carrier strike groups did the US deploy to the Middle East for the 2026 Iran War?
explanation: The US deployed two aircraft carrier strike groups to the Middle East as part of the largest military buildup in the region since 2003. This massive naval force, combined with the Israeli Air Force, conducted the sustained strikes.

question_text: Iran's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei had been in power since which year before being killed in the 2026 war?
explanation: Ali Khamenei became Supreme Leader of Iran in 1989, succeeding Ayatollah Khomeini who died that year. He held the position for over 35 years until his assassination in the 2026 Iran War.

question_text: Which son of Ali Khamenei was wounded (WIA) in the 2026 Iran War?
explanation: Mojtaba Khamenei, the son of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, was wounded in action (WIA) during the 2026 Iran War. He had been rumoured as a potential successor to his father before the war.

question_text: The Hezbollah Secretary General who led the organisation during the 2026 Lebanon War (after Hassan Nasrallah's death in 2024) was:
explanation: Naim Qassem became Hezbollah's Secretary General after Hassan Nasrallah was killed by Israel in September 2024. Qassem led Hezbollah during the 2026 Lebanon War phase of the Iran-Israel conflict.

question_text: The JCPOA (Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action), Iran's 2015 nuclear deal, was agreed between Iran and the group known as P5+1. Which countries comprise P5+1?
option_a: USA, UK, France, Russia, China + Germany
option_c: USA, UK, France, Israel, Russia, China
explanation: P5+1 = Five permanent members of the UN Security Council (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) + Germany. The JCPOA was signed in 2015 — Iran froze its nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief.

question_text: In which year did the USA unilaterally withdraw from the JCPOA nuclear deal?
explanation: US President Donald Trump unilaterally withdrew the US from the JCPOA on May 8, 2018 (his first term). Iran then resumed uranium enrichment, gradually raising it toward weapons-grade levels.

question_text: Israel bombed the Iranian consulate in Damascus (Syria) in April 2024, killing senior IRGC officials. This was located in which part of Damascus?
explanation: Israel bombed the Iranian consulate annexe adjacent to the Iranian Embassy in Damascus, Syria in April 2024. The strike killed several senior IRGC officers including General Mohammad Reza Zahedi.

question_text: Iran's first-ever direct missile and drone attack on Israel (April 13–14, 2024) was called:
explanation: Iran's first direct attack on Israel (April 13–14, 2024) was called 'Operation True Promise I'. It involved approximately 300 drones and missiles, most of which were intercepted by Israel, US, UK, France, and Jordan.

question_text: What percentage of Iran's uranium enrichment level had Iran reached before the wars began (as of 2024-25)?
explanation: Iran had enriched uranium to approximately 60% purity before the wars — just below the 90%+ threshold for weapons-grade uranium. This was far beyond the 3.67% limit under the JCPOA.

question_text: The 2026 Iran War was launched DURING which specific diplomatic activity?
option_a: IAEA Board of Governors meeting in Vienna
option_c: G20 emergency summit on Middle East
explanation: The February 28, 2026 US-Israel attacks were launched as a surprise DURING ongoing negotiations between Iran and the US on Iran's nuclear program. The timing shocked the international community.

question_text: The January 2026 Iranian protests, which saw security forces massacre thousands of civilians, were the largest in Iran since:
explanation: The 2025-2026 Iranian protests were described as the largest in Iran since the 1979 Islamic Revolution. The crackdown in January 2026 (with thousands of civilians killed) triggered US President Trump to threaten military action.

question_text: Which IRGC general, commander of Quds Force (overseeing proxy wars), was killed by the US in a drone strike in Baghdad in January 2020?
explanation: Qasem Soleimani, head of the IRGC Quds Force and architect of Iran's proxy strategy across the Middle East, was killed in a US drone strike at Baghdad International Airport on January 3, 2020. Esmail Qaani succeeded him.

question_text: The IRGC (Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps) is Iran's elite military force. Which of the following is NOT an IRGC component?
explanation: The IRGC has Ground Forces, Aerospace Force (missiles and drones), Naval Force, and Quds Force (overseas operations). 'IRGC Naval Aviation Wing' is not a standard component — the IRGC has a naval force but aviation falls under Aerospace.

question_text: Iran's 'Axis of Resistance' is a network of Iran-backed proxy groups. Which of the following is NOT part of the Axis of Resistance?
explanation: The Axis of Resistance includes Hezbollah (Lebanon), Hamas (Gaza), Houthis (Yemen), and Popular Mobilization Forces/Islamic Resistance in Iraq. The Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt is NOT part of this axis.

question_text: Iran's primary suicide drone (loitering munition) used against Israel and in the Twelve-Day War is known as:
explanation: The Shahed-136 (also called Geran-2 when used by Russia) is Iran's primary kamikaze/loitering munition drone. Iran used thousands of Shahed-series drones in operations against Israel. Russia also used Shaheds against Ukraine.

question_text: Hassan Nasrallah, the long-time Hezbollah Secretary General, was killed by Israel in which month and year?
explanation: Hezbollah Secretary General Hassan Nasrallah was killed by Israel in September 2024 in a massive airstrike on Hezbollah's headquarters in Beirut's southern suburbs. Naim Qassem succeeded him.

question_text: Israel's Iron Dome, David's Sling, and Arrow systems together form Israel's multi-tier missile defence. Which system is designed to intercept long-range ballistic missiles?
explanation: The Arrow (Hetz) system is Israel's upper-tier defence against long-range ballistic missiles. Iron Dome handles short-range rockets; David's Sling handles medium-range missiles. All were used during Iran's attacks.

question_text: The Houthis, who attacked Israel and US shipping in the Twelve-Day War period, operate from which country?
explanation: The Houthis (officially Ansar Allah) control northern Yemen including the capital Sanaa. They are backed by Iran and attacked Israel with drones and missiles during the conflict, and targeted shipping in the Red Sea.

question_text: Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), also called Hashd al-Shaabi, who fought alongside Iran in the 2026 war, are based in:
explanation: The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF/Hashd al-Shaabi) are Iran-backed Shia militia groups based in Iraq. They are part of Iran's Axis of Resistance and attacked US bases in Iraq and across the region.

question_text: The US military's main base in Qatar, targeted by Iran in the Twelve-Day War, is:
explanation: Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar is the largest US military base in the Middle East, hosting approximately 10,000+ US military personnel and a major forward command centre. Iran fired missiles at it after the US struck its nuclear sites.

question_text: Israel's military intelligence agency (the 'Institute for Intelligence and Special Operations') which ran operations inside Iran during the Twelve-Day War is called:
explanation: Mossad is Israel's national intelligence agency responsible for foreign intelligence and covert operations. During the Twelve-Day War, Mossad ran covert operations inside Iran, including assassinating nuclear scientists.

question_text: The Natanz Nuclear Facility in Iran is primarily known as:
explanation: The Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant is Iran's main uranium enrichment facility, located in Isfahan Province. It contains both above-ground and underground cascades of centrifuges and was the primary target in multiple strikes.

question_text: India's External Affairs Minister met Iranian FM Seyyed Abbas Araghchi on May 15, 2026 in New Delhi for bilateral discussions. India's EAM is:
explanation: S. Jaishankar (Dr. Subrahmanyam Jaishankar) is India's External Affairs Minister. He held a bilateral meeting with Iranian Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi in New Delhi on May 15, 2026.

question_text: The Iran-Israel war directly impacted India due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz because India:
option_a: Has a military base in Oman near the Strait
option_b: Imports significant quantities of oil and LNG from the Gulf
option_c: Exports goods to Iran through the Strait
option_d: Runs the Chabahar-Zahedan railway through the Strait
explanation: India imports a significant portion of its crude oil from Gulf countries (UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait) — most of which passes through the Strait of Hormuz. The 2026 closure severely impacted India's energy imports.

question_text: Chabahar Port, developed by India in Iran, is strategically important because it:
option_a: Allows India to access the Strait of Hormuz directly
option_b: Provides India access to Afghanistan and Central Asia bypassing Pakistan
option_c: Is Iran's main oil export terminal
option_d: Is the eastern terminal of the North-South Transport Corridor
explanation: Chabahar Port in Iran's Sistan-Baluchestan province gives India access to Afghanistan and Central Asia, bypassing Pakistan. India has invested heavily in this port and the Chabahar-Zahedan rail link.

question_text: India's position on the Iran-Israel-USA conflict has been to:
option_a: Support Israel unconditionally as a strategic partner
option_b: Support Iran as it supplies oil to India
option_c: Call for dialogue, diplomacy and de-escalation without taking sides
option_d: Abstain on all UN resolutions related to the conflict
explanation: India has consistently called for dialogue, diplomacy, and de-escalation without taking sides in the Iran-Israel-USA conflict. India has significant interests with both sides — strategic ties with Israel and energy/Chabahar ties with Iran.

question_text: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz in 2026 caused global oil prices to spike dramatically. Approximately what percentage of global oil passes through the Strait?
explanation: Approximately 20% of global crude oil (and 30% of global LNG) passes through the Strait of Hormuz daily — about 17-21 million barrels per day. Its closure in 2026 caused a major global energy crisis.

question_text: Which of the following is the CORRECT chronological order of key events in the Iran-Israel escalation?
option_a: October 7 Hamas attack → JCPOA withdrawal → Twelve-Day War → 2026 Iran War
option_b: JCPOA withdrawal → October 7 Hamas attack → Twelve-Day War → 2026 Iran War
option_c: Twelve-Day War → October 7 attack → JCPOA withdrawal → 2026 Iran War
option_d: JCPOA withdrawal → Twelve-Day War → October 7 attack → 2026 Iran War
explanation: Correct order: JCPOA withdrawal (2018) → October 7 Hamas attack (2023) → Twelve-Day War (June 2025) → 2026 Iran War (Feb 28, 2026). The 2024 Iran-Israel missile exchanges also occurred between the Hamas attack and the Twelve-Day War.

question_text: The Twelve-Day War and the 2026 Iran War are both considered part of which broader ongoing crisis?
explanation: Both the Twelve-Day War (June 2025) and the 2026 Iran War are considered part of the 'Middle Eastern Crisis (2023-present)', which began with the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023.

question_text: The US CENTCOM (Central Command) commander during the 2026 Iran War was:
explanation: General Michael Kurilla served as the US CENTCOM (United States Central Command) commander during the 2026 Iran War, overseeing US military operations across the Middle East.

question_text: Israel's current (2026) Prime Minister, who has led Israel through both the Twelve-Day War and the 2026 Iran War, is:
explanation: Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving Prime Minister, led Israel through the Gaza War (2023-25), Twelve-Day War (June 2025), and the 2026 Iran War. He faces ICC arrest warrant for actions in Gaza.

question_text: Israel's Defense Minister during the Twelve-Day War and 2026 Iran War is:
explanation: Israel Katz serves as Israel's Defense Minister during this period. He succeeded Yoav Gallant (who was dismissed by Netanyahu in November 2024). Eyal Zamir serves as IDF Chief of Staff.

question_text: The Iran-Israel proxy war that preceded the direct conflicts involved Iran supporting which two main groups against Israel?
explanation: Iran's main proxies against Israel are Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon. Iran also supports Houthis in Yemen and PMF in Iraq, but Hamas and Hezbollah are the primary anti-Israel proxies.

question_text: Iran's supreme nuclear enrichment facility Natanz is located in which Iranian province?
explanation: The Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant is located in Isfahan Province, Iran. It is Iran's main uranium enrichment facility and was one of the primary targets in both the Twelve-Day War and earlier strikes.

question_text: Which country hosted the US military base Al Udeid, struck by Iran in the Twelve-Day War?
explanation: Al Udeid Air Base is located in Qatar, about 30 km southwest of Doha. It is the largest US military base in the Middle East and hosts the CENTCOM forward headquarters. Iran struck it with missiles after the US bombed Iranian nuclear sites.

question_text: During the Twelve-Day War, approximately how many suicide drones (loitering munitions) did Iran fire at Israel?
explanation: Iran fired over 1,000 suicide drones (loitering munitions) along with 550+ ballistic missiles at Israel during the Twelve-Day War (June 2025), as part of Operation True Promise III.

question_text: The 2026 Iran protests (Jan 2026) that triggered US military threats were described as the largest since 1979. What was the immediate cause of these protests?
option_c: Continued government repression and massacre of civilians in ongoing unrest
option_d: Death of a prominent reformist leader
explanation: The 2025-2026 Iranian protests were an extension of growing unrest. In January 2026, Iranian security forces massacred thousands of civilians in their crackdown on the growing protest movement. This prompted Trump to threaten military action.

question_text: Which entity declared Iran non-compliant with nuclear obligations the day before the Twelve-Day War began?
option_b: IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency) Board of Governors
explanation: The IAEA Board of Governors passed a resolution on June 12, 2025 (the day before the Twelve-Day War began) declaring Iran non-compliant with its nuclear safeguards obligations. The resolution was tabled by USA, UK, France, and Germany.

question_text: Operation Epic Fury (the US codename for the 2026 Iran war that began Feb 28, 2026) was paired with what Israeli codename?
explanation: The Feb 28, 2026 US-Israel campaign was codenamed 'Operation Epic Fury' by the Pentagon and 'Operation Roaring Lion' by Israel. (The June 2025 Twelve-Day War was Israel's 'Operation Rising Lion'.) Epic Fury officially concluded on May 5, 2026.

question_text: How many Hezbollah fighters were killed in the 2026 Lebanon War phase (per US-Israel estimates)?
explanation: Per US and Israel estimates, approximately 1,900 Hezbollah fighters were killed in the 2026 Lebanon War phase of the conflict. The broader 2026 Lebanon war killed 2,000+ civilians and militants combined.

question_text: What was the significance of Iran striking the Akrotiri military base on Cyprus during the 2026 Iran War?
option_a: Cyprus is a member of the Axis of Resistance
option_b: It targeted a British sovereign base area — effectively attacking a NATO/EU member state's military asset
option_c: It was the first time a Middle Eastern country struck Europe
option_d: Akrotiri houses Israel's air defence radar
explanation: Akrotiri is a British Overseas Territory (Sovereign Base Area) on Cyprus. By striking it with a drone, Iran was attacking a military asset of the United Kingdom — a NATO and EU member — significantly widening the conflict geographically.

question_text: The US stated multiple rationales for launching the 2026 war on Iran. Which of the following was NOT a stated US rationale?
option_a: To prevent Iran from building a nuclear weapon
option_b: To destroy Iran's ballistic missile capabilities
option_c: To seize Iran's oil resources and redistribute them
option_d: To forestall an imminent Iranian threat
explanation: While the US cited multiple rationales — preventing nuclear weapons, destroying missile capabilities, forestalling threats, and regime change — 'seizing Iran's oil and redistributing it' was NOT a stated official US rationale (though critics alleged this as a motive).

question_text: Yahya Sinwar, Hamas's political bureau chief and architect of the October 7, 2023 attacks, was killed by Israeli forces on:
explanation: Yahya Sinwar was killed on October 16, 2024 during a chance encounter with an IDF patrol in the southern Gazan city of Rafah. He had succeeded Ismail Haniyeh as Hamas political bureau chief in August 2024. His body was identified through dental records and DNA. He was succeeded by his brother Mohammed Sinwar (later killed by Israel in 2025).

question_text: Ismail Haniyeh, Hamas's political bureau chief, was assassinated on July 31, 2024 in which city?
explanation: Ismail Haniyeh was assassinated in Tehran, Iran on July 31, 2024 — almost certainly by Israel — while attending the inauguration of new Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. The killing in Iran's capital was a major intelligence embarrassment for Tehran. Yahya Sinwar succeeded him on August 6, 2024.

question_text: Hassan Nasrallah, the long-time Hezbollah Secretary General, was killed by Israel on:
explanation: Hassan Nasrallah was killed on September 27, 2024 in a massive Israeli airstrike on Hezbollah's underground headquarters in Dahieh (southern Beirut suburbs). Israel used bunker-buster bombs. Hashem Safieddine (designated successor) was killed days later. Naim Qassem eventually became Secretary General.

question_text: The first Israel-Hamas Gaza ceasefire of 2025 took effect on:
explanation: The first phase of the Gaza ceasefire took effect on January 19, 2025, after an agreement announced January 15, 2025. Phase 1 ran until March 18, 2025, with 33 Israeli hostages and ~2,000 Palestinian prisoners released. The deal was brokered by the US (Trump's incoming team + Biden), Qatar, and Egypt.

question_text: The October 2025 Gaza peace plan that produced the second major ceasefire was a 20-point plan announced by:
explanation: The October 2025 Gaza ceasefire was anchored on President Donald Trump's 20-point peace plan. The last 20 living Israeli hostages were released around October 13, 2025, along with ~2,000 Palestinian prisoners. As of May 2026, Phase 2 talks remain stalled over Hamas disarmament.

question_text: The last body of the 28 deceased Israeli hostages, Ran Gvili, was recovered by the IDF on:
explanation: Ran Gvili's body, the last of the 28 deceased Israeli hostages held in Gaza, was recovered by the IDF on January 26, 2026. This completed the return of all hostages (living and deceased) under the October 2025 Trump plan.

question_text: Israeli forces demolished the UNRWA headquarters compound on January 20, 2026 in which neighbourhood of East Jerusalem?
explanation: On January 20, 2026, Israeli forces — accompanied by far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir — demolished the UNRWA headquarters in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of occupied East Jerusalem. The compound was set on fire and looted. UN Secretary-General Guterres condemned it. Israel cited a 2024 Knesset law banning UNRWA.

question_text: Who is the current UNRWA Commissioner-General who called the January 2026 demolition 'an unprecedented attack against a UN agency'?
explanation: Philippe Lazzarini, UNRWA Commissioner-General, condemned the January 20, 2026 demolition of the Sheikh Jarrah headquarters as 'an unprecedented attack against a United Nations agency and its premises' and called it a 'wake-up call' for the world.

question_text: Bashar al-Assad's regime in Syria was overthrown on December 8, 2024 by rebel forces led by:
explanation: Bashar al-Assad's regime fell on December 8, 2024 after a rapid 11-day offensive led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), under Abu Mohammed al-Jolani (later known by his real name Ahmed al-Sharaa). Assad fled to Moscow. The fall ended 53 years of Assad-family rule.

question_text: Syria's new President since December 2024 (formerly known as Abu Mohammed al-Jolani) is:
explanation: Ahmed al-Sharaa (the real name of Abu Mohammed al-Jolani) became Syria's transitional President in December 2024 after HTS overthrew Assad. He met Trump in Riyadh on May 14, 2025 — a meeting that capped a stunning year for the 43-year-old former al-Qaeda commander. US sanctions on Syria were lifted by Trump's executive order in 2025.

question_text: On May 14, 2025, US President Trump met Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa in which city?
explanation: Trump met al-Sharaa in Riyadh on May 14, 2025, hosted by Saudi Crown Prince MBS. Trump subsequently issued an executive order revoking the US Syria sanctions programme. The UN Security Council also lifted terror-related sanctions on al-Sharaa.

question_text: The US-Jordan joint airstrikes on ISIS targets in Syria on January 10, 2026 (90+ precision munitions on 35+ targets) were codenamed:
explanation: Operation Hawkeye Strike was ordered by President Trump on December 19, 2025 in response to an ISIS ambush near Palmyra on December 13, 2025 that killed 2 US soldiers and a US civilian interpreter. The strikes on January 10, 2026 involved F-15Es, A-10s, AC-130Js, MQ-9s, and Jordanian F-16s.

question_text: On March 30, 2026, the Knesset passed a controversial law (62-48 vote) prescribing what punishment for West Bank residents convicted of deadly terror acts?
explanation: The Knesset passed the 'Death Penalty for Terrorists Law' 62-48 on March 30, 2026. It mandates death by hanging as the default punishment for West Bank residents convicted of deadly terror by military courts (with execution within 90 days). In practice it applies only to Palestinians, not Israeli Jews. Strongly pushed by Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit. ACRI and Adalah filed petitions same day calling it racially discriminatory.

question_text: On December 30, 2025, Saudi Arabia's Royal Saudi Air Force struck a Yemeni port over an alleged UAE weapons shipment to the STC separatists. The port was:
explanation: Saudi Arabia struck Mukalla port in Hadramout province on December 30, 2025, targeting an alleged UAE weapons shipment from Fujairah to the Southern Transitional Council (STC) separatists. The Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council demanded UAE forces leave Yemen within 24 hours; the UAE announced voluntary withdrawal of its remaining forces — an unprecedented rift between the two Gulf powers.

question_text: The Southern Transitional Council (STC), targeted by Saudi strikes on Mukalla in December 2025, was historically backed by which country?
explanation: The Southern Transitional Council (STC) is a Yemeni separatist movement backed primarily by the UAE. The December 30, 2025 Mukalla strike marked an unprecedented public clash between Saudi Arabia and UAE — historical partners in the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis.

question_text: India's January 2026 operation to evacuate ~10,000 Indian citizens (mostly students) from Iran amid protests and instability was named:
explanation: Operation Swades was launched by India in mid-January 2026 to bring back its citizens from Iran. About 10,000 Indians were in Iran (2,500-3,000 medical students plus businesspeople and professionals). It was triggered by the largest Iranian protests since 1979 and the security crackdown.

question_text: Following the February 28, 2026 outbreak of the Iran war, India launched a second evacuation operation from Iran (and later Israel). This operation was called:
explanation: Operation Sindhu was India's evacuation of nationals from Iran (and later Israel) due to the deteriorating situation from the 2026 Iran war. By June 24, 2026, 1,100 Indians from Iran and Israel had arrived in India; 3,170 students were ultimately evacuated under the operation.

question_text: The Islamabad Talks of April 11-12, 2026 were led on the US side by Vice President JD Vance, alongside special envoys Steve Witkoff and:
explanation: The 300-member US delegation at the Islamabad Talks (April 11-12, 2026) was led by Vice President JD Vance, alongside special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The 70-member Iranian team was led by parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf with FM Abbas Araghchi.

question_text: After the death of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in Operation Epic Fury (Feb 28, 2026), Iran's interim leadership was announced by:
option_b: Ali Larijani (Secretary of Supreme National Security Council)
explanation: Ali Larijani, Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, announced a temporary leadership council after Khamenei's death on Feb 28, 2026. (Note: in some accounts Larijani was himself targeted by Israeli strikes during the war.) Larijani ruled out immediate talks, dramatically reshaping Iran's wartime succession.

question_text: Operation Epic Fury, the US codename for the 2026 Iran war, officially concluded on which date?
explanation: Operation Epic Fury — the US codename for joint US-Israel military operations against Iran that began February 28, 2026 — officially concluded on May 5, 2026, following the failed Islamabad Talks (April 11-12) and subsequent diplomatic stabilisation efforts. Separately, the porous Israel-Lebanon ceasefire from April 16 was extended 45 days on May 15, 2026.

question_text: Which consumer protection law in India defines unfair trade practices?
explanation: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 defines unfair trade practices under Section 2(47) as practices that take undue advantage of consumers, include misleading advertisements, and violate consumer rights.
